A link from a CMS stays a `string` too, checked with `isHref` or `Href.parse` where it is rendered, so that one bad entry does not take the page down.
- Build the URL as `route()` builds one: root-relative, in the file's spelling, with each value encoded (`new Href($"/blog/{Uri.EscapeDataString(slug)}")`), and without the base path, which the router adds as it does for every link. The props parse compares the literal segments with their case, so `new Href("/About")` fails it for `app/about/page.tsx`, although the server redirects `/About` to `/about` ([One URL per page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#one-url-per-page)). `LinkGenerator`'s overloads that take an `HttpContext` add the request's base path, so pass them `pathBase: PathString.Empty`.
- No query value or route value binds to an `Href`, also through `[AsParameters]`. A URL from the request, such as a `returnUrl`, stays a `string`, checked with `Page.IsLocalUrl` ([What a loader returns](#what-a-loader-returns)). An action input reads an `Href` from JSON, as a server action called with an object sends it, checked for its shape only. Form binding fills one only from a field named after the constructor's parameter (`next.url` for a property `Next`), also checked for its shape only, and never from the field `next` that a form posts: that leaves an `init` property `null` and fails a positional record's post with 400. So a `[FromForm]` input takes a `string` and makes the `Href` with `Href.TryCreate`.

## JSON endpoints

An API is a minimal API endpoint next to the pages. Return `TypedResults` (or declare `Results<...>`) and the endpoint gets request and response schemas in the generated `api` map, keyed by method and route template as written:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/api/projects/{slug}/stats", async Task<Results<Ok<ProjectStats>, NotFound, ForbidHttpResult>> (
        string slug, ClaimsPrincipal user, TaskBoardDb db, CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
    await db.AccessAsync(slug, user.UserId(), cancellationToken) switch
    {
        null => TypedResults.NotFound(),
        { IsMember: false } => TypedResults.Forbid(),
        var access => TypedResults.Ok(await StatsAsync(db, access.ProjectId, cancellationToken)),
    })
    .RequireAuthorization();
```

```ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useHref } from 'netjes';
import { api, endpointUrl } from '../generated/netjes.ts';

async function fetchStats(url: string) {
  const response = await fetch(url);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Stats request failed with ${response.status}`);
  return api['GET /api/projects/{slug}/stats'].response.parse(await response.json());
}

export function useProjectStats(slug: string) {
  const url = useHref(endpointUrl('GET /api/projects/{slug}/stats', { slug }));
  return useQuery({ queryKey: ['projects', slug, 'stats'], queryFn: () => fetchStats(url) });
}
```

`endpointUrl` fills the route with the encoded `slug`, and `useHref` puts the URL under the base path, which a hand-written `` fetch(`/api/projects/${slug}/stats`) `` misses when the app has one ([Endpoint URLs](#endpoint-urls)).

A route group's `"/"` keeps its slash in the key: `app.MapGroup("/api/posts/{slug}/likes").MapGet("/", ...)` is `api['GET /api/posts/{slug}/likes/']`. A JSON endpoint that browsers post to should require a JSON body, so a cross-site form post cannot reach it.

`MapGet` answers `GET` only. A `HEAD` to its URL goes to whatever else matches the URL, often the not-found page. To answer `HEAD` as well, map the endpoint with `MapMethods(pattern, [HttpMethods.Get, HttpMethods.Head], handler)`; its key stays `GET` and the route, as for `MapGet` ([HEAD requests](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#head-requests)).

## Endpoint URLs

`endpointUrl(key, params, search)` from the generated file builds the URL of one of the app's endpoints, with its values encoded. The key is written as in `api`: the method, then the route as the app wrote it. Every endpoint the app maps that is not a page or an action has keys, JSON or not: a JSON endpoint one for each of its methods except `HEAD`, and any other endpoint, such as a file, a feed, text or a redirect, one for `GET`, if it answers `GET`. A `POST` endpoint that is not JSON, such as a webhook, has none.

```tsx
import { useHref } from 'netjes';
import { endpointUrl } from '../generated/netjes.ts';

endpointUrl('GET /api/posts/{slug}/likes/', { slug: 'hello' });                // '/api/posts/hello/likes'
endpointUrl('GET /api/search', { q: 'net core', take: 10 }, { ref: 'nav' });    // '/api/search?q=net+core&take=10&ref=nav'
<a href={useHref(endpointUrl('GET /llms.txt'))}>llms.txt</a>
```

- `EndpointParams[key]` types the second argument from the endpoint's C# side. It holds each parameter of the route template, typed from the handler parameter that binds it (a `string` when none does), and then each query string value the handler binds, named as binding reads it: `[FromQuery(Name = "v")] int version` is `v`, and a member of an `[AsParameters]` type keeps its C# name, such as `Page`, which binding reads in any case. A name the endpoint does not bind is a type error. Parameters that read nothing from the URL are left out: headers, the body, services, `HttpContext`, `CancellationToken`, `ClaimsPrincipal`, and a type with `BindAsync`, which reads the request itself.
- The third argument is open. Its values go in the query string after the typed ones, for keys the endpoint does not bind, such as `utm_source`, or that a `BindAsync` type reads. It is a `SearchParamsInput`, as for `route()`.
- The types are what binding accepts. A number is a `number`, a `bool` a `boolean`, and a string or another type with `TryParse` (`Guid`, `DateOnly`) a `string`. An array is a `readonly` list and `StringValues` a `string` or a list. An enum takes its C# names and its values, `'Open' | 'InProgress' | 0 | 1`: the query string binds those, whatever names the JSON writes with `JsonStringEnumConverter`. A `[Flags]` enum takes any `string` or `number`.
- A route value is required unless routing fills in a default (`{page=1}`), or the template makes it optional (`{id?}`, a catch-all such as `{**path}`) and the handler parameter that binds it can be left out. So `{id?}` bound by `int id` is required, since binding answers 400 without a value, and `{id?}` bound by `int? id` is not. `{slug}` is required even when the handler takes a `string? slug`, since the template needs it. An optional value that is a whole segment is required too when a segment that has to be there follows it: `/a/{x?}/b` does not match `/a/b`, so `x` is required. A query value can be left out when its parameter has a default or a nullable type, and a list always.
- `null` and `undefined` leave a value out, and `''` leaves out a route value, while a query value of `''` is written empty (`?q=`), as in `route()`. An optional route value left out drops its segment, or its part of a segment with the `.` before it (`{name}.{ext?}`), and a query value left out its key. A route value with a default is filled in with the default, unless it is a whole segment at the end of the URL, which is left out. A required route value throws `netjes: endpoint '<key>' needs the route value '<name>'` instead, and so does an optional one left out before a value that is given: for `/a/{x?}/{y?}`, `y` alone would be read as `x`.
- Route values are encoded with `encodeURIComponent`, except that a `{**path}` value keeps its slashes; a `{*path}` value has them encoded. The query string is written by `URLSearchParams`, which writes a space as `+`. The URL routes to the same endpoint as the one `LinkGenerator` writes, but it is not always the same text: a value equal to its default is kept, for example.
- The URL is root-relative and has no base path. Pass it through `useHref` for a `fetch` or an `<a href>`, as above, so that it works under `UsePathBase` ([Base path](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#base-path)). `<Link>` refuses it as a type error: an endpoint is not a page, and a client navigation to it asks the server for a page first ([Endpoints next to pages](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#endpoints-next-to-pages)).
- Netjes's own endpoints have no keys: `/_netjes/image`, `/_netjes/antiforgery` and the vitals beacon, which `MapPages()` maps, and the locale redirect (`MapLocaleRedirect`). Nor do server actions and page actions, which `serverActions` and `<Form>` call, endpoints that name no HTTP method (`app.Map`, `MapHealthChecks`, `MapFallback`), static assets (`MapStaticAssets`) or MVC conventional routes, whose actions share one route. `MapSitemap` and `MapRobotsTxt` have keys (`GET /sitemap.xml`, `GET /robots.txt`), and so does an endpoint marked `ExcludeFromDescription`, which leaves it out of OpenAPI only. An MVC attribute route has a key, with its route values as strings and no query values: MVC reports no binding for an action's parameters.
- The keys and types follow the C# side when the file is generated: run `npx netjes generate` after changing an endpoint, and a renamed route or parameter is a type error where the old one is used. The templates are in the generated file. Once any component calls `endpointUrl`, all of them reach the browser in the chunk that holds the file, which pages share, also those that never call it ([Security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#errors-and-configuration)).

## Server state with TanStack Query

Netjes provides a TanStack Query `QueryClient`: one per render on the server, and one per page load in the browser, which lasts across client navigations. There is no provider to set up. A loader seeds it with `.WithQuery(key, data)`, and a component that calls `useQuery` with the same key renders that data on the server and on the first client render, without waiting for a fetch:

```csharp
app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, PostStore store) =>
    store.Find(slug) is { } post
        ? Page.Props(new PostProps(ToDetail(post)))
            .WithQuery(["likes", slug], new LikesResponse(slug, store.LikesOf(slug)))
        : Page.NotFound());
```

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

const likes = useQuery({ queryKey: ['likes', slug], queryFn: () => fetchLikes(slug) });
// likes.data is there on the first render
```

Keep each query key in one place on each side (a function in C#, a key factory in TypeScript), so the seed and the query match. Layout loaders can seed queries too.

- Seeded data is fresh for the client's `staleTime`, one minute by default, and is fetched again once stale. Data the browser fetched more recently is kept: an older payload, such as an output-cached page or a page shown again on back, does not replace it. Netjes moves the server's timestamps onto the browser's clock first, so a clock that is off does not make data look older or newer than it is.
- `staleTime` and `Cache-Control` belong to two different caches, and neither reads the other. `staleTime` is how long the page's TanStack Query cache counts a query's data as fresh. While data is fresh, a mount or a window focus does not call the `queryFn`, whatever `Cache-Control` the earlier answer came with, so an endpoint that answers `no-cache` is not asked again until the query is stale.
- A refetch of a stale query, or of one that `.Invalidate(key)` names, does call the `queryFn`, and a `fetch` in it goes through the browser's HTTP cache: it is answered from there when the earlier answer is still fresh by its `Cache-Control` (`max-age`), and sent to the server otherwise. A `staleTime` of 0 leaves a query to the HTTP cache: the query is stale at once, so every mount and window focus refetches it, and the endpoint's `Cache-Control` decides how often that reaches the network. A seeded query is then fetched again as it mounts. The headers of an endpoint that is not a page are in [Caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md#endpoints-that-are-not-pages).
- After a server action, `.Invalidate(key)` refetches the queries under a key and `.WithQuery(key, data)` sets one, without a refetch ([Actions and forms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md#revalidation)).
- An action or form post that signs someone in or out clears the client, seeded queries included, in every tab of the app ([Signing in and out](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md#signing-in-and-out)).
- A query whose fetch fails is tried three more times, after 1, 2 and 4 seconds, before it shows the error, and a failed mutation is not tried again: TanStack Query's defaults. `netjes({ query: { defaultOptions: { queries: { retry: 1, retryDelay: 500 } } } })` sets other numbers for the whole app; there they can only be plain values, since they are written into the bundle ([Vite plugin](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/vite-plugin.md#options)). A function, such as a `retry` that looks at the error, goes on the query itself: `useQuery({ retry })`. Component tests try a failed query as often as the app does, without the waits ([Testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md#queries-that-fail)).
- Configure the client in `vite.config.ts` with `netjes({ query: { defaultOptions } })`, or remove it with `netjes({ query: false })` ([Vite plugin](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/vite-plugin.md)).

## Slow data: `Page.Defer`

A value that is slow and not essential, such as comments or an activity feed, can follow the page instead of holding it up. Make the prop a `Deferred<T>` and fill it with `Page.Defer(...)`:

```csharp
public sealed record TaskPageProps(TaskDetail Task, Deferred<IReadOnlyList<ActivityItem>> Activity);

// A task of its own: give it its own DbContext, never the request's.
Page.Props(new TaskPageProps(task, Page.Defer(ActivityAsync(contexts, projectId, number, http.RequestAborted))));

// Or let Netjes run the work in a DI scope of its own, started once the page's payload is written:
// a scoped DbContext from that scope is not shared with the request's loaders.
Page.Props(new TaskPageProps(task, Page.Defer(services =>
    LoadActivityAsync(services.GetRequiredService<TaskBoardDb>(), projectId, number, http.RequestAborted))));
```

The generated schema types the prop with `deferred(...)` from `netjes/zod`, as a promise whose value is validated when it arrives. Read it with React's `use()` inside a Suspense boundary, or let the folder's `loading.tsx` be the fallback:

```tsx
function ActivityFeed({ activity }: { activity: PromiseLike<ActivityItem[]> }) {
  const items = use(activity);
  return <ol>{items.map((item) => <li key={item.id}>{item.summary}</li>)}</ol>;
}

<Suspense fallback={<p>Loading activity…</p>}>
  <ActivityFeed activity={activity} />
</Suspense>
```

The page goes out first and each value streams in when its task completes, on documents and client navigations alike. [Rendering and streaming](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md) covers what crawlers, the static export and browsers without JavaScript get, timeouts and errors.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md -->

# Actions and forms

This guide is for app developers. It covers how a page changes data: server actions, which are C# endpoints that React calls through typed references, and page actions, which take a form post at the page's own URL. Both work without JavaScript. The guide also covers validation, what a failed post hands back, the checks every post goes through, revalidation, what signing in or out does to the client, and uploads and downloads. Server actions are C# endpoints rather than `'use server'` functions ([ADR 0011](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0011-server-actions-as-csharp-endpoints.md)).

## A server action

Map a server action with `MapAction`, a name and a minimal API delegate. It answers `POST /_netjes/actions/{name}`:

```csharp
// Features/Home/HomePage.cs
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc; // FromFormAttribute

public sealed record GreetInput
{
    public string? Name { get; init; }
}

public sealed record Greeting(string Text);

app.MapAction("home.greet", ([FromForm] GreetInput input) =>
    string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(input.Name)
        ? ServerAction.Invalid("name", "Tell us your name.")
        : ServerAction.Ok(new Greeting($"Hello, {input.Name.Trim()}!")));
```

`[FromForm]` is in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc`, which a project's implicit usings do not include, so the file that uses it (or `[FromQuery]`, `[FromRoute]`, `[FromHeader]`, `[FromServices]`) needs `using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;`. `[AsParameters]` is in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http`, which implicit usings cover. The samples below leave it out.

```tsx
// components/HelloForm.tsx
import { Form, useAction } from 'netjes';
import { serverActions } from '../generated/netjes.ts';

export function HelloForm() {
  const [state, formAction, pending] = useAction(serverActions['home.greet']);
  const error = state?.ok === false ? state.errors['name']?.[0] : undefined;
  return (
    <Form action={formAction}>
      <input name="name" defaultValue={state?.ok === false ? String(state.values?.['name'] ?? '') : ''} aria-invalid={error ? true : undefined} />
      {error && <p>{error}</p>}
      <button type="submit" disabled={pending}>{pending ? 'Saying hello…' : 'Say hello'}</button>
      {state?.ok && <p role="status">{state.result.text}</p>}
    </Form>
  );
}
```

That is the form `netjes new` writes. With JavaScript it calls the action with `fetch` and shows the result in place. Without JavaScript the browser posts the form, and the page comes back with the error or the result ([Forms without JavaScript](#forms-without-javascript)).

- Names are letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_`, and must be unique; `feature.verb` reads well. `MapAction` throws at startup otherwise.
- The delegate binds like any minimal API handler. A `[FromForm]` parameter binds form fields, which a `<Form>` posts and which also work without JavaScript. A parameter without it binds a JSON body, for calls from code. Services, `ClaimsPrincipal`, `HttpContext` and `CancellationToken` bind as usual. A delegate minimal APIs cannot bind, such as one with two inferred bodies or with `[FromForm]` fields next to a JSON body, stops the app at startup with an `InvalidOperationException` that names the action and gives minimal APIs' reason.
- `MapAction` returns a `RouteHandlerBuilder`: `.RequireAuthorization()`, `.RequireRateLimiting(...)` and filters work as on any endpoint. Check what the user may do inside the action as well, as for any endpoint that changes data.
- Under `npm run dev`, `dotnet watch` applies a change inside an action to the running app, but maps a new `MapAction` only after a restart (Ctrl+R): until then a post to it answers 405, and `generated/netjes.ts` gains its reference on that start or with `npx netjes generate`.

### Results

| Result | What the client gets |
|---|---|
| `ServerAction.Ok(result)` | Success with a result: `{ ok: true, result }`. Returns `ServerActionResult<T>`, which types the result in the generated reference. |
| `ServerAction.Ok()` | Success without a result. |
| `ServerAction.Invalid(field, message)`, `ServerAction.Invalid(errors)` | Status 422 with the errors per field: `{ ok: false, status: 422, errors }`. |
| `ServerAction.Redirect(url)` | Success, then the client navigates to `url` (relative or http(s), checked as `Page.Redirect` checks it). |
| `ServerAction.Forbidden()`, `ServerAction.NotFound()` | 403 or 404. A call from React throws `ServerActionError`, with the reason phrase (`Forbidden`, `Not Found`) as its message, to the nearest error boundary; a post without JavaScript gets the error page. |

Field names in `errors` are written with the app's JSON naming policy, so `Title` comes back as `title`, matching the field and the zod schema. Chain these on any result:

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `.Revalidate(tags)` | Evict output-cached pages with these tags, then refresh the client's page. |
| `.RevalidatePath(paths)` | Evict the output-cached pages at these paths, then refresh the client's page. |
| `.Refresh()` | Refresh the client's page: every loader runs again. |
| `.Invalidate(queryKeys)` | Invalidate these TanStack Query keys, and those they prefix, so they are fetched again. |
| `.WithQuery(key, data)` | Set a TanStack Query entry on the client, without a fetch. |

```csharp
return ServerAction.Ok(new CreatedTask(number))
    .RevalidatePath($"/projects/{access.Slug}")
    .Invalidate(ProjectLayout.StatsKey(access.Slug));
```

## Calling an action from React

The generated `serverActions` map holds a typed reference to every `MapAction`. Its input is what the action reads: `FormData` for a `[FromForm]` action, the JSON input type otherwise (nullable and defaulted properties optional, computed ones left out), and `void` for an action that binds only services. Its result is the type given to `ServerAction.Ok(result)`, or `void` for an action that returns the untyped `ServerActionResult`.

```ts
export const serverActions = {
  "auth.logout": serverAction<void, void>("auth.logout"),
  "posts.like": serverAction<z.input<typeof LikeInput>, LikesResponse>("posts.like", { result: LikesResponse }),
  "tasks.create": serverAction<FormData, CreatedTask>("tasks.create", { result: CreatedTask }),
} as const;
```

Call a reference with an object, sent as JSON, or with `FormData`, sent as a form post. It resolves to an `ActionState`: `{ ok: true, result }`, or `{ ok: false, status, errors, values }` after a 422. Any other failure (403, 404, 413, 500, a refused token) throws a `ServerActionError` with the `status`. Its `withheld` is true when the server sent no message, as for an exception in the action while error details are off: the message is then Netjes's own, `Server action <name> failed with status 500`, which an error page that renders the message only when `!error.withheld` leaves out ([`ServerActionError`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/react-api.md#serveractionerror)). The Blog's like button calls its action from a click, with an optimistic count:

```tsx
const likePost = serverActions['posts.like'];

const [pending, startTransition] = useTransition();
const [count, addLike] = useOptimistic(likes.data?.likes, (current) => (current ?? 0) + 1);

<button type="button" onClick={() => startTransition(async () => {
  addLike(undefined);
  await likePost({ slug });
})}>
  {count} likes
</button>
```

`serverAction<TInput, TResult>(name, { result })` from `netjes` writes such a reference by hand, with a schema to parse the result. An action that answers `ServerAction.Redirect(...)` resolves with no result even when its type promises one, and by then the router has moved on.

### Calls as the page starts

In the browser a call goes through the client router, which adds the antiforgery token and the URL to return to, and acts on the answer. The router registers itself in an effect, which React runs after the page's own effects, and a call can come sooner: a form submitted while the page hydrates, or a call from a component's `useEffect` or `useLayoutEffect` as it mounts. Such a call waits for the router, for up to 10 seconds, and then goes out as usual. Links, `router.push`, `router.refresh()` and page action forms reach the router directly and need no wait.

A call with no router on its way fails at once with an error saying that the action "was called before the page was ready": on the server, where no router registers, and in a component test without `createTestApp`'s `Wrapper` ([Testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md#answering-server-actions)). If the router does not register within the 10 seconds, because React threw its render away, the call fails with the same error.

### `useAction` and `<Form>`

[`useAction(action, options)`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/react-api.md#useaction) wraps React's `useActionState`: it returns `[state, formAction, isPending]`. Pass `formAction` to `<Form action>`:

- React runs the action, so `useFormStatus()` works in the form's buttons.
- On the server the form renders as a real post to the action, with the antiforgery token and the page's URL to return to, so the same form works without JavaScript.
- After a failed post without JavaScript, `state` starts as that failure.
- `options.initialState` sets the state before the first submission (default `null`).
- `options.onSubmit(formData)` runs inside the action's transition, before the call: the place for `useOptimistic` updates, which React keeps until the action and the refresh after it have finished.

```tsx
const [shown, addPending] = useOptimistic<ShownProject[], ShownProject>(projects, (current, next) => [...current, next]);
const [state, formAction] = useAction(serverActions['projects.create'], {
  onSubmit: (data) => addPending({ slug: String(data.get('slug') ?? ''), name: String(data.get('name') ?? ''), pending: true }),
});
```

React resets a form after its action runs. To keep what the user typed after a failure, give each field `defaultValue={state.values.name}`: a failed state carries the submitted values of the fields the action declares, with or without JavaScript ([What a failed post hands back](#what-a-failed-post-hands-back)).

## Validation

`MapAction` and `MapPageAction` check the DataAnnotations of their inputs before the action runs. A server action answers with their errors as `ServerAction.Invalid`, also without JavaScript; a page action renders its page again with them ([Validation in page actions](#validation-in-page-actions)). No setup is needed:

```csharp
public sealed record CreateTaskInput
{
    [Required] public string ProjectSlug { get; init; } = "";

    [Required(ErrorMessage = "Give the task a title."), StringLength(200)]
    public string Title { get; init; } = "";

    public string? Priority { get; init; }
}

app.MapAction("tasks.create", async ([FromForm] CreateTaskInput input, ...) => ...);
```

- Attributes count on properties and on a record's constructor parameters (`record SignUpInput([Required, EmailAddress] string Email, ...)`).
- An input that implements `IValidatableObject` is validated once its attributes pass. Its errors without a member name are keyed `""`.
- A JSON input whose type lists derived types with `[JsonDerivedType]` is checked by the attributes of the type the call sends, also when the declared type is abstract or has none.
- When there are errors, the action does not run.
- A `[FromForm]` input is never `null`. For a post that carries none of its fields, such as a form whose only fields are unchecked checkboxes, form binding builds no object, so the action gets an empty input, as if each field were missing. It is checked like any other: its `[Required]` members come back as field errors, and an input that passes reaches the action. Declare the parameter nullable (`[FromForm] NoteInput? input`) to get `null` instead ([ADR 0017](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0017-a-form-input-without-fields-is-empty-not-null.md)).
- `builder.Services.AddValidation()` is not needed for this. It is for the app's other minimal API endpoints, which keep their 400 problem details.
- Rules that need data, such as a name that is taken, go in the action: `return ServerAction.Invalid("email", "There is already an account with this email.")`.
- `MapAction` and `MapPageAction` read the attributes as they map the action. One that cannot be read, such as a `[Display]` whose resource type has no property of that name, or a validation attribute whose constructor throws, stops the app at startup, naming the action, the parameter and the property. So does one on a derived type that a JSON input lists with `[JsonDerivedType]`.

Give a form input `init` properties, as above, rather than constructor parameters. ASP.NET Core's form binding builds a positional record only from a post that has every one of its constructor's fields, and refuses any other post with 400 before the action runs: the user gets the error page, or a `ServerActionError` from the call with JavaScript. A browser leaves an unchecked checkbox out of the post, and a list with nothing checked or chosen, so a positional record with a `bool` or a list refuses a valid post. With `init` properties a missing field keeps its default (`false` for a checkbox), and `[Required]` names the fields that must be there. A positional record is fine for text fields only, which a browser posts even when they are empty; bind a checkbox next to it as a parameter of its own: `([FromForm] SignInInput input, [FromForm] string? returnUrl, [FromForm] bool? stay, ...)`. Netjes warns at startup about a positional form input whose constructor takes a `bool` or a list ([Route warnings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#a-form-input-that-refuses-a-post-without-a-checkbox)).

Form binding builds a form input only through its one public constructor. From a type with several public constructors or none, or from an abstract class or an interface, it builds nothing, whatever the post holds, so the action would get an empty input or `null`. `MapAction` and `MapPageAction` stop the app at startup for such a type, naming the action and the type: give it one public constructor, a parameterless one with `init` properties or a positional record's, or use a concrete type in its place. The same goes for the types of the properties form binding fills (those with a public getter and setter, not marked `[IgnoreDataMember]`) and the items of its lists. A type it reads from one field, one with a `TryParse` method or one that implements `IParsable<T>`, such as a strongly-typed id, may have any constructors.

A checkbox group, several fields with one name, binds to a `string[]` property of the input type, for repeated fields (`Tags=a&Tags=b`) and indexed ones (`Tags[0]=a`) alike, and stays empty when nothing is checked:

```csharp
public sealed record TagInput { public string[] Tags { get; init; } = []; }

app.MapAction("posts.tag", ([FromForm] TagInput input) => ...);
```

A top-level `[FromForm] string[] tags` parameter does not work: ASP.NET Core's minimal APIs refuse it ("TryParse method found on string with incorrect format"), so Netjes stops the app at startup, naming the action and that reason. Bind the list as a property of an input type, as above.

Other top-level lists bind in ways a form rarely fits:

- An array of numbers, dates or other values with a `TryParse` method (`[FromForm] int[] ids`) binds from repeated fields of its name (`ids=1&ids=2`), and is empty when none is posted.
- A list or dictionary of any other kind (`[FromForm] List<string> tags`, `[FromForm] List<LineInput> lines`, `[FromForm] Dictionary<string, string> notes`) binds from fields named by index or key alone, without the parameter's name (`[0]=a`, `[0].product=…`, `[gift]=…`), whatever `[FromForm(Name = ...)]` says. A checkbox group named `tags` never reaches it, and it is `null` when no such field is posted. Netjes leaves that `null`, unlike an input object without any of its fields ([ADR 0017](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0017-a-form-input-without-fields-is-empty-not-null.md)): an empty list would also stand for checked boxes posted under the parameter's name, which form binding drops.

Both work as properties of an input type, where fields carry the property's name and a list keeps its default (`= []`) when nothing is posted.

## Forms without JavaScript

Every `<Form action={formAction}>` is also a plain HTML form. Without JavaScript, or before the page's JavaScript has run, the browser posts it to `/_netjes/actions/{name}` with the antiforgery token and a hidden `__netjes_return` field holding the page's URL:

- **Success:** a 303 back to the page, or to the action's `ServerAction.Redirect` target.
- **`Invalid`:** the page is rendered again in the same request, status 422, with the errors and the declared fields' values, and `useAction` starts with that state. The response goes out `Cache-Control: no-store`, since it holds what was typed.
- **`Forbidden`, `NotFound` and errors:** the error page with that status.

The page rendered for a failure runs the pipeline again from `UseNetjes`'s routing, as a GET of the return URL. Middleware registered before `app.UseNetjes()` does not run for it, so guard pages with endpoint authorization, not with a middleware in front. The return URL must be a page of the app: one that routes anywhere else, such as a static file or an API, renders the home page instead, or the error page with 422 where `/` is no page either.

After an `Invalid` result, the address bar of a browser without JavaScript shows the action's URL (`/_netjes/actions/home.greet`) while the page is the one the form is on. Reloading asks to post the form again, and opening that URL with a GET is a 404, since an action answers only `POST`. This is how a plain form post behaves, and it only matters when users reload or share the address after a failure. If it does matter, use a page action: it posts to the page's own URL, so the address bar keeps showing the page ([page actions](#page-actions)).

Test forms with JavaScript turned off. Playwright's `test.use({ javaScriptEnabled: false })` does that ([Testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md)).

## What a failed post hands back

A failure hands back what was typed only for the fields the action declares:

- its `[FromForm]` parameters, by name;
- the fields form binding reads into a `[FromForm]` type, by their C# or JSON names, nested and indexed ones included (`address.street`, `tags[0]`, `lines[0].product`, `notes[gift]`);
- the `[FromForm]` members of an `[AsParameters]` type.

It never hands back files, the antiforgery token, Netjes's own `__netjes_` fields, or a field whose name marks it as private. An action that reads the form itself (`IFormCollection`, `HttpRequest`) declares nothing, so it hands back nothing.

Without JavaScript the values are written into the page. A value over 16 KB comes back empty, and the values stop at 64 KB in all, field names included. With JavaScript the browser keeps the submitted values itself, and the server names the fields it may hand back, up to 64 KB of names.

`NetjesOptions.PrivateFormFields` lists the words that mark a field as private. The defaults are `password`, `passwd`, `pwd`, `pass`, `pw`, `passcode`, `passphrase`, `secret`, `token`, `apikey`, `privatekey`, `credential`, `pin`, `otp`, `totp`, `mfa`, `recovery`, `cvc`, `cvv`, `csc`, `cc`, `card`, `iban`, `ssn` and `bsn`. Names are compared ignoring case:

- A word of five letters or more matches anywhere in the name, with `_`, `-` and `.` ignored: `newPassword`, `password2`, `api_key`, `recoveryEmail`.
- So does a word written with those separators: `auth-code` also hides `authCode`.
- A shorter word matches as a word of the name, or at the start or end of one: `PINCode`, `card_number`, `cardnumber`, `newpwd`, and also `passengerName` and `compass`, but not `spinner`. `cc` and `csc` cover the browser's autocomplete names (`cc-number`, `cc-csc`).

Hiding a field by mistake only costs a retype. Set your own list in code to replace the defaults: `options.PrivateFormFields = ["password", "secret", "card"]`. Configuration (`Netjes:PrivateFormFields`) adds its words to the defaults instead ([Options](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/options.md#actions-and-forms)).

## Page actions

A page action takes a form post at the page's own URL, for a page whose form should post where the page is. Map it with `MapPageAction` and the page's pattern, next to the page's loader:

```csharp
public sealed record SignForm
{
    public string? Name { get; init; }
    public string? Message { get; init; }
}

public sealed record GuestbookProps(
    IReadOnlyList<GuestbookEntry> Entries,
    IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string>? Errors = null,
    SignForm? Values = null);

app.MapPageLoader("/guestbook", (GuestbookStore store) => Page.Props(new GuestbookProps(store.Recent())));

app.MapPageAction("/guestbook", ([FromForm] SignForm form, GuestbookStore store) =>
{
    var errors = Validate(form);
    if (errors.Count > 0)
    {
        return Page.Props(new GuestbookProps(store.Recent(), errors, form)).WithStatus(StatusCodes.Status422UnprocessableEntity);
    }

    store.Sign(form.Name!.Trim(), form.Message!.Trim());
    return Page.Redirect("/guestbook");
});
```

```tsx
// app/guestbook/page.tsx
export default definePage(pages['/guestbook'], function Guestbook({ entries, errors, values }) {
  const submitting = useNavigation().state === 'submitting';
  return (
    <Form method="post">
      <input name="name" defaultValue={values?.name ?? ''} aria-invalid={errors?.name ? true : undefined} />
      {errors?.name && <p>{errors.name}</p>}
      <textarea name="message" defaultValue={values?.message ?? ''} />
      <button type="submit" disabled={submitting}>Sign the guestbook</button>
    </Form>
  );
});
```

- A `<Form method="post">` without an `action` posts to the current URL. With JavaScript the client router posts it with `fetch` and treats the answer like a navigation: it follows a redirect, or shows the page the action rendered, in place of the current history entry when the URL stays the same.
- Return `Page.Redirect(...)` after a change (a 303 after a post), or `Page.Props(...)` to render the page again. The action supplies all the page's props itself: the page's loader does not run for it, though its layouts' loaders do.
- The DataAnnotations of its inputs are checked before the delegate runs, as for a server action; a failure renders the page again with the errors ([Validation in page actions](#validation-in-page-actions)). Checks the delegate makes itself, such as one that needs data, return the page's props with the errors and values, as above.
- A `[FromForm]` input is never `null` unless the parameter is declared nullable: a post with none of its fields gets an empty input, checked like any other, as for a server action.
- The delegate binds like a minimal API POST handler: route values, `[FromForm]` fields, services. One minimal APIs cannot bind, such as one with two inferred bodies, form fields next to a JSON body, or a `[FromRoute]` naming no route value, stops the app at startup, naming the page file and its URL. So does a form input that form binding could never build ([Validation](#validation)).
- The `[FromForm]` type is in the generated `forms` map: `forms['/guestbook']`.
- A page with a page action cannot be exported to static files.

### Validation in page actions

A page action's inputs are checked like a server action's, with or without `AddValidation()`: their DataAnnotations, then `IValidatableObject`. When a check fails, the delegate does not run. The page is rendered again in the same request from its loader, with status 422 and `Cache-Control: no-store`, and `usePageActionState()` returns the errors and the submitted values of the fields the action declares ([What a failed post hands back](#what-a-failed-post-hands-back)). With JavaScript the client router shows that page in place; without it the browser shows it, and the address bar keeps the page's URL.

```csharp
public sealed record SignForm
{
    [Required(ErrorMessage = "Tell us who you are."), StringLength(40)]
    public string? Name { get; init; }

    [Required(ErrorMessage = "Leave a message."), StringLength(280)]
    public string? Message { get; init; }
}

app.MapPageAction("/guestbook", ([FromForm] SignForm form, GuestbookStore store) =>
{
    store.Sign(form.Name!.Trim(), form.Message!.Trim());
    return Page.Redirect("/guestbook");
});
```

```tsx
// app/guestbook/page.tsx
export default definePage(pages['/guestbook'], function Guestbook({ entries }) {
  const failed = usePageActionState();
  return (
    <Form method="post">
      <input name="name" defaultValue={String(failed?.values.name ?? '')} aria-invalid={failed?.errors.name ? true : undefined} />
      {failed?.errors.name && <p>{failed.errors.name[0]}</p>}
      <textarea name="message" defaultValue={String(failed?.values.message ?? '')} />
      <button type="submit">Sign the guestbook</button>
    </Form>
  );
});
```

`failed` has the shape of `useAction`'s failure state, `{ ok: false, status: 422, errors, values }`: `errors` is keyed with the app's JSON naming policy, as for a server action, and `values` by the names the form posted. It is null on every other render, also after a server action's failure, which `useAction` reads. An error that only the delegate can find, such as a name that is taken, goes in the page's props, as in the first example.

## Antiforgery and the origin check

Every server action and page action requires a valid antiforgery token and a same-origin request. `AddNetjes()` registers antiforgery; put `app.UseAntiforgery()` in the pipeline after `UseNetjes()` and after authentication:

```csharp
app.UseNetjes();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.UseAntiforgery();
```

- **The token.** Each page's payload carries a token, and `<Form>` and the action references send it, in a hidden field or a header. A page action requires it even when it binds no form fields, such as a delete button. A call refused for its token gets 400 with `X-Netjes-Antiforgery: invalid`, and the client sends that call again once, with a fresh token; no other answer is retried, since the action may have run. Output-cached pages carry no token: the client fetches one from `/_netjes/antiforgery` before the first post, so forms on cached pages need JavaScript ([Caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md)).
- **The origin.** A post whose `Sec-Fetch-Site` is `cross-site`, or whose `Origin` is not the request's host, gets 403. `NetjesOptions.AllowedActionOrigins` adds origins, such as a public host a proxy rewrites; it helps only for same-site ones, since a cross-site post is always refused. Behind a proxy that rewrites `Host`, call `UseForwardedHeaders()` so the app sees its public host.
- **`.DisableAntiforgery()`** on a page action turns off both checks, for a payment or identity provider that posts a form back from its own site. On a server action it turns off the token check only; the origin check stays.

[Security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md) covers these checks in full, with the antiforgery cookie's settings.

## Body limits

A server action accepts a request body of up to 1 MB (`NetjesOptions.ActionBodySizeLimit`, like Next.js's `serverActions.bodySizeLimit`). A larger one gets 413, apart from a form post without JavaScript sent chunked, without a `Content-Length`: that one gets 400, because the antiforgery check fails to read its token from the body. Calls from the client send the token in a header, so they get 413 either way. The option only lowers the server's limit, never raises it, and `null` leaves the server's limit. Give one action its own limit, higher or lower, with `[RequestSizeLimit(bytes)]` or `[DisableRequestSizeLimit]` on its delegate or group, or `.WithMetadata(new RequestSizeLimitAttribute(bytes))`; like any such limit, it replaces the server's.

```csharp
app.MapAction("photos.upload", [RequestSizeLimit(20 * 1024 * 1024)] (IFormFile photo, PhotoStore photos) => ...);
```

Page actions keep the server's limit (30 MB with Kestrel).

## Revalidation

After an action, the client refreshes what changed:

- `.RevalidatePath("/projects/web")` and `.Revalidate("posts")` evict output-cached pages by path or by tag, then refresh the page on screen, so it shows the change. `IPageCache` does the same from anywhere else, such as a webhook ([Caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md)).
- `.Refresh()` refreshes the page on screen without evicting anything.
- `.Invalidate(["projects", slug, "stats"])` makes TanStack Query fetch those queries again; `.WithQuery(key, data)` sets one without a fetch.
- `ServerAction.Redirect(url)` navigates instead.

A refresh runs every loader of the page again, layouts included, in the same history entry, without scrolling. If the user moved to another page while the action ran, the router neither redirects nor refreshes. Every action and form post also drops the pages the router prefetched.

## Signing in and out

An action that signs someone in or out changes what every page shows. Script cannot read `Set-Cookie`, so when a call from the client router sets or deletes a cookie, the response carries `X-Netjes-Cookies: changed`, and the router acts on it as soon as it arrives ([ADR 0014](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0014-signing-in-or-out-clears-what-back-shows.md)):

- It forgets the pages it keeps for back and forward, and its prefetched pages, which showed whoever was signed in before. Back and forward load those pages from the server again.
- Navigations and prefetches on their way went out with the old cookies, so they start over.
- It loads the page on screen from the server once, as Next.js does: by the action's redirect or revalidation, or else by a refresh.
- The built-in `QueryClient` is cleared, seeded queries included; the action's own `.WithQuery` entries are applied after that. A memoized component whose props did not change keeps its last result until it renders or refetches.
- The app's other tabs in the same browser send the same cookies, so the tab that made the call tells them ([ADR 0021](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0021-signing-in-or-out-reaches-the-other-tabs.md)). Each forgets its pages, clears its `QueryClient` and loads the page on screen from the server again, so every tab shows the user the change signed in, or none.

A sign-out action needs nothing more than signing out:

```csharp
app.MapAction("auth.logout", async (HttpContext http) =>
{
    await http.SignOutAsync(CookieAuthenticationDefaults.AuthenticationScheme);
    return ServerAction.Redirect("/");
});
```

The header follows these rules:

- Cookies the action writes count, its own `OnStarting` callbacks included. The antiforgery cookie does not, and neither do cookies a middleware wrote before the action ran or as the response starts, such as cookie authentication's sliding renewal.
- Server actions and page actions are both marked, when the client router made the call. A post without JavaScript is not marked; the browser loads the next page in full anyway.
- A sign-in that changes no cookie, such as one kept in a server-side session, is not seen. Set or delete a cookie in the action to mark it.
- Only the tab that made the call sees the header, and it tells the app's other tabs (those under the same base path) on a `BroadcastChannel`, which every current browser has. In a browser without one, another tab keeps its router's memory and its query cache until it makes such a call itself.
- A proxy in front of the app must pass `X-Netjes-Cookies` and `X-Netjes-Antiforgery` through.

A form post is never sent twice: one still on its way when another call's header arrives shows what it answered, and the router keeps that page for no history entry, so it comes from the server when the user returns to it. Pages also go out with `Cache-Control: no-store, private` by default, so the browser's own cache does not show the previous user's pages on Back after a full page load ([Caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md)).

## `<Form>` in detail

| Prop | What it does |
|---|---|
| `method` | `'get'` (default) or `'post'`. A GET form navigates to its action with the fields as the query string. |
| `action` | Where to submit: a URL (default: the current one, where page actions listen), or a form action function such as `useAction`'s `formAction`. |
| `replace` | For a GET form: replace the history entry instead of adding one. |
| `reloadDocument` | Let the browser submit the form itself, with a full page load. |

The other props are those of a `<form>`, and a `ref` gets the `<form>` element. Without JavaScript every form is a native form; with it, `<Form>` submits with `fetch` and handles the answer:

- A page, or a redirect to one, is shown as a navigation.
- An HTML document that is not a Netjes page is shown as the browser would show it, and is never requested again as a GET.
- A response with `Content-Disposition: attachment` is saved as a download.
- Anything else, or no answer, leaves the page and what was typed as they are, and `useNavigation()` reports the failure with its status ([Navigation state](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#navigation-state)).

A submit button's `formaction`, `formmethod` and `formtarget` are honoured. A form or button whose target is not `_self`, and an action on another origin, are left to the browser. Under a base path, use `<SubmitButton formAction="/x">` instead of a plain button with `formAction`, so the base path is added with and without JavaScript.

POST forms carry the antiforgery token when the page has one. A form that posts to your own minimal API endpoint validates that token through ASP.NET Core's form binding, as any endpoint that binds a form does.

## Uploads and downloads

Bind uploaded files as `IFormFile` (or `IFormFileCollection`) in a page action or a server action, and give an action that takes large files its own size limit ([Body limits](#body-limits)). Files are never handed back after a failure.

For an upload that must also work without JavaScript, post the form to a page action with `encType="multipart/form-data"`. With JavaScript, `<Form>` sends it as multipart too:

```tsx
<Form method="post" encType="multipart/form-data">
  <input type="file" name="photo" accept="image/*" />
  <button type="submit">Upload</button>
</Form>
```

```csharp
app.MapPageAction("/photos", async (IFormFile photo, PhotoStore photos, CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
{
    await photos.SaveAsync(photo, cancellationToken);
    return Page.Redirect("/photos");
});
```

A server action called with `FormData` that holds a file sends it as multipart as well, so `useAction` uploads with JavaScript. Without JavaScript the browser sends files only from a form with `encType="multipart/form-data"`, and React warns about an `encType` on a form whose action is a function, which is why the page action is the way for uploads that must work either way.

A form post that answers with a file (`Content-Disposition: attachment`) is downloaded, but the client router reads the whole file into memory first. For a large file, give the form `reloadDocument`, so the browser streams it to disk, or link to a GET endpoint with a plain `<a download href={useHref(endpointUrl('GET /export.csv'))}>`, which the browser downloads itself ([Endpoint URLs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md#endpoint-urls)).

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md -->

# Rendering and streaming

This guide is for app developers who want to know how a Netjes page becomes HTML: the Node processes that render React, streamed documents and `loading.tsx`, slow data with `Page.Defer`, what crawlers get, what happens when no Node process is ready, components that load late or only in the browser, and the error pages. Routing and loaders have guides of their own: [routing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md) and [data loading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md).

## How a page is rendered

A request for a page goes through ASP.NET Core first. The endpoint for the page file runs its C# loaders (the layouts' and the page's), and Netjes builds the page payload: which page and layouts to show, their props, the route parameters, the shared props and the seeded queries. The next step depends on who asked:

- A document request (a browser loading the URL) sends the payload to a Node process, the sidecar, which renders the whole HTML document with React and streams it back. The payload is embedded in the document, and the browser hydrates it. Once the client router runs there, `<html>` carries `data-netjes-hydrated`, which end-to-end tests wait for ([testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md#wait-for-hydration)).
- A client navigation (`<Link>`, `router.push`, a `<Form>` post) asks the same URL for the payload as JSON. No Node process is involved: the browser loads the page module and renders it itself.

Only document requests need the sidecar. Redirects, not-found and forbidden results, authorization and the response status are all decided in .NET before anything is rendered.

## The sidecar pool

Netjes starts the Node processes when the app starts and stops them when it stops. You do not run or deploy them yourself: `UseNetjes()` and `AddNetjes()` are enough, as long as `node` is on the path (`NetjesOptions.NodeExecutable` names another one).

- In development there is one process. It also runs the Vite dev server (port 5173, `ViteDevPort`), which compiles your pages on demand, so an edit shows on the next request.
- In production each process imports the server build in `dist/server/`. `NetjesOptions.SidecarProcesses` sets how many run (default 1). A process renders one page at a time on one core, so an app whose pages take real CPU time to render wants about one per core. Each render goes to the ready process with the fewest renders in flight.

```json
{
  "Netjes": {
    "SidecarProcesses": 4
  }
}
```

The app does not start until every process has reported ready, within `StartupTimeout` (60 seconds). When a process cannot be started at all (Node.js is not found, or the sidecar script is not installed or built), or in development the Vite dev server does not start, the app logs why in one log entry, with what to do, and exits with code 1. A process listens on a random port on `127.0.0.1`, accepts only requests that carry the token .NET gave it, and exits when the app's end of its standard input closes, so it never outlives the app.

### Timeouts

| Option | Default | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| `RenderTimeout` | 15 s | How long a process may take to render the shell of a streamed document: everything outside Suspense boundaries that are still waiting. In production also how long a health ping waits for an answer, and never less than 5 s ([Restarts](#restarts)). |
| `StreamTimeout` | 60 s | How long a whole document may take, deferred values and Suspense boundaries included. A complete document (for a crawler, below) waits up to this long. |

A render that runs out of time fails with the error page.

### Restarts

A process that exits is restarted after 1 second, then after 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds for each crash in a row, and after 30 seconds from then on. The delay goes back to 1 second once a process has stayed up for 30 seconds. Each exit is logged with the last lines the process printed.

In production, a process that stops answering without exiting (stuck in a loop, deadlocked, stopped by a signal) is restarted the same way. Netjes sends a health ping (`GET /health`) to a process that has answered no render for 5 seconds; one that gives no answer within `RenderTimeout`, and never less than 5 seconds, is taken out of the ready ones and killed, with an error in the log, and then restarts as a crashed one does. A render that had been sent to it fails with the error page. A process kept busy by a long render, but for less than that, is left alone, as is one that waits on data while it renders. In development nothing is pinged, since the process also runs the Vite dev server and can stop at a breakpoint in your code. A sidecar script of your own (`Netjes:SidecarScript`) must answer `GET /health`, with any status and without reading a request body.

Renders while a process is down go like this:

- A render that has already been sent to the process when it dies fails with the error page. Netjes never sends it again, because it may be the render that brought the process down.
- A render that finds its process gone before anything was sent goes to another ready process, or, when there is none, waits for the restart within its own `RenderTimeout` (`StreamTimeout` for a complete document). A render with deferred values stays on the process it started on and waits for that one.
- In production, a document request that finds no process ready at all does not wait: it gets the [client-rendered fallback](#when-no-sidecar-is-ready).

Waiting for a restart applies with `ClientRenderFallback` off, in development, to `netjes export`, and to the render that is first to find its process gone. Other production documents get the fallback.

### Health

`AddNetjes()` on the health checks builder adds a check named `netjes`:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks().AddNetjes();
// ...
app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz");
```

It reports Healthy when every process is ready, Degraded while some are restarting (renders go to the others), and Unhealthy when none is ready. A process that stopped answering counts as restarting from the moment it is taken out. The template's Docker health check calls `/healthz`. See [deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md#health-checks).

## Streamed documents

A document streams. The sidecar sends the shell as soon as it is ready, with a fallback in place of each Suspense boundary that is still waiting, and sends the content of those boundaries as it becomes ready. The browser hydrates the shell while the rest is still arriving, so the page is interactive before its slow parts are there. A page with an external `beforeInteractive` script hydrates once that script has loaded or failed ([Metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md#code-that-runs-before-the-first-paint)).

A boundary is either a `loading.tsx` file, which wraps the page below its folder in `<Suspense fallback={<Loading />}>`, or a `<Suspense>` you write in a component. A page waits inside a boundary for two things: a `Page.Defer` value it reads with `use()`, and code that loads late (`React.lazy`, `dynamic()`).

A boundary whose content is ready when the shell goes out is written in place, at its position in the HTML, however large it is. So a page that waits on nothing renders complete, and shows without JavaScript. Only what is still waiting comes later, after the shell, with a small inline script that puts it in place of the fallback. Without JavaScript that script does not run, and the fallback stays. ([ADR 0012](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0012-streamed-documents-and-deferred-values.md) explains the choice.)

Under a hash-based Content-Security-Policy, which output-cached pages need, those inline scripts are blocked, so such pages must not stream. See [security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#content-security-policy).

## Slow data with Page.Defer

`Page.Defer` puts a value in the props that is still being computed. The page renders without waiting for it, and the value streams to the page when it is ready, like a slow `fetch` behind a Suspense boundary in a Next.js server component. Use it for parts of a page that can come a moment later: comments, an activity feed, recommendations.

```csharp
public sealed record PostProps(PostDetail Post, Deferred<IReadOnlyList<PostSummary>> Related);

app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, PostStore store, HttpContext http) =>
    store.Find(slug) is { } post
        ? Page.Props(new PostProps(
            new PostDetail(post.Slug, post.Title, post.Body, post.Tags, post.PublishedOn),
            Page.Defer(RelatedAsync(store, slug, http.RequestAborted))))
        : Page.NotFound());
```

The prop's type is `Deferred<T>`. In the generated types it is a `deferred()` schema, which `definePage` parses into a thenable. Read it with React's `use()` inside a Suspense boundary:

```tsx
import { definePage } from 'netjes';
import { Suspense, use } from 'react';
import { type PostSummary, pages } from '../../../generated/netjes.ts';

function Related({ related }: { related: PromiseLike<PostSummary[]> }) {
  const posts = use(related);
  return <ul>{posts.map((post) => <li key={post.slug}>{post.title}</li>)}</ul>;
}

export default definePage(pages['/blog/[slug]'], function Post({ post, related }) {
  return (
    <article>
      <h1>{post.title}</h1>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Finding related posts…</p>}>
        <Related related={related} />
      </Suspense>
    </article>
  );
});
```

The value is validated against its schema when it arrives. `deferred(schema)` from `netjes/zod` builds the same schema by hand.

### The two overloads

| Overload | When the work starts | Services |
|---|---|---|
| `Page.Defer(Task<T> task)` | When you call it: you hand over a task that is already running. | Whatever the task captured, in the request's own scope. |
| `Page.Defer(Func<IServiceProvider, Task<T>> load)` | Once the page's payload is written, after the loaders have finished. | A DI scope of its own, disposed when the value is done. |

A task that uses a scoped service runs at the same time as the rest of the request, and an EF Core `DbContext` must not be used by two operations at once. The TaskBoard example creates a context of its own for the deferred work, from an `IDbContextFactory<TaskBoardDb>`:

```csharp
var activity = Page.Defer(ActivityAsync(contexts, access.ProjectId, number, http.RequestAborted));

static async Task<IReadOnlyList<ActivityItem>> ActivityAsync(
    IDbContextFactory<TaskBoardDb> contexts, Guid projectId, int number, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    await using var db = await contexts.CreateDbContextAsync(cancellationToken);
    return await db.Activity
        .Where(a => a.ProjectId == projectId && a.TaskNumber == number)
        .OrderByDescending(a => a.At)
        .Take(30)
        .Select(a => new ActivityItem(a.Id, a.Summary, a.Actor.Name, a.At))
        .ToListAsync(cancellationToken);
}
```

The second overload does the same without the factory: it hands the work a service provider of its own scope, so the `TaskBoardDb` it resolves is not the one the loaders use.

```csharp
var activity = Page.Defer(services => ActivityAsync(
    services.GetRequiredService<TaskBoardDb>(), access.ProjectId, number, http.RequestAborted));

static async Task<IReadOnlyList<ActivityItem>> ActivityAsync(
    TaskBoardDb db, Guid projectId, int number, CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
    await db.Activity
        .Where(a => a.ProjectId == projectId && a.TaskNumber == number)
        .OrderByDescending(a => a.At)
        .Take(30)
        .Select(a => new ActivityItem(a.Id, a.Summary, a.Actor.Name, a.At))
        .ToListAsync(cancellationToken);
```

`Page.Defer` works in the props of pages and layouts, anywhere in the props object, and in any number.

### On the wire

- A document carries a placeholder for each value, and the value follows in the same response, as a small inline script, once it is ready.
- A client navigation gets NDJSON instead of JSON: the payload on the first line, then one line per value as it completes.

A value that throws, or has not arrived when `StreamTimeout` runs out, rejects on the client, and `use()` throws it to the nearest `error.tsx`. With error details on (`IncludeErrorDetails`, on in the Development environment), the message is the exception's. With them off, the server sends an empty error in its place, and the client rejects with the message "Something went wrong" and `error.withheld` true. A value that did not arrive in time says "The value did not arrive in time", and a value whose task was cancelled says "The value was cancelled", in every environment and not withheld. The failure is logged as a warning (category `Netjes.Deferred`).

## Complete documents

Some readers get the whole document at once, with every boundary in place and no fallbacks:

- Crawlers and link previews, whose `User-Agent` matches `NetjesOptions.CrawlerUserAgents` (a case-insensitive regular expression; the default covers search engine bots, social previews, Lighthouse and the like).
- Every document, when `NetjesOptions.StreamDocuments` is `false`.
- `netjes export`, which writes complete documents to files (see [static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md)).

The response then starts once every deferred value has arrived, up to `StreamTimeout`. The values still follow as inline scripts, for the browser to hydrate what they rendered. Client navigations stream their NDJSON either way.

## When no sidecar is ready

In production, a document request that finds no Node process ready (they have all crashed or stopped answering, and are restarting) does not wait for one. Loaders and authorization run as usual and the response has the status it would have had, but .NET writes the document itself: a head with the stylesheets, the client entry and the CSP nonce, the `<title>`, description and robots from the loader's `PageMetadata`, and a body with only the page payload. The browser renders the page instead of hydrating it, and `Page.Defer` values stream in after it as usual. ([ADR 0013](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0013-client-rendered-fallback.md) has the reasoning.)

- Each such document logs a warning, `No Node sidecar was ready to render {Route} ({Path}); the page was sent for the browser to render.`, and adds one to the `netjes.sidecar.fallbacks` counter on the `Netjes` meter, tagged `netjes.route`.
- It is never stored in the output cache, and it goes out with `Cache-Control: no-store` in place of any header the page set, and without the headers a CDN reads ahead of `Cache-Control` (`CDN-Cache-Control`, `Surrogate-Control` and the others listed in [caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md#cdns-and-proxies)), so no browser, and no CDN that goes by the response's headers, keeps it once the processes are back.
- Visitors without JavaScript, and crawlers and link previews that run none, get an empty page with the title, description and robots from C#. Layout title templates, and the metadata that page and layout files export, apply once the page renders.
- Once the page has rendered, the client router runs as it does on a hydrated page and puts the same `data-netjes-hydrated` on `<html>`, so end-to-end tests wait for it here too ([testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md#wait-for-hydration)).
- The health check reports Unhealthy while it lasts.
- A render that reached a process and failed there, or timed out, still gets the error page.
- Development never falls back, since its process also runs the Vite dev server the browser loads from, and neither does `netjes export`.

`NetjesOptions.ClientRenderFallback = false` (`Netjes__ClientRenderFallback=false`) turns it off: such a request then waits for a restart, up to `RenderTimeout` (`StreamTimeout` for a complete document), and gets the error page if none comes.

## Components that load late or only in the browser

`dynamic()` loads a component's module on demand, in a chunk of its own, like `next/dynamic`:

```tsx
import { dynamic } from 'netjes';

const Chart = dynamic(() => import('./Chart.tsx'), { loading: Spinner });
const Map = dynamic(() => import('./Map.tsx'), { ssr: false, loading: Spinner });
```

With `ssr` (the default), the component renders on the server like any other; on a page the browser has not loaded the chunk for yet, it suspends until the module is there. With `ssr: false`, the server and the first render in the browser show `loading`, and the component renders after hydration: use it for code that needs `window` or a browser-only library.

`clientOnly(Component, { fallback })` renders an existing component only in the browser, after hydration, and `fallback` (default nothing) on the server and before that.

Both are in the [React API reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/react-api.md).

## Error pages

If something fails while Netjes serves a page, it renders the nearest boundary file instead, with the response's status:

- An exception in a loader, in an action without JavaScript, or in the React render: the nearest `error.tsx` above the segment that failed, inside the layouts above it, with status 500 (or the status of a `BadHttpRequestException`). A layout loader that throws renders the boundary above its own layout.
- `Page.NotFound()`, `Page.Forbidden()`, `Page.Unauthorized()`, and empty 401, 403 and 404 responses (from authorization, say): the nearest `not-found.tsx`, `forbidden.tsx` or `unauthorized.tsx`, else the error page. A user who fails a layout loader's `RequireAuthorization(...)` gets that section's own boundary (or the nearest above it) inside the layouts above the section, and the section's loader never runs.
- If the error page fails to render too: `app/global-error.tsx`, without any layout. If that is missing or fails as well: a plain HTML page with the status.

An `error.tsx` gets `{ error, reset }`, with the status as `error.status`. In production `error.message` is the status's reason phrase ("Internal Server Error"), so nothing about the exception reaches the browser, and `error.withheld` is true, so the page can leave the message out; `error.stack` is undefined. In development it is the exception's message, not withheld, and the stack is there too: the JavaScript stack for a render that failed in the sidecar (`SsrRenderException.JsStack`), the .NET one otherwise. `NetjesOptions.IncludeErrorDetails` sets this either way. Both are plain text, without the terminal colour codes Vite puts in its errors, and the message can take several lines, such as the code frame Vite reports for a syntax error in a page: show it with `white-space: pre-wrap` (`whitespace-pre-wrap` in Tailwind CSS), as the built-in error page and the template's `error.tsx` do. A status rendered without an exception, such as `Page.Forbidden()` where no `forbidden.tsx` is, gets its reason phrase as the message in every environment, and that message is not withheld.

Every such failure is logged: unhandled exceptions as errors, bad requests as warnings (category `Netjes.Rendering.PageErrorMiddleware`). The [routing guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md) describes where each boundary file goes.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md -->

# Caching

This guide is for app developers who want pages served from a cache, or need to know what browsers and proxies keep. It covers the `Cache-Control` Netjes sends by default, `CachePage` on ASP.NET Core output caching, the rules that apply to a page under any output caching, what differs for the endpoints that are not pages (JSON APIs, text files), revalidation, draft mode, and what to watch for with CDNs and cookies. The client's own cache of server state (TanStack Query) is in [data loading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md).

## What browsers keep by default

Page responses, documents and client payloads alike, go out with `Cache-Control: no-store, private`, unless the page set the header itself or, outside the Development environment, the output cache stores the response. That is what Next.js sends for its dynamic pages, and for the same reason: a page carries per-user data (shared props, an antiforgery token), and browsers show a page they kept on Back and Forward without asking the server again. A kept page would show a signed-in user's page on Back after they signed out.

Back past a full page load therefore fetches the page again, unless the browser's back/forward cache restores it (Chrome restores `no-store` pages while the site's cookies are unchanged). A page that should stay in the browser's cache sets its own `Cache-Control`, in its loader or an endpoint filter, and then can come back on Back after a sign-out.

The response that sets the antiforgery cookie, which is a visitor's first page, goes out with ASP.NET Core's own `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store` and `Pragma: no-cache` instead, so no browser or proxy keeps it either. Later pages reuse that cookie and get the default.

Some responses always get `no-store` in place of the page's own header: draft pages and the redirects loaders return in draft mode (`no-store, private`), the [client-rendered fallback](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md#when-no-sidecar-is-ready), and the page rendered again for a failed form post, which holds what was typed (`no-store`): a server action's post without JavaScript, and a page action's post with or without it. Server action answers and `/_netjes/antiforgery` go out `no-store` too. All of them also go out without the headers a CDN reads ahead of `Cache-Control` ([CDNs and proxies](#cdns-and-proxies)).

Static files are ASP.NET Core's: in production, the content-hashed files Vite writes under `/assets` are sent with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, and the other files in `public/` with no `Cache-Control`.

## Output-cached pages

`CachePage` caches a page on ASP.NET Core output caching, like incremental static regeneration in Next.js: the page is rendered at most once per `duration` and served from the cache in between.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddOutputCache();
// ...
app.UseNetjes();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.UseAntiforgery();
app.UseOutputCache(); // after UseNetjes and after authentication

app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, PostStore store) => /* ... */)
    .CachePage(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30), "posts");
```

`CachePage(duration, params tags)` works on anything that takes endpoint conventions: a page loader, `MapPages()` for every file page, a group, or a minimal API that returns `Page.Render`. Each endpoint it is put on carries the duration and tags as `CachedPageMetadata`, which app code and tests can read ([endpoint metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/csharp-api.md#endpoint-metadata)).

The order in the pipeline matters:

- `UseOutputCache()` after `UseNetjes()`. Before it, the output cache runs before routing, so no endpoint's policy applies, `CachePage` included, and Netjes logs a warning naming the order.
- `UseOutputCache()` after `UseAuthentication()`, so the output cache can see who is signed in. ASP.NET Core's default policy neither serves nor stores a response for a signed-in user or a request with an `Authorization` header.

### In the Development environment

In the Development environment no page is output-cached, under `CachePage` or any other policy: every request renders the page, nothing is stored, and an output-cached page goes out `Cache-Control: no-store, private` unless it set its own header. Code changes between any two requests there (Vite serves the sources, the sidecar imports them again, hot reload swaps loaders), and a stored page would go on serving markup and styles from before an edit, which React then fails to hydrate with the new modules. Everything else is as in production: the keys, the antiforgery token left out of a page the cache could store, and the warnings below. The app logs once, at Information, that pages are not output-cached there. Endpoints that are not pages, images included, are cached as anywhere, except those `CachePage` marks, such as the JSON endpoints of a group it is put on: the page rules apply to them, so they run on each request too ([ADR 0023](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0023-pages-are-not-output-cached-in-development.md)).

So `UseOutputCache()` can stay in every environment. Data that is slow or costly to load, such as a remote API that bills per call, is cached in the service that loads it (`IMemoryCache`, `HybridCache`), which helps in production too. To see what the output cache stores, run the built app (`npx netjes build`, then `npx netjes start`), or test it in a host in another environment with Netjes in development mode ([testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md#the-app-over-http)): the environment decides, not `Netjes:Mode`.

### What is stored

Outside the Development environment, the output cache stores a page's response when:

- the request is a `GET` or `HEAD` without a signed-in user or an `Authorization` header,
- the status is 200 and the response sets no cookie,
- the document carries no CSP nonce (a stored nonce would be every visitor's; Netjes logs a warning once per page, see [security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#content-security-policy)),
- and the request is not in draft mode, not the page rendered for a failed form post, and not the client-rendered fallback.

A render that is not stored is one visitor's page, and gets the default `no-store, private`, as does every output-cached page in the Development environment. Netjes judges that when the response starts: a refusal the output cache makes later, such as for a body over its `MaximumBodySize`, leaves the response without `Cache-Control`. Stored responses carry no `Cache-Control` of their own.

### How entries are keyed

Each entry is keyed on:

- the scheme, the host, and the path and query string exactly as sent, case included. Loaders get route and query values as sent, so `/s/Ab` and `/s/aB` can be different pages, and each query string is a page of its own (`?tag=a&tag=b` and `?tag=b&tag=a` are two entries). A literal segment in another case (`/About` for `app/about/page.tsx`), and under `TrailingSlash.Never` a trailing slash, is redirected before the output cache sees the request, so such a spelling gets no entry of its own when a browser sends it. A request target that browsers do not send, with `.` or `..` segments (`/./About`) or in absolute form (`GET http://example.com/About`), is not redirected: it is answered, and its page can be stored under `/About`, as before ([One URL per page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#one-url-per-page)).
- whether it is a document or a client payload, and for a payload, which of the page's layouts the client already holds (it then leaves their props out).
- the client build. During a rolling deploy, instances on the old and the new build do not serve each other's entries.
