The cache's size limit counts response bodies, not keys, and every host and query string makes a new entry. In production, pin `AllowedHosts` to your host names and size the cache:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddOutputCache(options => options.SizeLimit = 200 * 1024 * 1024); // bytes; ASP.NET Core's default is 100 MB
```

### What a stored page leaves out

A response the output cache may store carries no antiforgery token, since the stored copy would hand one visitor's token to everyone it is served to. Pages under `CachePage` never carry one. Before a server action call or a `<Form>` post, the client fetches a token from `/_netjes/antiforgery`, and again after each action or navigation, since signing in or out changes it. So forms on cached pages need JavaScript: without it the post has no token and is refused.

### Shared props and cookies

A stored entry is every visitor's, shared props included. Shared props and the loaders of cached pages must not depend on cookies or other per-visitor state. Shared props built from the signed-in user are fine, since signed-in users never get a cached page.

As a backstop, a render the output cache will store that reads `Request.Cookies` (draft mode's cookie aside) logs a warning once per page: the render was stored and will be served to every visitor. It is still stored, because refusing would turn caching off behind any middleware that reads a cookie on each request (cookie authentication, sessions, a cookie culture provider). Reads of the raw `Cookie` header are not seen. Read per-visitor values on the client, or leave the page uncached. `UseAuthentication()` placed after `UseOutputCache()` also triggers the warning. In the Development environment, where nothing is stored, the warning says instead that outside Development the render is stored.

### Under any output caching

The keys and rules above hold however a page is output-cached, not only with `CachePage`:

- `.CacheOutput()` plain, named (`.CacheOutput("pages")`) or built (`.CacheOutput(p => p.Expire(...))`),
- an `[OutputCache]` attribute on the loader,
- conventions on `MapPages()`,
- a base policy of the app (`options.AddBasePolicy(...)`).

The differences: under those, a response the output cache will not store keeps its antiforgery token, while `CachePage` pages never carry one. And an endpoint that is no page but renders one (a minimal API returning `Page.Render` or `Page.Redirect`) gets these keys only from `CachePage`. Under other output caching its pages are not stored, and Netjes logs a warning once per endpoint.

A policy's own keys still add to these: `SetVaryByQuery("page")` cannot narrow the key, since the query string as sent is part of it already. ([ADR 0016](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0016-page-cache-rules-under-any-output-caching.md) explains why the rules apply under every policy.)

`CachePage` and `.CacheOutput(...)` on one endpoint do not combine. Of the output-cache policies on an endpoint, ASP.NET Core applies the last, so a `.CacheOutput(...)` after `CachePage` replaces the policy `CachePage` set: the later policy decides how long the page is kept and how its entries are tagged, and revalidating one of `CachePage`'s tags no longer evicts the page (`RevalidatePath` still does). The rest of `CachePage` stays: the page carries no antiforgery token, and its `CachedPageMetadata` still holds the duration and tags `CachePage` was given, not those that apply.

## Endpoints that are not pages

The sections above are about pages. This section is about the minimal API endpoints an app maps next to them to return data or files: a JSON API, a text file such as `llms.txt`, a webhook. Netjes adds no `Cache-Control` to their answers, and its page rules do not apply to the entries the output cache keeps for them: ASP.NET Core's own keys and rules decide ([ADR 0016](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0016-page-cache-rules-under-any-output-caching.md) says why the page rules stop at pages). An endpoint that `CachePage` is put on, directly or through its route group, gets the page rules for its entries, and one that renders a page with `Page.Render` is covered above; this section is about the rest. The differences from a page, each explained below:

| | A page | An endpoint that is not a page |
|---|---|---|
| `Cache-Control` | `no-store, private`, unless the page sets its own or the output cache stores the response | The handler's own; none when the handler sets none |
| The path in an entry's key | As sent | Compared without regard to case: all spellings share one entry |
| The query string in the key | The whole query string, as sent | Every key varies the entry, unless the policy narrows it with `SetVaryByQuery` |
| `RevalidatePath` | Evicts the page | Does not evict it: evict by tag |
| The Development environment | Rendered on each request, never stored | Output-cached as anywhere |

### Headers

Netjes adds no `Cache-Control` to the answer of such an endpoint. The header its handler sets goes out as set. When the handler sets none, Netjes adds none, also to the 400 that minimal API binding answers for a value that does not bind (`take=x` for an `int?`). `CachePage` does not change that. A JSON endpoint in a group it is put on gets the page rules for its cache entries, but no `Cache-Control` from Netjes, in the Development environment too: the default `no-store, private` is a page's. Without a `Cache-Control`, a browser or a CDN uses its own defaults, so set one on an answer that may be kept, in the handler or in an endpoint filter:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/api/search", (string q, SearchIndex index, HttpContext http) =>
{
    http.Response.Headers.CacheControl = "public, max-age=300";
    return TypedResults.Ok(index.Search(q));
});
```

Output caching adds no `Cache-Control` either. It stores the response headers that are set before the body is written, and sends them again with every answer it serves, with an `Age` header added. So a stored answer goes out with the `Cache-Control` of the response it was stored from, or with none when that response had none.

For the endpoints Netjes maps itself:

- `/_netjes/image` sends `public, max-age=` the image option `CacheDuration` (7 days) and an `ETag` with an image or a 304 ([images](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/images.md#the-image-endpoint)). Its error answers, such as the 400 for a width it does not allow, send none.
- `MapSitemap` sends `public, max-age=` its `cacheFor` (an hour by default), and `no-store` on the 404 it answers under a base path that is too long ([metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md#sitemap-and-robots)). `MapRobotsTxt` and `MapLocaleRedirect` ([locales](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#locales)) send none.
- Server action answers and `/_netjes/antiforgery` send `no-store` ([above](#what-browsers-keep-by-default)).

### Keys and the query string

The output cache keys the entry of such an endpoint on the method, the scheme, the host, the path and the query string, by ASP.NET Core's rules, without the build and the other parts of a page's key. A page's entry is keyed on its path and query string as sent. Two things differ for the endpoint.

The path is compared without regard to case, route values included. `/llms.txt` and `/LLMS.TXT` share one entry, and so do `/codes/Ab` and `/codes/aB` for `MapGet("/codes/{code}", ...)`. The handler answers whichever spelling arrives first, and every other spelling is served that answer until the entry expires or is evicted, so a handler that answers two spellings differently, such as one that compares a route value exactly, runs only for the spelling that arrives first. There are two ways to change that:

- A condition on the policy stores one spelling. `.CacheOutput(p => p.With(context => context.HttpContext.Request.Path.Value == "/llms.txt"))` stores the answer for the path `/llms.txt` only. A request for `/LLMS.TXT` is neither served from the cache nor stored in it, so the handler answers each one.
- `AddOutputCache(options => options.UseCaseSensitivePaths = true)` gives each spelling an entry of its own. It applies to every endpoint the output cache handles, not to one.

Every query key varies the entry. `?page=1`, `?page=2` and `?page=1&utm_source=feed` are three entries, and a visitor, a crawler or a link can make up more. The cache's size limit counts response bodies, not keys ([How entries are keyed](#how-entries-are-keyed)), so enough query strings for a large body fill it: a 400 KB text file takes about 100 MB, ASP.NET Core's default limit, once 256 query strings have stored it. While the cache is full, no new response is stored, a page's included, until older entries expire or are evicted. `SetVaryByQuery` narrows the key:

- `p.SetVaryByQuery([])` keeps one entry whatever the query string says. The call has no form without arguments, so an empty array stands for no keys.
- `p.SetVaryByQuery("page")` varies the entry on the keys it lists and ignores the others, so `?page=1` and `?page=1&utm_source=feed` share one.

That is safe for an endpoint whose answer does not depend on the keys it leaves out and whose body does not repeat the URL. A page's payload repeats its URL, which is why a page's key cannot be narrowed this way ([Under any output caching](#under-any-output-caching)).

### What is stored, and how to evict it

ASP.NET Core's default policy decides what is stored. It stores the answer to a `GET` or `HEAD` request that has no `Authorization` header and no signed-in user (which is why `UseOutputCache()` goes after `UseAuthentication()`), when the status is 200 and the response sets no cookie. Any other answer reaches the handler again on the next request.

`RevalidatePath` and `IPageCache.RevalidatePathAsync` evict by a tag that the page rules add to the entries of pages, so they never evict the entry of an endpoint that is not a page. Give the policy a tag instead, and evict that: `.Revalidate("docs")` on a server action's result, or `IPageCache.RevalidateTagAsync("docs")` from anywhere else ([Revalidating](#revalidating)).

For example, a text file that is stored once whatever the query string, for ten minutes, and evicted when the docs change:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/llms.txt", (DocsStore docs) => Results.Text(docs.AsText(), "text/plain; charset=utf-8"))
    .CacheOutput(p => p.SetVaryByQuery([]).Expire(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)).Tag("docs"));
```

### In the Development environment and in draft mode

In the Development environment these endpoints are output-cached as anywhere: only pages, and the endpoints `CachePage` marks, render on each request there ([In the Development environment](#in-the-development-environment)). A change to what a handler returns shows once its entry has expired or been evicted, or the app has restarted.

Draft mode bypasses them as it bypasses pages: while the draft cookie is on, nothing is served from the cache to that visitor, and nothing that answers the request is stored. The image endpoint is the one exception ([Draft mode](#draft-mode)).

## Revalidating

A server action evicts cached pages with `.Revalidate(tags)` or `.RevalidatePath(paths)` on its result. The client then loads the page on screen again:

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc; // [FromForm]

app.MapAction("posts.publish", async ([FromForm] PublishPost input, PostStore posts) =>
{
    await posts.PublishAsync(input.Slug);
    return ServerAction.Ok().Revalidate("posts").RevalidatePath($"/blog/{input.Slug}");
});
```

- `Revalidate(tags)` evicts every entry tagged with one of these tags: the tags given to `CachePage(duration, tags)`, or by any other output-cache policy.
- `RevalidatePath(paths)` evicts the entries of each path, documents and payloads, with any query string. The path is matched without regard to case or a trailing slash, and without the base path (`/blog/hello`, not `/docs/blog/hello` under `UsePathBase("/docs")`).

Outside actions (a webhook from your CMS, a background job), inject `IPageCache`:

```csharp
app.MapPost("/webhooks/cms", async (CmsEvent change, IPageCache cache) =>
{
    await cache.RevalidatePathAsync($"/blog/{change.Slug}");
    await cache.RevalidateTagAsync("posts");
    return Results.NoContent();
}).RequireAuthorization("cms");
```

Without output caching both do nothing. Eviction is the app's own: with several instances, it reaches the others only through a store they share (see [deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md#several-instances)), and it never reaches a CDN.

## Draft mode

Draft mode lets an editor see unpublished content on pages that are otherwise cached, like Next.js's `draftMode()`. Turn it on from an endpoint you protect, and read it in loaders with `IDraftMode`:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/preview/on", (IDraftMode draft) =>
    {
        draft.Enable();
        return Results.LocalRedirect("/");
    })
    .RequireAuthorization("editors");

app.MapGet("/preview/off", (IDraftMode draft) =>
{
    draft.Disable();
    return Results.LocalRedirect("/");
});

app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, IDraftMode draft, PostStore posts) =>
        posts.Find(slug, includeDrafts: draft.IsEnabled) is { } post ? Page.Props(new PostProps(post)) : Page.NotFound())
    .CachePage(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));
```

- `Enable()` sets a cookie signed with ASP.NET Core Data Protection that lasts `NetjesOptions.DraftModeDuration` (one hour). It is `HttpOnly`, and outside Development `SameSite=None; Secure`, so a CMS on another site can show the preview in a frame (allow that with `SecurityHeaders.DraftFrameAncestors`, see [security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#security-headers)).
- While it is on, output caching is bypassed for that visitor under any policy, for [endpoints that are not pages](#endpoints-that-are-not-pages) as well: nothing is looked up, and nothing that answers a draft request is stored, a redirect a loader returns included. Each draft request has a cache key of its own, so editors previewing a page at once do not wait for each other.
- Draft pages go out `Cache-Control: no-store, private`, without the headers a CDN reads ahead of it ([CDNs and proxies](#cdns-and-proxies)). So does a redirect a page or layout loader returns while draft mode is on, since where a draft leads (an unpublished slug, say) is draft content too.
- In React, `useDraftMode()` returns `{ isEnabled }`, for a "Leave preview" banner.
- The image endpoint is the exception: an image is the same for editors and visitors, so editors share its cache.

## CDNs and proxies

Netjes sends no CDN headers. A stored page goes out without `Cache-Control`, so a CDN in front of the app keeps it only under rules you give the CDN, and `Revalidate` and `RevalidatePath` evict the app's own output cache only.

Page responses carry `Vary: X-Netjes-Data, X-Netjes-Segments`: the same URL answers with a document or a client payload, and a payload depends on the layouts the client holds. A cache that keeps pages has to keep those apart, or pass every request with `X-Netjes-Data` through to the app.

Where Netjes sends `no-store` whatever the page set (draft pages and draft redirects, the client-rendered fallback, the page for a failed form post, action answers and antiforgery tokens), it also removes the headers a CDN or proxy reads ahead of `Cache-Control`, in any casing: `CDN-Cache-Control` and any other header whose name ends in `-Cache-Control` (a CDN's own, such as `Cloudflare-CDN-Cache-Control`), `Surrogate-Control`, `Edge-Control` and `X-Accel-Expires`. A CDN that reads one of them would otherwise keep a draft, or go on serving the fallback, whatever `Cache-Control` says. Netjes does this when it renders the response and again as the response starts, after the `Response.OnStarting` callbacks of loaders, actions and middleware registered after `UseNetjes`. A callback of middleware ahead of `UseNetjes` runs after Netjes's, so what it adds still goes out. On every other response, the headers a page sets go out as they are ([ADR 0019](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0019-forced-no-store-removes-cdn-cache-headers.md)).

## Images

The `<Image>` endpoint (`/_netjes/image`) is output-cached whenever the app uses output caching, for signed-in visitors too, and sends long-lived `Cache-Control` and an `ETag`. See [images](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/images.md).

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/images.md -->

# Images

This guide is for app developers. It covers the `<Image>` component and the `/_netjes/image` endpoint behind it, the counterparts of `next/image` and `/_next/image`: where images may come from, the widths and qualities served, the formats, the limits that keep the endpoint safe under load, and how images are resized, through an `IImageProcessor` such as the optional SkiaSharp package ([ADR 0008](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0008-pluggable-image-processing.md)).

## Showing an image

```tsx
import { Image } from 'netjes';

{/* A fixed size: a 1x and a 2x copy. */}
<Image src="/img/avatar.png" width={64} height={64} alt="Ada Lovelace" />

{/* Responsive: every configured width, and the browser picks by `sizes`. Above the fold, so `priority`. */}
<Image
  src="/hero.png"
  width={1600}
  height={800}
  sizes="(max-width: 64rem) 100vw, 64rem"
  priority
  alt="Gradient in the blog's accent colours"
  className="h-auto w-full"
/>
```

`<Image>` renders an `<img>` with its `width` and `height`, so the page keeps the space and does not shift as it loads. It loads lazily and decodes asynchronously, and its `srcset` points at resized copies from the endpoint:

- Without `sizes`, a fixed-size image gets two candidates: the smallest configured width that covers `width`, as `1x`, and the one that covers twice that, as `2x`.
- With `sizes`, it gets every configured width as a `w` candidate, and the browser picks one by the layout.
- `priority` loads it eagerly with high fetch priority and preloads it from the document head. Use it for the image a visitor sees first.
- `quality` (1–100, default 75) is rounded to the nearest quality the server accepts.
- `unoptimized` serves `src` as it is. SVGs, `data:` URLs and `blob:` URLs are always served as they are.

`src` is a path in `public/` (`/img/hero.png`) or a URL on an allowed remote host. `alt` is required; give `""` for a decorative image. Every other `<img>` attribute, such as `className` or `style`, passes through, and a `ref` gets the `<img>` element. Under a [base path](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#base-path), write `src` as if the app were at the root.

The configured widths, qualities and the endpoint's path reach the component with the first document, so the server's configuration is the only one. A static host has no image endpoint, so pages from `netjes export` need `unoptimized` on their images ([Static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md#what-cannot-be-exported)).

## The image endpoint

`app.MapPages()` maps `/_netjes/image?url=…&w=…&q=…` for `GET` and `HEAD`. It reads the source, hands it to the registered `IImageProcessor` with the width, quality and an output format the browser accepts, and answers with the result:

- `Cache-Control: public, max-age=…` for `CacheDuration` (7 days), an `ETag` (a matching `If-None-Match` gets 304), and `Vary: Accept`.
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; sandbox;`, so an image opened on its own, an SVG above all, runs no script.

A `HEAD` is answered as a `GET` is, with the same status and headers and without the body. The endpoint reads and processes the image for it all the same ([HEAD requests](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#head-requests)).

If the app uses output caching (`AddOutputCache()` and `UseOutputCache()`), the endpoint's answers are cached: keyed by the width, the quality, the image as it is fetched and the negotiated format, not by the `Host` header. Requests with an `Authorization` header or a signed-in user are cached too, unlike under ASP.NET Core's default policy, since an image from `public/` or an allowed host is the same for everyone. Editors in draft mode share this cache. Serve private images from an endpoint of your own. The output cache keys every entry by the method as well, so a `HEAD` is cached apart from the `GET`: the first `HEAD` for an image processes it once more and stores a copy of its own.

Without an image processor the endpoint serves the original bytes, cached as above. `Netjes:Images:Path` moves the endpoint; it is used with one leading slash and none trailing, and other spellings of it get 400.

## Where images come from

**Local images** come from `public/` in development and from the client build in production, where Vite has copied `public/`. A local `url` must be a plain path:

- no query, no fragment, no `.`, `..` or empty segments, and no backslash;
- spelled as its file is stored, case included. On Windows and macOS, `/img/HERO.png` for `hero.png` gets 400, and so do an 8.3 short name, a segment with a trailing dot or space, and an accented name in another Unicode form.

This keeps one cache entry per image and size. The endpoint lists a path's directories the first time the path is asked for, then remembers it (up to 4096 paths, after which it starts over). A file renamed while the app runs is still served under its old spelling, where the file system still opens it that way, until then or until the app restarts.

**Remote images** come only from the hosts in `Netjes:Images:RemoteHosts`:

```json
{
  "Netjes": {
    "Images": {
      "RemoteHosts": ["images.example.com", "*.cdn.example.com"]
    }
  }
}
```

- `images.example.com` allows that host; `*.example.com` allows its subdomains, not `example.com` itself.
- Over https only, unless `RemoteRequireHttps` is `false`, and on the scheme's default port, unless `RemotePorts` lists another.
- Redirects are never followed: a remote host that redirects gets 502.
- The host's address must be public. Loopback, private, link-local (`169.254.169.254`, where cloud metadata services live), shared and unique-local addresses are refused after DNS resolution, so an allowed name pointed at an internal service is never reached. An IPv6 address that carries an IPv4 one (IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, NAT64 on `64:ff9b::/96` or a `/96` inside `64:ff9b:1::/48`, 6to4 on `2002::/16`) is judged by the IPv4 address inside, and Teredo is refused. A NAT64 prefix of your own network, or another RFC 6052 layout, cannot be recognised from the address: where DNS64 makes those, restrict the app's egress at the network as well.
- Fetches never use a proxy: `HTTP_PROXY` and `HTTPS_PROXY` are ignored, because through a proxy the address check would see the proxy. Where all egress must go through a proxy, remote images fail with 502 or 504; allow the app direct egress to its `RemoteHosts`, or serve those images from `public/`.
- The fetch has `RemoteTimeout` (10 seconds) for its headers and body together.

A remote URL is cached as it is fetched: host lower-cased, default port, dot segments and fragment dropped. Its path and query string are sent upstream as written, so `//a.png`, `/A.png` or a trailing `?` may be one image to the host and still be separate entries here. Allow only hosts you trust.

## Widths, qualities and formats

The endpoint serves only the widths in `Netjes:Images:Widths`, by default Next.js's device and image sizes: 16, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128, 256, 384, 640, 750, 828, 1080, 1200, 1920, 2048 and 3840. It accepts `DefaultQuality` (75) and the qualities in `Qualities` (by default only 75). A width or quality it does not serve, or one written with leading zeros (`w=0640`), gets 400. Configured lists replace the defaults:

```json
{
  "Netjes": {
    "Images": {
      "Widths": [320, 640, 1280, 1920],
      "Qualities": [50, 75, 90]
    }
  }
}
```

The endpoint goes by a source's bytes, not its file extension or `Content-Type`: it serves PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP and AVIF, and SVG when `AllowSvg` is on (it is off by default, because SVG can carry script; SVGs are served unprocessed). Anything else is refused, 400 for a local file and 502 for a remote one, and an image goes out typed as what its bytes are. The output format is the first of the processor's formats that the request's `Accept` header names, or the source's own format.

## Limits

| Option | Default | What it limits |
|---|---|---|
| `MaxSourceBytes` | 20 MB | The largest source read, local (400) or remote (502). |
| `MaxConcurrency` | one per CPU | Images read and processed at once. A request takes its slot before it reads the source. |
| `MaxRemoteFetches` | 16 | Remote images fetched at once, in slots of their own, so a slow host cannot hold up local images. A fetch keeps its slot until its image is processed. |
| `MaxQueue` | 1000 | Requests that may wait for a slot, in each of the two pools. More get 503 with `Retry-After`. |
| `RemoteTimeout` | 10 s | A remote fetch, headers and body together (then 504). |

Peak memory is about `MaxConcurrency` × (2 × `MaxSourceBytes` + 4 bytes × the processor's `MaxPixels`) + `MaxRemoteFetches` × `MaxSourceBytes`, so lower these in a small container. If most images are remote and their hosts are slow, raise `MaxRemoteFetches` rather than `MaxConcurrency`: a fetch waits on the network, while each processing slot can take a CPU and the memory of a decoded image.

| Status | When |
|---|---|
| 400 | A bad or non-canonical query, a width or quality not served, a host or port not allowed, a local file that is not a served image, is spelled otherwise than stored or is too large, or a local image the processor refuses. The body says which. |
| 404 | No such local file. |
| 502 | A remote image that is refused: a redirect, an error status, a non-public address, not an allowed image, too large, or refused by the processor. |
| 503 | The queue is full; `Retry-After` says when to try again. |
| 504 | A remote fetch took longer than `RemoteTimeout`. |

A `HEAD` takes its slots as a `GET` does, within the same limits. Each image can have a cache entry for `GET` and one for `HEAD`, and under `UsePathBase`, where the endpoint answers with and without the base path, two of each. Size the output cache (`SizeLimit`) for the images it holds as well as the pages ([Caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md)).

## Resizing with SkiaSharp

Without a processor, images are served as they are. The `Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp` package resizes them and encodes WebP:

```bash
dotnet add package Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp
```

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNetjes();
builder.Services.AddNetjesSkiaImages(o => o.MaxPixels = 25_000_000);
```

`AddNetjesSkiaImages` registers `SkiaImageProcessor`, before or after `AddNetjes()`. It:

- resizes to the requested width, never larger than the source, and applies the EXIF orientation;
- encodes WebP when the browser accepts it, and the source's own format otherwise;
- decodes large JPEGs at a reduced size;
- refuses an image whose header declares more than `MaxPixels` pixels (default 40 million, about 160 MB decoded) before decoding it, since a file of a few kilobytes can claim 40000×40000;
- decodes `MaxConcurrency` images at once (default one per CPU). `Netjes:Images:MaxConcurrency` limits the whole endpoint, reading included.

It decodes PNG, JPEG and WebP only, and only bytes that start with the declared format's signature, so no other codec SkiaSharp bundles (BMP, ICO and the rest) parses them, even when your own code calls the processor. GIFs (which may be animated) and AVIFs pass through unchanged. An image it cannot decode is refused, not passed through.

SkiaSharp's native codecs parse whatever a file in `public/` or an allowed host holds, so keep SkiaSharp current. If SkiaSharp ships a security update before `Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp` moves to it, add package references to the newer `SkiaSharp` and `SkiaSharp.NativeAssets.Linux.NoDependencies` yourself.

## Writing an image processor

Register your own `IImageProcessor` to resize with another library:

```csharp
public sealed class MyImageProcessor : IImageProcessor
{
    public IReadOnlyList<string> OutputFormats => ["image/webp", "image/jpeg"];

    public ValueTask<ProcessedImage> ProcessAsync(ImageSource source, ImageTransform transform, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        // source.Content: the bytes; source.ContentType: what they are (image/png, image/jpeg, image/gif, image/webp, image/avif).
        // transform.Width: a configured width; transform.Quality: 1-100; transform.Format: one of OutputFormats, or null for the source's.
        if (TooLarge(source))
        {
            throw new ImageRejectedException("The image has too many pixels.");
        }

        return ValueTask.FromResult(new ProcessedImage(Resize(source, transform), transform.Format ?? source.ContentType));
    }
}

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IImageProcessor, MyImageProcessor>();
```

- `OutputFormats` lists the formats it can encode, preferred first. The endpoint passes one the browser names in `Accept`, or `null` to keep the source's.
- `source.ContentType` is the format the bytes are, whatever the file's extension or the remote `Content-Type` said.
- Do not upscale past the source.
- Throwing `ImageRejectedException` answers with its message: 400 for a local image, 502 for a remote one.

All of the endpoint's options are listed in [Options](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/options.md).

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md -->

# Metadata

This guide is for app developers. It covers what goes in a page's `<head>`: titles, descriptions, Open Graph and Twitter tags, canonical and alternate links, from page and layout files or from a C# loader. It also covers `sitemap.xml` and `robots.txt`, and loading third-party scripts with `<Script>`. The API follows the Next.js Metadata API.

## Titles and tags from page files

A page or a layout exports `metadata`:

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
import type { Metadata } from 'netjes';

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: { default: 'Netjes Blog', template: '%s · Netjes Blog' },
  openGraph: { siteName: 'Netjes Blog', type: 'website' },
};
```

```tsx
// app/guestbook/page.tsx
export const metadata: Metadata = { title: 'Guestbook' }; // <title>Guestbook · Netjes Blog</title>
```

Netjes merges the metadata of the layouts above a page (outermost first), then the page's own, then what the page's C# loader sent, and writes the result as tags that React puts in the head. Each later one replaces what the earlier ones set, field by field: `openGraph`, `twitter`, `alternates`, `icons` and `other` are merged key by key, everything else is replaced. On a client navigation the tags change with the page.

### Titles

`title` is a string, or an object:

| Title | Effect |
|---|---|
| `'Guestbook'` | Goes through the nearest `template` from a layout above. |
| `{ template: '%s · Docs' }` | In a layout: the first `%s` is replaced by the title of each page below it. |
| `{ default: 'Netjes Blog' }` | In a layout: the title of the pages below it that set none. In a layout or a page it goes through the nearest `template` from a layout above, like a string title, and never through a `template` in the same object. |
| `{ absolute: 'Home' }` | Used as it is, skipping every template. |

The Blog's docs layout nests a template inside the root one: `export const metadata: Metadata = { title: { template: '%s · Docs · Netjes Blog' } };` makes a docs page's title `Routing · Docs · Netjes Blog`.

A layout below the root can set a `default` as well. Say the Blog's docs layout set both a default and a template:

```tsx
// app/docs/layout.tsx
export const metadata: Metadata = { title: { default: 'Docs', template: '%s · Docs · Netjes Blog' } };
```

A docs page that sets no title is then `Docs · Netjes Blog`: the default goes through the root layout's template, `%s · Netjes Blog`, and not through the template beside it. A page's `title: 'Routing'` is still `Routing · Docs · Netjes Blog`, and so is `title: { default: 'Routing' }`, since a page's default goes through the nearest template above it like a string. To keep a title bare, set `absolute` instead of `default`: `{ absolute: 'Docs' }` is `Docs`, whatever templates are above it.

### Fields

| Field | Written as |
|---|---|
| `title` | `<title>` |
| `description` | `<meta name="description">` |
| `keywords` | `<meta name="keywords">`, joined with commas |
| `authors: [{ name, url? }]` | `<meta name="author">` per author (the name) |
| `robots` | `<meta name="robots">`: a string as it is, or `{ index, follow }` as `index, follow`, `noindex, nofollow` and so on |
| `alternates.canonical` | `<link rel="canonical">` |
| `alternates.languages: { 'nl': '/nl' }` | `<link rel="alternate" hreflang>` per language |
| `openGraph` | `og:title`, `og:description`, `og:url`, `og:site_name`, `og:type`, `og:locale`, and `og:image` per image, each followed by its `og:image:width`, `og:image:height` and `og:image:alt` when set |
| `twitter` | `twitter:card`, `twitter:site`, `twitter:creator`, `twitter:title`, `twitter:description`, and `twitter:image` per image, each followed by its `twitter:image:alt` when set |
| `icons: { icon, apple }` | `<link rel="icon">`, `<link rel="apple-touch-icon">` |
| `themeColor` | `<meta name="theme-color">` |
| `other: { name: content }` | `<meta name content>` per entry |

An image's `alt` is written only when it is not empty, and its `width` and `height` only when they are above zero. URLs are written as given, so give crawlers absolute image URLs: under a [base path](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#base-path), an icon in `public/` needs the base path in front (`useBasePath()` in a layout that renders the `<link>` itself).

Another case of a page's literal segments, and with `TrailingSlash.Never` a trailing slash, is redirected to the file's spelling, so a crawler that follows such a link indexes the page once ([One URL per page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#one-url-per-page)). Each query string is still a URL of its own, though, so a page reached with query strings that show the same content, such as `?utm_source=newsletter` or a sort order, names the URL to index with `alternates.canonical`: `export const metadata: Metadata = { alternates: { canonical: '/blog' } }`, or `Alternates` in a loader's `PageMetadata` when the URL has route values.

### Open Graph and Twitter

`openGraph.images` and `twitter.images` take one image or an array of them, as in Next.js: each is a URL, as a string or a `URL`, or `{ url, width, height, alt }` with the details optional. An empty entry, or an image with an empty URL, is left out.

Once the layouts', the page's and the C# metadata are merged, the link preview tags that are not set fill in as they do in Next.js:

- With `openGraph` metadata, `og:title` and `og:description` take the page's title and description where `openGraph` sets none.
- With `openGraph` or `twitter` metadata, `twitter:title`, `twitter:description` and the `twitter:image` tags take the Open Graph title, description and images that `twitter` does not set, and the page's title and description where there is no Open Graph one either. A title taken this way does not go through a template again: an Open Graph title is used as set, the page's title as its layouts' templates made it.
- Where `twitter` sets no `card`, `twitter:card` is `summary_large_image` when `twitter.images` has an image and `summary` when it has none; with no `twitter` metadata at all, the Open Graph images decide. So `twitter: { site: '@acme' }` next to Open Graph images writes a `summary` card with those images: set `card: 'summary_large_image'` for the large one.

An empty title or description counts as not set, so it takes the fallback, and no `og:` or `twitter:` title or description tag is written empty. An empty `twitter.images` list does count as set: it keeps the Open Graph images out of the Twitter tags, and the card is `summary` unless `twitter` sets one.

### Special pages

`not-found.tsx`, `error.tsx`, `forbidden.tsx` and `unauthorized.tsx` export `metadata` too, and the layouts' title templates apply to them. An `error.tsx`'s metadata applies when the server renders it; an error caught in the browser keeps the page's title.

### `<title>` and `<meta>` elements

React 19 hoists `<title>`, `<meta>` and `<link>` elements rendered anywhere into the head, so a component can render them itself. Below a layout that sets a title, use `metadata` instead: the layout's title is still written, so a `<title>` element makes a second one.

## Metadata from C#

For a title or description that depends on data, the loader sends it with `.WithMetadata(...)`, the counterpart of Next.js's `generateMetadata`:

```csharp
app.MapPageLoader("/blog", (string? tag, PostStore store) =>
    Page.Props(new BlogIndexProps(tag, store.Tags(), store.Posts(tag)))
        .WithMetadata(new PageMetadata { Title = tag is null ? "Blog" : $"Posts tagged {tag}" }));
```

It is merged over the files' metadata, so the layouts' title templates still apply: `Posts tagged dotnet · Netjes Blog`. `PageMetadata` has `Title`, `Description`, `Keywords`, `Robots` (`new PageMetadataRobots(Index: false)`), `Alternates` (`Canonical`, `Languages`), `OpenGraph` (`Title`, `Description`, `Url`, `SiteName`, `Type`, `Locale`, `Images`), `Twitter` (`Card`, `Site`, `Creator`, `Images`; each image is a `PageMetadataImage`, and a plain URL string converts to one), `ThemeColor` and `Other`. Icons and authors are set in the files only.

```csharp
.WithMetadata(new PageMetadata
{
    Title = post.Title,
    Description = post.Summary,
    Alternates = new PageMetadataAlternates(Canonical: $"https://blog.example/blog/{post.Slug}"),
    OpenGraph = new PageMetadataOpenGraph { Type = "article", Images = [new PageMetadataImage($"https://blog.example/img/{post.Slug}.png", 1200, 630, post.Title)] },
})
```

A layout loader's result can carry metadata too, but only the page loader's reaches the head.

If no Node sidecar is ready and the browser renders the page itself, the document Netjes writes has the title, description and robots from C# only; the layouts' templates and the files' metadata apply once the page has rendered ([Rendering and streaming](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md)).

## The `lang` attribute

`<html lang>` is `NetjesOptions.Lang`, `en` by default. With [locale routing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#locales) it follows the request culture.

## Sitemap and robots

```csharp
var siteUrl = new Uri(app.Configuration["SiteUrl"] ?? "http://localhost:5080");
app.MapSitemap(siteUrl);
app.MapRobotsTxt(siteUrl);
app.MapPages();
```

`MapSitemap(siteUrl, cacheFor)` serves `/sitemap.xml`, the counterpart of `app/sitemap.ts`, from the route table:

- every page without parameters, and each dynamic page's URLs from its `.StaticParams(...)` ([Static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md));
- not the pages that require authorization, their own or through a fallback policy, unless they are `.AllowAnonymous()`;
- not the pages marked `.ExcludeFromSitemap()`.

URLs are absolute, under `siteUrl` and the app's base path, with the base path percent-encoded as a URL path. The list of pages is built at most once per `cacheFor` (an hour by default), so `StaticParams` does not run on every request. The XML is kept for the first eight base paths it is requested under in each `cacheFor`, which is one in a normal app. When the base path can come from a client (an `X-Forwarded-Prefix` the app accepts from untrusted addresses), any further one is built from the kept list on each request instead. Under a base path longer than 256 characters as the XML writes it (percent-encoded, with each `&` as `&amp;`), `/sitemap.xml` is not found (404, `Cache-Control: no-store`, logged at debug level) and nothing is built: every URL would repeat the base path, so one small request could ask for a large answer. The sitemap itself is sent with `Cache-Control: public, max-age` set to `cacheFor`.

`MapRobotsTxt(siteUrl, disallow)` serves `/robots.txt`: `Disallow` for each path given (or `Allow: /` when none is), and a `Sitemap:` line with the URL `MapSitemap` is served at: `/sitemap.xml` under `siteUrl` and the app's base path. Both endpoints allow anonymous requests. Both answer `HEAD` as well as `GET`, since crawlers and link checkers send `HEAD` too: a `HEAD` gets the status and headers of a `GET`, without the body ([HEAD requests](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#head-requests)). Each answers one spelling, as a page does: `/ROBOTS.TXT` and `/Sitemap.xml` get a 308 to `/robots.txt` and `/sitemap.xml`, and so do `/robots.txt/` and `/sitemap.xml/` under `TrailingSlash.Never` ([One URL per page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#one-url-per-page)).

`netjes export` writes both, as `sitemap.xml` and `robots.txt` ([static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md#sitemap-and-robotstxt)). The exported sitemap lists only pages the export writes, so it leaves out the pages marked `.ExcludeFromExport()`, which the sitemap the app serves still lists. Both files take their URLs from the `siteUrl` of the Production environment, which the export runs in, so the example's `http://localhost:5080` fallback would publish links to localhost: the export warns about a loopback `siteUrl`, and `SiteUrl=https://www.example.com npx netjes export` sets the right one. `.ExcludeFromExport()` on either call leaves its file out of the export.

Crawlers read `robots.txt` only at the root of the host. Under a base path, serve the root file from whatever answers the root, with the `Sitemap:` line from the app's own `robots.txt`. The `disallow` paths are written as given, so include the base path in them.

Leave `/_netjes/` out of `disallow`. `<Image>` serves every image through `/_netjes/image`, so a crawler that may not fetch it cannot index your images. The other endpoints there take posts (server actions and web vitals) or hand out an antiforgery token, which a crawler has no use for.

## Third-party scripts: `<Script>`

`<Script>` loads a third-party script, like `next/script`: `afterInteractive` and `lazyOnload` scripts do not block the page, and `beforeInteractive` ones run before the page's code. Each script is added to the document once, by its `id` or `src`, however many components render it, except inline `beforeInteractive` code, which the server writes wherever a component renders it. An `afterInteractive` or `lazyOnload` script renders nothing where it stands; a `beforeInteractive` one is written into the server-rendered document ([below](#code-that-runs-before-the-first-paint)).

```tsx
import { Script } from 'netjes';

<Script src="https://analytics.example/script.js" strategy="lazyOnload" onLoad={() => console.log('loaded')} />

<Script id="consent-defaults">{`window.dataLayer = window.dataLayer || [];`}</Script>
```

| `strategy` | When the script runs |
|---|---|
| `afterInteractive` (default) | Added once the page has hydrated. |
| `lazyOnload` | Added after the page's `load` event, when the browser is idle. |
| `beforeInteractive` | In a server-rendered document: inline code runs where it stands, as the parser reaches it, before what follows it is painted; an external script runs once the shell is parsed, in order with the others, before the page's own code and hydration. A component that mounts in the browser adds it as `afterInteractive` does. |

- Inline code goes in as the children, with an `id`, which a script without `src` needs.
- `onLoad` and `onError` are called once the script has loaded or failed, also for a component that renders a script another one added before it.
- Other attributes, such as `integrity`, `crossOrigin` or `data-*`, are set on the element.
- Under a [Content-Security-Policy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md) with a nonce, `<Script>` puts the page's nonce on the script. For an inline script of your own, read it with `useNonce()`.

### Code that runs before the first paint

A `beforeInteractive` script with inline code is written into the server's HTML where the component stands, so the browser runs it as its parser reaches it, before it parses or paints anything below it. That is the place for code the first paint depends on, such as a theme read from storage, set on `<html>` before any of the page shows:

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
import { type LayoutProps, Script } from 'netjes';

const theme = `
  let theme = 'light';
  try { theme = localStorage.getItem('theme') ?? (matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches ? 'dark' : 'light'); } catch {}
  document.documentElement.dataset.theme = theme;
`;

export default function RootLayout({ children }: LayoutProps) {
  return (
    <>
      <Script id="theme" strategy="beforeInteractive">{theme}</Script>
      {children}
    </>
  );
}
```

React leaves an attribute that such a script sets on `<html>` or `<body>` as it is when it hydrates the page ([Layouts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#layouts)). After a hydration error, React renders the page in the browser instead and replaces the attributes of both elements with its own, and the script does not run again.

- A browser runs inline code only once the stylesheets before it in the document have loaded, so it runs after the head's stylesheets, and before the page's own code. Put it first in the root layout, as above; a script takes no focus, so a skip link after it is still the first element Tab reaches.
- An external script (`src`) is preloaded from the head, so the browser fetches it while it parses the document. Once the shell is parsed, Netjes runs the external `beforeInteractive` scripts in it one after the other, in the order they stand in the document, with the page's nonce. They do not hold up the parser or the page's rendering: the page shows while they load. Hydration waits for them: the page's own modules run, and the page responds to clicks, once each of them has loaded or failed, so a host that is slow to answer delays the page's interactivity. A script the browser does not run, one with `noModule` or a `type` that is neither JavaScript nor `module`, such as the `text/plain` a consent manager looks for, is not preloaded and not waited for. It is still added to the head, with its `id` and attributes, where the consent manager finds it.
- All the inline code in the shell runs before any external script, so inline code cannot use what an external `beforeInteractive` script defines.
- A page with a `beforeInteractive` script runs its own modules once the shell is parsed, instead of while the rest of the shell arrives ([ADR 0044](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0044-before-interactive-scripts-run-before-the-pages-code.md)).
- Keep these scripts in the shell, outside any Suspense boundary that may still wait when the shell goes out (a `loading.tsx` included). In such a boundary, inline code runs when the boundary's content arrives, and an external script runs when that part of the page hydrates, not before the page's code.
- Render each one in one place, such as the root layout: a server-rendered document carries the inline code of every `beforeInteractive` script a component renders, so the same code rendered by two components runs twice. An external script runs once per `id`, or `src` when it has none, as with the other strategies.
- On a page the browser renders itself (after a client navigation, when no sidecar was ready, or in a `createTestApp()` test) a component that mounts adds the script after it mounts, as `afterInteractive` does. A script the server's document already ran is not added again.
- `onLoad` and `onError` are called once an external script has loaded or failed, and `onLoad` once inline code has run, after the component mounts.
- `async`, `defer` and `type="module"` do not apply. In development Netjes warns about them: an external script runs in order whatever `async` and `defer` say, and inline code with `type="module"` would wait until the whole document is parsed.
- Under a nonce-based policy the script carries the page's nonce. Under a hash-based one, list the hash of the inline code as the document carries it: Netjes writes the `s` of `<script` and `</script` (in any case) as `\u0073` (`\u0053` for `S`), as React does in its own scripts, so the code cannot end its element. JavaScript reads that as the same letter in strings, template literals, regular expressions and names, and the hash is of the text with it. Code without `<script` or `</script` in it is written as it is. A component that adds the code in the browser writes the same text, so the one hash allows it on both paths. `inlineScriptHashes(await renderDocument(...))` from `netjes/testing` lists the hash of each such script on a page ([the document](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md#the-document)), and an external script's host goes in `script-src` ([security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#hash-based)).

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md -->

# Static export

This guide is for app developers who want to publish a Netjes app, or part of one, as static files on a host without .NET: what `netjes export` writes, how dynamic pages list their URLs, what cannot be exported, the sitemap, `robots.txt` and other files from endpoints, and how exported pages behave in the browser, Content-Security-Policy included. It is the counterpart of Next.js's `output: 'export'`. The command's options are in the [CLI reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/cli.md#netjes-export).

## What the export does

```bash
npx netjes export          # builds, then writes out/
npx netjes export site     # into site/ instead
npx netjes export --no-build
```

`netjes export` builds the app (as `netjes build` does), runs it once in Production, and requests every page through it over HTTP: the same pipeline a visitor hits, so loaders, layout loaders, middleware and output caching apply as usual. It writes:

- `out/index.html` for `/`, and `out/<path>/index.html` for every other page,
- `out/404.html`, the not-found page,
- `out/sitemap.xml` and `out/robots.txt` when the app maps `MapSitemap` and `MapRobotsTxt`, the sitemap listing only pages the export writes ([below](#sitemap-and-robotstxt)),
- a file at its URL for each endpoint marked `.IncludeInExport()`, such as `out/llms.txt` ([below](#other-endpoints-as-files-includeinexport)),
- a copy of the client build (`dist/client`, without Vite's `.vite/` folder).

As with Next.js, the loaders run once, at export time. The pages then hydrate in the browser as usual.

## Dynamic pages: StaticParams

A page with route parameters is exported once for each set of values its loader lists with `.StaticParams(...)`, like `generateStaticParams`:

```csharp
app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, PostStore store) => /* ... */)
    .StaticParams<PostStore>(store => store.All.Select(post => new { slug = post.Slug }));

app.MapPageLoader("/docs/[...path]", (string path, DocsStore docs) => /* ... */)
    .StaticParams<DocsStore>(docs => docs.All.Select(doc => new { path = doc.Path.Split('/') }));
```

- One object per page, with a property for each route parameter. A catch-all takes an array of segments (or a string with `/` between them); an optional catch-all may leave it out.
- `.StaticParams<TService>(service => ...)` resolves the service for you; `.StaticParams(services => ...)` takes the `IServiceProvider`, in a scope of its own.
- Each value becomes a directory name, so it must not be empty, `.` or `..`, or contain `/`, `\`, `:` or a NUL character. The export refuses it otherwise.
- `MapSitemap` uses the same lists for the dynamic pages in `sitemap.xml` (see [metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md)).

Every listed page must answer 200. A loader that returns `Page.NotFound()` for a listed value fails the export, naming the URL.

## What cannot be exported

`.ExcludeFromExport()` leaves a page out, on its loader, its page action or `MapPages()`. On a layout loader, it leaves out every page below the layout:

```csharp
app.MapPageLoader("/guestbook", (GuestbookStore store) => /* ... */).ExcludeFromExport(); // needs a server
```

Without it, the export stops before it writes anything, naming each problem, when a page:

- is dynamic and has no `.StaticParams(...)`,
- has a page action (`MapPageAction`), since form posts need a server,
- requires authorization, through `RequireAuthorization()` on it or a layout loader above it, or through a fallback policy (unless the page is `.AllowAnonymous()`),
- would write the same file as another page on some file system: paths that differ only in case, Unicode normalisation or trailing dots and spaces, or a `.StaticParams` value that lands on another page's URL,
- would write the same file as `404.html`, the export's own `.netjes-export` marker or an endpoint written as a file ([below](#other-endpoints-as-files-includeinexport)), or needs a directory where one of those is a file,
- has a path segment that Windows reserves for a device (`con`, `nul.txt`, `com1`).

Server actions, minimal APIs that are not marked `.IncludeInExport()`, `/_netjes/antiforgery`, web vitals collection and the image endpoint have no static counterpart: an exported page that calls them gets the static host's 404. `<Image>` points its `src` and `srcset` at the image endpoint, so give images on exported pages `unoptimized`, which uses the file as it is.

### Loaders that read the query string

The export requests each URL without a query string, and a static host serves the file it wrote for every query string: `/blog?tag=react` gets `blog/index.html`, which the loader rendered with no tag. A page whose loader reads the query string is still exported, as the page without one, and the export logs a warning in the category `Netjes.Export.QueryString` for that loader. It does the same for a layout loader that reads the query string above a page it writes, naming the pages below the layout. The warning does not change the exit code (a loader that requires the value fails the export, as below):

```text
warn: Netjes.Export.QueryString[0]
      app/blog/page.tsx reads 'tag' from the query string, but netjes export writes /blog without one, and a static host serves that file for every query string. To export a page for each value, make it a route parameter with .StaticParams(...); to keep the page on a server, exclude it with .ExcludeFromExport().
```

There are two fixes:

- Make the value a route parameter and list its values with `.StaticParams(...)`: `/blog/tags/[tag]` instead of `/blog?tag=`, exported once for each tag.
- Keep the page on a server: `.ExcludeFromExport()` on its loader, or on the layout loader for every page below the layout.

If the page without a query string is what the static site should show, keep it, and set the category's log level to `Error` (`Logging:LogLevel:Netjes.Export.QueryString`, see [logs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md#logs)) to silence the warning. That silences it for every loader and every endpoint marked `.IncludeInExport()`, including those added later; the export's own messages, in `Netjes.Export.StaticExportService`, still appear.

A loader that requires the value cannot be exported as it is. A parameter with no default value and a type that is not nullable, such as `int page`, or `string q` with nullable reference types on, has to have one: minimal APIs answer 400 to the export's request without it, so the export fails on that page, and a layout loader that requires one fails every page below it. The warning then says so, names only the keys the loader requires, and adds a third fix: give the parameter a default value or a nullable type (`int page = 1`, `string? q`) to export the page without one. An array never requires a value: without one, it binds an empty array.

A parameter counts when minimal API binding takes its value from the query string: one marked `[FromQuery]`, which the warning names by the attribute's `Name` when it has one, or one without a binding attribute that is a string or a type with `TryParse` whose name is no route parameter's, or an array of those or `StringValues`, whatever its name, since a route value binds only to a single value (see [route warnings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#a-loader-parameter-that-reads-the-query-string-instead-of-a-route-value)). Members of an `[AsParameters]` type count as parameters. The check cannot see a loader that reads `HttpContext.Request.Query` itself, or a parameter whose type binds itself with `BindAsync`. A layout loader's warning names the pages below the layout and never `404.html`, which the export renders under the root layout too, so a root layout loader that reads the query string renders that file without one as well. Nor can it see code in the browser, where `useSearchParams()` sees no query string on an exported page either (see [In the browser](#in-the-browser)).

## Sitemap and robots.txt

An app that maps `MapSitemap` and `MapRobotsTxt` ([metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md#sitemap-and-robots)) gets both files in the export. The export requests them from the app after the pages, as it requests the pages, and writes what the app answers:

- `sitemap.xml` lists the pages the export writes, in the order it writes them: each page without parameters, and each dynamic page for every value of its `.StaticParams(...)`, except the pages marked `.ExcludeFromSitemap()`. A page marked `.ExcludeFromExport()` has no file on the static host, so the exported sitemap leaves it out, while the sitemap the app serves still lists it.
- `robots.txt` is the file the app serves: its `Disallow` or `Allow` lines and its `Sitemap:` line.

Both build their URLs from the `siteUrl` that the app passes to `MapSitemap` and `MapRobotsTxt` when it runs in the Production environment, which is the environment the export runs in. Pass the static host's URL there, for example from configuration, with the app reading `app.Configuration["SiteUrl"]`:

```bash
SiteUrl=https://www.example.com npx netjes export
```

When that URL is a loopback address, such as the `http://localhost:5080` that the [metadata guide's example](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md#sitemap-and-robots) falls back to, the export still writes both files, and logs a warning for each in `Netjes.Export.StaticExportService`, since their links would point at the machine of whoever opens them:

```text
warn: Netjes.Export.StaticExportService[0]
      /sitemap.xml is written with the site URL http://localhost:5080, a loopback address, so its links point at the machine of whoever opens them. Pass the static host's URL to MapSitemap and MapRobotsTxt in the Production environment that netjes export runs in, for example through configuration.
```

To leave either file out of the export, add `.ExcludeFromExport()` to its Map call: `app.MapSitemap(siteUrl).ExcludeFromExport()`. `robots.txt` always has a `Sitemap:` line, so when you leave the sitemap out, leave `MapRobotsTxt` out too, or its `Sitemap:` line names a file the static host does not have.

A `robots.txt` or `sitemap.xml` in `public/`, which the build copies into the client build, or one that a Vite plugin writes there, next to the matching Map call fails the export before it writes anything. The app serves the client build ahead of routing, so that file is what a server answers at the URL, and the endpoint never runs there. Remove the file or the Map call, or keep the file and add `.ExcludeFromExport()` to the Map call.

## Other endpoints as files: IncludeInExport

`.IncludeInExport()` writes a `GET` endpoint of the app into the export as a file at its URL, like a Next.js route handler with `dynamic = 'force-static'`. `MapSitemap` and `MapRobotsTxt` carry it already:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/llms.txt", (DocsStore docs) => Results.Text(docs.Index(), "text/plain")).IncludeInExport();
app.MapGroup("/feeds").MapGet("news.xml", (PostStore posts) => Results.Text(posts.Rss(), "application/rss+xml")).IncludeInExport();
```

The export requests each one after the pages and `404.html`, with a `GET` and no query string, and writes the body of a 200 byte for byte: `out/llms.txt` and `out/feeds/news.xml`, since a route group's prefix is part of the URL. Only the body is written. The response's headers, `Content-Type` and `Cache-Control` among them, are not, and the static host sends its own; most choose the type from the file's extension. Any other status, a redirect included, fails the export, naming the URL. `.ExcludeFromExport()` wins over `.IncludeInExport()` on the same endpoint, and `.IncludeInExport()` on a page's loader or on `MapPages()` changes nothing, since pages are exported anyway.

The export stops before it writes anything, naming the endpoint, when one marked `.IncludeInExport()`:

- does not answer `GET`, as one mapped with `MapPost` alone; `MapMethods` with `GET` among its methods counts, and so does `Map`, which answers every method,
- has route parameters, such as `/feeds/{name}.xml`, since the export writes each endpoint once,
- has a path segment that cannot be a file or directory name: `.`, `..`, or one with `\`, `:` or a NUL character,
- has a URL whose last segment has no file extension (`/feed` rather than `/feed.xml`), which a static host needs to send the file with its type,
- requires authorization, through `RequireAuthorization()` on it or on its route group, or through a fallback policy (unless it is `.AllowAnonymous()`),
- has the path of a file in the client build, such as one copied from `public/` ([above](#sitemap-and-robotstxt)), where paths that differ only in case, Unicode normalisation or trailing dots and spaces count as one, as Windows and macOS treat them,
- would write the same file as a page, `404.html`, the `.netjes-export` marker or another such endpoint, compared the same way, or would be a file where one of those needs a directory, or the other way round (`/notes.txt` next to `app/notes.txt/page.tsx`),
- has a path segment that Windows reserves for a device (`con.txt`).

An endpoint that reads the query string is written as it answers without one, and the export warns about it in `Netjes.Export.QueryString`, by the rules for page loaders ([above](#loaders-that-read-the-query-string)):

```text
warn: Netjes.Export.QueryString[0]
      GET /feed.xml reads 'tag' from the query string, but netjes export writes /feed.xml once, without one, and a static host serves that file for every query string. To keep it on a server, exclude it with .ExcludeFromExport().
```

One that requires a value there, through a parameter with no default value and a type that is not nullable, answers 400 to the export's request, so the export fails on it, and its warning says so.

## Where the output goes

The output directory is replaced as a whole, so it is checked before anything is written to it. It must be inside the app, and must not overlap `app/`, `public/`, `dist/` or the folder of the generated types. An existing directory is replaced only when it is empty or a previous export, which the export marks with a `.netjes-export` file. A folder name that starts with two dots, such as `..site`, is an ordinary name; only `..` itself means the folder above.

`netjes export` checks the first rule before it builds, against the project folder: the folder it runs in, with the app's `.csproj`, or the one `--cwd` names. On macOS and Linux it takes that folder by its real path, with any symlink resolved, as the app sees its own folder, and resolves a relative output folder against it. A folder outside the project folder, or the project folder itself, ends the command with exit code 1 before anything is built. On macOS and Windows that check ignores letter case, as .NET does. After the build, the app checks every rule before it renders a page, against `Netjes:Root`, which is the project folder unless it is set.

`netjes export --no-build` skips what `netjes build` does (the types and both Vite bundles) and the command's own check of the folder, and leaves every rule to the app. It still resolves a relative output folder against the project folder, by its real path on macOS and Linux, as above. So an app whose `Netjes:Root` is a folder above the project folder can export to a folder inside that one, such as `../site`; and a folder the app refuses costs a compile and a start before the export stops.

## Redirects

A page whose loader returns `Page.Redirect(url)` is written as a small page that refreshes to the target, with a link to it, the target written exactly as the loader sent it. Other redirects fail the export, naming the URL:

- a redirect the page did not make itself: a login redirect, HTTPS redirection, a URL rewriter rule,
- one that points at the export server's own address (use a relative URL),
- a target that is neither a path on the site nor an http(s) URL,
- a target that starts with a quote, which a meta refresh would drop.

## In the browser

Exported pages carry no antiforgery token, since there is no server to check it. They hydrate as usual, and links and `router.push` work, but every navigation is a full page load: the client router asks for the next page's data, gets a static HTML file instead, and loads it as a document. Assets are linked from the site root, so serve the export at the root of its host.

Query strings reach no loader, since the loaders ran at export time (see [above](#loaders-that-read-the-query-string)), and no hook either. On an exported page, `useSearchParams()` reads the URL the page was exported for, which has no query string, whatever the address bar shows: it returns an empty `URLSearchParams`, and with a schema, what the schema makes of no values. For the same reason, `<Link>` never marks a link with a query parameter as the current page there. Until the router reads the address itself, read `window.location.search` in an effect, and parse it with the schema you would give `useSearchParams`:

```tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';
import { z } from 'zod';

const filters = z.object({ tag: z.string().optional() });

// On an exported page: the query string in the address bar, once the page has hydrated.
function useExportedSearch() {
  const [search, setSearch] = useState<z.infer<typeof filters>>({});
  useEffect(() => {
    const parsed = filters.safeParse(Object.fromEntries(new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)));
    if (parsed.success) setSearch(parsed.data);
  }, []);
  return search;
}
```

The first render matches the exported HTML, as hydration needs, and the effect then renders the page again with the values. Every navigation on an exported site loads a document, so the effect runs for each URL. `Object.fromEntries` keeps the last value of a key that repeats; `getAll(key)` on the `URLSearchParams` reads every value.

The redirect of another spelling of a page's URL ([One URL per page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#one-url-per-page)) is the server's, and the export writes none. It requests each page at its file's spelling and writes it where it always has, `out/about/index.html` for `/about`, whatever `RedirectLiteralCase` and `TrailingSlash` say. What `/About` or `/about/` answers on a static host is up to that host.

## Deferred values and Suspense

Each page is exported as a complete document, the one crawlers get (see [rendering](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md#complete-documents)). The export waits for the page's `Page.Defer` values, up to `StreamTimeout`, and writes what they render in place of their Suspense fallback (`loading.tsx`, or a `<Suspense>` in the page), with no script to reveal it. So an exported page shows its deferred content without JavaScript, and under a static host's Content-Security-Policy that runs no inline script.

The values also follow in inline scripts, for the client to hydrate that content. Under a policy that blocks those scripts, the content shows on load but its boundary does not hydrate: the first update that renders the boundary again (a state change in the page around it) replaces it with the fallback, for good. Two ways out:

- keep `Page.Defer` out of exported pages that update around their deferred content, or
- list the scripts' hashes in the host's policy, next to `CSP_SCRIPT_HASHES` from `netjes`, the hashes of the inline scripts that every document carries with the same text, such as the bootstrap (`NetjesContentSecurityPolicy.ScriptHashes` in C#; see [security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#hash-based)). In an exported file those scripts are fixed text, and change only when a value does, so their hashes change only when you export again with other data.

A value that fails, or misses `StreamTimeout`, leaves its fallback in the file, and the nearest `error.tsx` replaces it once JavaScript runs. The export logs a warning and still succeeds.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/redirects-rewrites-headers.md -->

# Redirects, rewrites and headers

This guide is for app developers looking for what Next.js configures in `next.config.js`: `redirects`, `rewrites`, `headers`, `basePath` and `i18n`. In Netjes these are ASP.NET Core features, configured in `Program.cs` (or `appsettings.json`), next to authentication and the rest of the pipeline.

## Redirects

Next.js's `redirects()` is the URL Rewriting middleware, placed before `UseNetjes()`:

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Rewrite;

app.UseRewriter(new RewriteOptions()
    .AddRedirect("^old-blog/(.*)", "blog/$1", statusCode: StatusCodes.Status308PermanentRedirect)
    .AddRedirectToHttpsPermanent());
app.UseNetjes();
```

For redirects that depend on data (a renamed slug), return `Page.Redirect(...)` from the page's loader instead. It works for document requests and client navigations alike: the client router follows it without a full page load. See [security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#redirects) for the URLs it accepts, and `Page.LocalRedirect` for URLs that come from the request.

Netjes sends one redirect of its own: another case of a page's literal segments (`/About` to `/about`) and, with `TrailingSlash.Never`, a trailing slash, which is what Next.js's `trailingSlash` setting decides ([One URL per page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#one-url-per-page)). It runs at the end of `UseNetjes()`, after routing, on the URL the client sent, so it never redirects a request the rewriter changed. A canonical rule of the app's own, such as one that sends `www.example.com` to `example.com`, goes in the rewriter ahead of its rewrites, where it sees the URL as it was sent.

## Rewrites

Internal rewrites, where the URL stays and another page answers (Next.js's `rewrites()`), are the rewriter too:

```csharp
app.UseRewriter(new RewriteOptions().AddRewrite("^docs/latest/(.*)", "docs/v2/$1", skipRemainingRules: true));
```

The page answers at the URL the client sent, and Netjes does not redirect it to its file's spelling: under `TrailingSlash.Never`, `/docs/latest/intro/` is answered as it is, while `/docs/v2/intro/` goes to `/docs/v2/intro`.

Rewrites to another host (an external `destination` in Next.js) are a reverse proxy, such as [YARP](https://microsoft.github.io/reverse-proxy/) (MIT), mapped next to the pages:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddReverseProxy().LoadFromConfig(builder.Configuration.GetSection("ReverseProxy"));
// ...
app.MapReverseProxy(); // e.g. /api/legacy/{**rest} → https://legacy.example.com
```

## Headers

Netjes already sends `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` with every response that passes through `UseNetjes()`, so an app needs no middleware of its own for it, and `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` and `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` with every document (see [security headers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#security-headers)). It leaves out any of them that the app has set itself. An app that sends its own `X-Frame-Options`, as below, decides about framing alone: Netjes then adds neither framing header. With `frame-ancestors` in the app's policy, documents get the `X-Frame-Options` it implies, `DENY` or `SAMEORIGIN`, instead of the default `SAMEORIGIN`.

Set headers for all pages with a small middleware, or for some pages with an endpoint filter, where Next.js has `headers()`:

```csharp
app.Use((http, next) =>
{
    http.Response.Headers["X-Frame-Options"] = "DENY";
    http.Response.Headers["Permissions-Policy"] = "camera=(), microphone=()";
    return next(http);
});

app.MapPages().AddEndpointFilter(async (context, next) =>
{
    context.HttpContext.Response.Headers["X-Robots-Tag"] = "noindex";
    return await next(context);
});
```

For a Content-Security-Policy, use `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy` rather than a header of your own, so the nonce Netjes puts on its scripts matches the header, or call `HttpContext.GetCspNonce()` when you write the policy yourself. A policy with `{nonce}` keeps pages out of the output cache; a hash-based one lets them be cached, but its pages must not stream, and its `script-src` lists `NetjesContentSecurityPolicy.ScriptHashes`, the hashes of Netjes's inline scripts. [Security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#content-security-policy) explains both, and [static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md#deferred-values-and-suspense) what a static host's policy does to exported pages. NetEscapades.AspNetCore.SecurityHeaders (MIT) covers the other headers declaratively.

## Base path

Next.js's `basePath` is `UsePathBase` in .NET and the `basePath` option of the Vite plugin, set to the same value:

```csharp
app.UsePathBase("/docs"); // before UseNetjes()
```

```ts
netjes({ basePath: '/docs' }) // vite.config.ts: built asset URLs get the prefix
```

Write links, form actions, redirects and `router.push` paths as if the app were at the root; Netjes adds the base. `usePathname()` leaves it out. For a raw URL such as `<link rel="icon">`, prefix it yourself with `useBasePath()`, or build it with `useHref(path)`, as with Next.js. [Base path](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#base-path) in the routing guide has the rules.

## Internationalized routing

Next.js's `i18n` routing is a `[lang]` folder with Netjes's locale routing turned on ([Locales](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#locales) in the routing guide):

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNetjesLocalization(o => o.SupportedCultures = ["en", "nl"]); // the first is the default
builder.Services.AddLocalization();
// ...
app.UseNetjes();
app.UseNetjesLocalization(); // after UseNetjes: it reads the [lang] route value
app.MapLocaleRedirect();     // "/" → "/nl" for a Dutch browser
```

Loaders run with `CultureInfo.CurrentCulture` set, so formatting and `IStringLocalizer<T>` follow the URL.

- Only the URL decides. Pages outside `[lang]` get the default culture, not one from a cookie or `Accept-Language`, because an output-cached copy would otherwise serve the first visitor's language to everyone. If such pages are not cached and should follow the browser, add `AcceptLanguageHeaderRequestCultureProvider` to `RequestLocalizationOptions.RequestCultureProviders` yourself (and vary any caching by `Accept-Language`).
- Netjes turns off parent-culture fallback, so a name matches only a configured culture exactly: list `nl-BE` as well as `nl` if both should match. The `/` redirect from `MapLocaleRedirect` is separate: it sends an `nl-BE` browser to `/nl`.
- An unsupported locale renders the 404 page in the default culture. Any other endpoint whose route has the locale parameter (a minimal API at `/{lang}/api/...`) answers a bare 404 for one too, so give a parameter that is not a locale another name.
- A supported locale in another case (`/EN/about`) reaches loaders and `params.lang` as configured (`en`).
- The route parameter is `lang` unless you set `NetjesLocalizationOptions.RouteParameter`.

The document's `<html lang>` follows the locale, and `useLocale()` returns it in React. Send the page's strings through shared props:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNetjes(options => options.UseSharedProps(http =>
{
    var strings = http.RequestServices.GetRequiredService<IStringLocalizer<SharedResource>>();
    return ValueTask.FromResult(new SiteStrings(strings.GetAllStrings().ToDictionary(s => s.Name, s => s.Value)));
}));

public sealed record SiteStrings(Dictionary<string, string> Messages);
```

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md -->

# Security

This guide is for app developers putting a Netjes app in front of real users. It lists what Netjes does by default and what is left to you: the security headers, Content-Security-Policy, the antiforgery and origin checks on actions, request body limits, redirects, the image endpoint, the Node sidecar, the secret that signs layout keys, host names and HTTPS, and the development server. To report a vulnerability, follow [SECURITY.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/SECURITY.md).

## Defaults at a glance

| What | Default | Change it with |
|---|---|---|
| `X-Content-Type-Options` on every response through `UseNetjes()`; `Referrer-Policy` and framing headers on documents | On | `Netjes:SecurityHeaders` |
| Content-Security-Policy | Off | `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy` |
| Antiforgery token and same-origin check on server actions and page actions | On | `.DisableAntiforgery()` on a page action; `AllowedActionOrigins` |
| Server action body limit | 1 MB | `ActionBodySizeLimit`, `[RequestSizeLimit]` |
