| Fields a failed form hands back | Only declared ones, never private ones | `PrivateFormFields` |
| `Cache-Control` on pages | `no-store, private` | Your own header; see [caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md) |
| Error details in error pages | Development only | `IncludeErrorDetails` |
| Remote images | None allowed | `Netjes:Images:RemoteHosts` |
| Layout key secret | Random per process | `SegmentKeySecret` |
| HSTS, HTTPS redirection, `AllowedHosts` | ASP.NET Core's; the template turns on HSTS and HTTPS redirection outside Development | ASP.NET Core |

## Security headers

Every HTML document Netjes renders (pages, not-found and error pages, the plain fallback error page) carries these, unless the app has set that header itself:

| Header | Value |
|---|---|
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | `nosniff` |
| `Referrer-Policy` | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` |
| `X-Frame-Options` | `SAMEORIGIN`, or what the policy's `frame-ancestors` implies (below) |
| `Content-Security-Policy` | `frame-ancestors 'self'` added to `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy` when you set one without `frame-ancestors`, unless the app sent `X-Frame-Options` |

Every other response that passes through `UseNetjes()` gets `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` too: client payloads (JSON), static files from `public/` and the client build, `robots.txt`, `sitemap.xml`, `/_netjes/antiforgery`, the app's own endpoints, and answers from the output cache. Under a policy such as `script-src 'self'`, any response from the app's origin can be loaded as a script or a stylesheet, and with `nosniff` the browser refuses to run a script whose `Content-Type` is missing or not a JavaScript type, or to apply a stylesheet whose `Content-Type` is missing or not `text/css`. Nor does it take a response with no `Content-Type` for HTML: a page that an endpoint writes itself with `Response.WriteAsync` shows as plain text, and none of its scripts run, unless the endpoint sets `Response.ContentType = "text/html; charset=utf-8"` first. Netjes adds it as the response starts, only when the response does not have it by then, so a value the app sets is kept and an answer from the output cache carries it once. A response that middleware registered before `UseNetjes()` writes itself, without passing the request on, does not get it. These responses get none of the other headers in the table. The image endpoint sends `nosniff` and a sandboxing Content-Security-Policy of its own, whatever `Enabled` says (see [the image endpoint](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/images.md#the-image-endpoint)).

An app that sends `X-Frame-Options` itself decides about framing alone: Netjes adds neither framing header, so nothing contradicts it.

An app with `frame-ancestors` in a Content-Security-Policy that goes out (its own header, or else `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy`) gets the `X-Frame-Options` that the directive implies, for browsers that know only that header, and no `frame-ancestors` from Netjes:

| `frame-ancestors` | `X-Frame-Options` |
|---|---|
| `'none'`, an empty list, or other sites only, such as `https://partner.example` | `DENY` |
| `'self'`, `*` or a scheme source such as `https:`, with or without other sites | `SAMEORIGIN` |

Every policy counts, whether it comes in a header of its own or joined to others by commas, and the strictest decides: when one of them implies `DENY`, the document gets `DENY`. A `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` header does not count. Directive names and keywords such as `'self'` are compared ignoring case. Browsers obey `frame-ancestors` over `X-Frame-Options`, which cannot name another site, so to let a partner frame your pages, send `frame-ancestors 'self' https://partner.example`: browsers that support `frame-ancestors` let the partner frame them, and a browser that knows only `X-Frame-Options` keeps them to your own site.

Netjes sets `X-Frame-Options` on a document before the visitor's antiforgery cookie is stored. ASP.NET Core antiforgery adds `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` with each new token cookie, but only to a response that has no `X-Frame-Options` yet, so on documents it adds none: a visitor's first page, a returning visitor's, and a page from the output cache all get the same header. Four limits remain:

- A host source that names your own site counts as another site: `frame-ancestors https://www.example.com` on `https://www.example.com` gets `DENY`. Netjes does not compare sources with the request's host, which behind a proxy is not always the one the browser sees. Write `'self'` for your own site.
- Code that stores antiforgery tokens before the page renders, such as a loader or a middleware that calls `IAntiforgery.GetAndStoreTokens`, has antiforgery add its `SAMEORIGIN` to a visitor's first page before Netjes decides, and Netjes keeps it as the app's own. Set `AntiforgeryOptions.SuppressXFrameOptionsHeader = true` to have Netjes follow the policy there too.
- Netjes decides when the page renders, so it does not see a policy that a middleware writes later, in a `Response.OnStarting` callback. Set such a policy before the page renders, or send `X-Frame-Options` yourself.
- A page whose loader or render throws is answered with its error page on a cleared response, so the headers set before the exception are gone, your own `Content-Security-Policy` and `X-Frame-Options` included. That error page gets `SAMEORIGIN`, or the `X-Frame-Options` that the `frame-ancestors` of `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy` implies, with the option's policy. To have your policy on those pages too, set it in `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy`.

On responses that are not documents, and on every response with `Enabled = false`, antiforgery still adds its `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` with each new token cookie; `AntiforgeryOptions.SuppressXFrameOptionsHeader` turns it off.

`NetjesOptions.SecurityHeaders` (`Netjes:SecurityHeaders`) has two settings:

- `Enabled = false` turns all of them off, `nosniff` on the other responses included; the image endpoint keeps its own. To preview the app in an editor's frame, such as VS Code's Simple Browser, set it in `appsettings.Development.json`, and turn off the header that antiforgery adds in code, since ASP.NET Core does not bind `AntiforgeryOptions` from configuration:

  ```json
  { "Netjes": { "SecurityHeaders": { "Enabled": false } } }
  ```

  ```csharp
  if (builder.Environment.IsDevelopment())
  {
      builder.Services.AddAntiforgery(o => o.SuppressXFrameOptionsHeader = true);
  }
  ```

- `DraftFrameAncestors = ["https://cms.example"]` lets those sites frame pages in [draft mode](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md#draft-mode), for a CMS that shows the preview in a frame. Draft documents then get `frame-ancestors 'self' https://cms.example` (in Netjes's own policy, or a header with only that directive) and keep `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, which still holds if a middleware rewrites the policy without `frame-ancestors`. A browser without `frame-ancestors` support cannot show the preview. Published pages stay same-origin. It is ignored when the app sets its own `X-Frame-Options` or `Content-Security-Policy`, or has `frame-ancestors` in `ContentSecurityPolicy`; put the sites there instead. Each entry must be one CSP source, such as `https://cms.example` or `https://*.cms.example`; anything else stops the app at startup.

To send other headers, or other values on some pages, see [redirects, rewrites and headers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/redirects-rewrites-headers.md#headers).

## Content-Security-Policy

Netjes sends no Content-Security-Policy until you set `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy`. It then sets the header on every document, unless the app sent one itself, with `frame-ancestors 'self'` added when the policy has no `frame-ancestors`. There are two kinds of policy, and the choice depends on whether your pages are output-cached.

### Nonce-based

Put `{nonce}` where the per-request nonce goes:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNetjes(options =>
    options.ContentSecurityPolicy = "script-src 'nonce-{nonce}' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'");
```

Netjes makes a nonce for each document and puts it on everything it renders: the module scripts and preloads, the stylesheets, the payload, the scripts that stream deferred values and reveal Suspense boundaries, and Vite's `csp-nonce` meta (for the styles Vite injects in development). `useNonce()` returns it for inline scripts or styles of your own, and `<Script>` uses it. A `beforeInteractive` `<Script>` with a `src` is written into the document as an entry that the client entry turns into a script, with the nonce, before the page hydrates ([code that runs before the first paint](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md#code-that-runs-before-the-first-paint)). The client entry takes only entries that carry the document's nonce, so markup that reaches the page some other way, such as HTML from a user that a sanitizer let through, cannot make it run a script.

A document with a nonce is never stored in the output cache: a stored copy would give every visitor the same, readable nonce. Netjes renders such a page each time and logs a warning once per output-cached page. For cached pages, use a hash-based policy.

If you write the policy yourself, for example with a headers library, call `HttpContext.GetCspNonce()` for the request's nonce, before the page renders, and Netjes puts the same one on what it renders. A nonce the library makes itself is on none of it, so browsers refuse what the rest of the policy does not allow, and Netjes warns about it ([what Netjes checks](#what-netjes-checks)). The output cache rule applies to that nonce as well.

### Hash-based

A policy without `{nonce}` makes no nonce, so pages under it can be output-cached. It must allow, by their hashes, the inline scripts that Netjes writes with the same text into every document. `NetjesContentSecurityPolicy.ScriptHashes` lists those hashes:

```csharp
options.ContentSecurityPolicy =
    $"script-src 'self' {NetjesContentSecurityPolicy.ScriptHashes}; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'";
```

`ScriptHashes` holds a `'sha256-…'` source for each such script, in its quotes and separated by spaces. In this version there is one, the bootstrap in the head that collects streamed values, so the value is `'sha256-FSjVV+FzmXP8KKrLKLdvst/5N/bEWSkde01XzpGKRgs='`. A Netjes version that changes the bootstrap, or adds a script like it, changes the value. So build the policy from `ScriptHashes` rather than pasting the hash: a pasted hash would block the script after such an upgrade. A policy written in JavaScript, such as a static host's headers for [exported pages](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md), gets the same value from the npm package: `import { CSP_SCRIPT_HASHES } from 'netjes'`.

Keep `'self'`: a hash allows only the inline script it was computed from, and the built app's module scripts are files the app serves, which `'self'` allows. Leave out `'strict-dynamic'`, which needs a nonce here: next to it, browsers ignore `'self'`, and the module scripts carry no nonce under this policy and no `integrity` attribute for a hash to match, so browsers refuse them and the page does not hydrate. Inline `<Script>` code of your own needs its hash listed too: for `afterInteractive` and `lazyOnload`, the hash of the code as you passed it; for `beforeInteractive`, the hash of the code as the document carries it, which differs where the code holds `<script` or `</script` ([code that runs before the first paint](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/metadata.md#code-that-runs-before-the-first-paint)). An external `<Script>` from another origin needs that origin in `script-src`, as any other script from there does. Without a nonce, the client entry turns every entry of an external `beforeInteractive` script in the document into a script, one in HTML from a user that a sanitizer let through included: the hosts the policy allows bound what such markup can load, so list only those the app needs, and let no `<script>` element through a sanitizer.

In the Development environment the module scripts come from the Vite dev server, on another origin, so a policy without a nonce lists that origin as well; [in development](#in-development) shows how.

A form action that is a function makes React add an inline script of its own, which replays a submission made before the page hydrates. A server action from `useAction` in `<Form action>` adds none, since Netjes renders that form with the action's URL. Any other function does, in `<Form action>`, in `<SubmitButton formAction>` (server actions included) or on a plain `<form>` or `<button>`. The script's text follows the React version, so `ScriptHashes` leaves it out. List its hash for the React version you run (Chromium names the hash in the console when it blocks the script), or keep such actions off pages under the policy. While the script is blocked, a submission made before the page hydrates is lost; after hydration, React runs the action without it.

No hash covers what streams after the shell: each script that delivers a `Page.Defer` value carries that value, and React's scripts that reveal Suspense boundaries name the boundaries of that render. A hash-based policy blocks both, so a page served under one must not stream: no `Page.Defer`, and no Suspense boundary still waiting when the shell goes out (lazy code under `loading.tsx` included). Pages from `netjes export` are the exception, since their scripts are fixed text; see [static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md#deferred-values-and-suspense).

### zod in the browser

Neither kind of policy needs `'unsafe-eval'` for zod. In the browser, the client entry turns zod's compiled parsers off (zod's `jitless` setting) before any of the app's modules run, in development, in production and in exported pages ([ADR 0036](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0036-zod-runs-without-compiled-parsers-in-the-browser.md)). Without that, zod would compile each object schema's parser into a function made from a string, after testing once whether it may. A policy refuses the test when its `script-src` leaves out `'unsafe-eval'`, as both policies above do, or when it has no `script-src` and its `default-src` leaves it out; a policy with neither directive lets zod compile. Although zod catches the error and the page works, the browser reports the refusal as a violation of `script-src` (blocked URI `eval`) on every document: it fires a `securitypolicyviolation` event, and sends a report to the policy's `report-uri` or `report-to` endpoint when it has one. Chromium logs nothing to the console for it when the policy has a `script-src`. When the policy leaves scripts to `default-src`, Chromium logs one error, which reads in full "Note that 'script-src' was not explicitly set, so 'default-src' is used as a fallback."

This holds in every browser, with or without a policy, for every zod object schema made in the page: the generated props schemas that `definePage` and `defineLayout` parse with, `api[...].response.parse(...)`, and the app's own search-param and form schemas. A Web Worker has a global object of its own, which the setting does not reach: a worker of the app's own that parses with zod calls `z.config({ jitless: true })` before it makes a schema. Netjes has no setting to keep the compiled parsers. An app's own call of zod's `z.compile(schema)` is left alone: it makes a function from a string whatever the setting says, so a policy that refuses zod's test reports it.

The cost shows where one schema parses many objects: a list of 1,000 small objects takes about 0.5 ms to parse, against about 0.09 ms with compiled parsers. A new schema's first parse of one object, such as a page's props, is faster, since nothing is compiled.

It takes zod 4.4.0 or newer, which reads the setting however many copies of zod the page loads. zod 4.0 to 4.3 do not read it, and still test once per document: upgrade zod to 4.4.0 or newer (an app made with `netjes new` asks for `^4.6.7`). Server rendering in the Node sidecar, and the app's Vitest tests, do not run the client entry, so they keep the compiled parsers.

### What Netjes checks

Netjes sends the policy as written, in every environment, and compares it with what each document needs. When it refuses something, `Netjes.Rendering.PageRenderer` logs a warning that names the directive and what to change, once per policy (a nonce that changes from document to document does not make it another policy). Every policy in the `Content-Security-Policy` header that goes out counts, your own or `NetjesOptions.ContentSecurityPolicy`, several joined by commas included. A report-only policy does not count, and nor does a policy that a middleware writes in a `Response.OnStarting` callback, after the page renders. The warnings are about:

- the scripts, in the list that script elements follow: `script-src-elem`, else `script-src`, else `default-src`. A list that holds the document's nonce allows them all, since Netjes puts that nonce on every script it writes. Netjes warns when any other list refuses the bootstrap (it holds neither every hash in `ScriptHashes` nor `'unsafe-inline'` without a hash, a nonce or `'strict-dynamic'` beside it), has `'strict-dynamic'`, which leaves the module scripts nothing to be allowed by, or refuses the module scripts (it holds none of `'self'`, `*`, `http:`, `https:` or a host source). Netjes does not judge which host a host source names: behind a proxy, the request's host is not always the one the browser sees. So a list of other hosts only gets no warning, and nor does `self` without its quotes, which browsers read as a host named `self`. When the list is `default-src`, a warning says to add the missing source there; a `script-src` added instead takes the place of `default-src` for every script, so it needs `'self'` as well;
- a nonce that is not the document's, such as one your own code makes without `GetCspNonce()`. It is on none of what Netjes renders, and next to it `'unsafe-inline'` does not count, so when the rest of its list refuses one of the scripts, or in Development the inlined styles, Netjes warns once, about the nonce;
- in Development, the Vite dev server's scripts, its socket and the inlined styles ([in development](#in-development)).

A policy that allows all of it, but blocks something else, such as a script that streams a deferred value, gets no warning. Netjes compares no more than about 100 different policies, so an app that writes another one for each request does not make it keep them all. The static export (`netjes export`) is not checked: its files go out under the static host's policy.

### In development

In the Development environment the browser loads the page's module scripts from the Vite dev server, on another origin than the app's, and Vite's client in the page opens a WebSocket to it, which brings your edits to the page (hot module replacement). Netjes keeps the policy as written there too, so a policy also has to allow these:

- **The dev server's scripts.** The document's nonce in `script-src` covers them, from `{nonce}` or `GetCspNonce()`: Netjes puts it on `@vite/client` and on the client entry, and the modules they load inherit it. A list without it lists the dev server's origin, or browsers refuse the scripts and the page does not hydrate. The origin is `http://localhost:5173`, on another port when `ViteDevPort` (`Netjes:ViteDevPort`) moves it, or the one in `NETJES_VITE_ORIGIN` when browsers reach the dev server at another address.
- **The socket.** A policy with `connect-src`, or with `default-src` and no `connect-src`, lists the socket's address in it: `ws://` and the dev server's host and port, such as `ws://localhost:5173` (`wss://` for an `https` origin), or `ws:`. A nonce does not cover connections, `'self'` stands for the app's own origin, whose port is another, and an `http://` source never matches a `ws://` address. Without it, browsers refuse the socket, and an edit shows only once you reload the page. When `server.hmr` in the Vite config moves the socket (its `host`, `port`, `clientPort` or `protocol`), list the address it gives instead.
- **The styles.** In Development the document carries the app's CSS inline, in `<style>` elements, and Vite's client adds more of them as modules load and change. Both carry the nonce when the document has one (Vite reads it from the `csp-nonce` meta). So the list that style elements follow, `style-src-elem`, else `style-src`, else `default-src`, needs that nonce or `'unsafe-inline'`, which counts only with no hash or nonce beside it; otherwise pages show without their styles. A client build links its CSS as files instead.
- **Images and fonts.** Vite serves the files the app imports, such as the URL that `import logo from './logo.png'` gives, and the files its CSS names with `url()`, from the dev server's origin too. So a policy with `img-src` or `font-src`, or with `default-src` and not them, lists that origin there, or those files do not load. `media-src` does the same for imported audio and video.

Netjes warns about the first three once per policy; it cannot see which images or fonts a page uses, so it does not check those. Under a policy without `'unsafe-eval'`, the browser can also report a violation of `script-src` with the blocked URI `eval` in Development, from the development code of React or Vite rather than from zod. The page still hydrates, the built app does not report it, and Netjes does not check for `'unsafe-eval'`. The simplest policy for Development is none: set the policy outside Development only.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNetjes(options =>
{
    if (!builder.Environment.IsDevelopment())
    {
        options.ContentSecurityPolicy =
            $"script-src 'self' {NetjesContentSecurityPolicy.ScriptHashes}; connect-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'";
    }
});
```

To try the policy in Development as well, widen it there with the dev server's origin and its socket:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNetjes(options =>
{
    var scripts = $"'self' {NetjesContentSecurityPolicy.ScriptHashes}";
    var connections = "'self'";
    if (builder.Environment.IsDevelopment())
    {
        // The Vite dev server, which serves the scripts there, and its socket, on the same host and port unless
        // server.hmr in the Vite config moves it.
        var devServer = new Uri(builder.Configuration["NETJES_VITE_ORIGIN"] ?? $"http://localhost:{options.ViteDevPort}");
        scripts += $" {devServer.GetLeftPart(UriPartial.Authority)}";
        connections += $" {(devServer.Scheme == "https" ? "wss" : "ws")}://{devServer.Authority}";
    }

    options.ContentSecurityPolicy = $"script-src {scripts}; connect-src {connections}; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'";
});
```

A policy with `style-src` adds `'unsafe-inline'` to it in Development in the same way, and one with `img-src`, `font-src` or `default-src` the dev server's origin.

## Server actions and page actions

Every server action (`MapAction`) and page action (`MapPageAction`) needs a valid ASP.NET Core antiforgery token and a same-origin request. Put `app.UseAntiforgery()` in the pipeline, after authentication. `<Form>`, `useAction` and `serverAction()` send the token; pages that carry none (output-cached ones) fetch it from `/_netjes/antiforgery` first.

- A token the server refuses: a client call gets 400 with `X-Netjes-Antiforgery: invalid`, which no other response carries, and the client sends that call once more with a fresh token (no other 400 proves that the action did not run). A post without JavaScript gets the 400 error page.
- The origin check, like Next.js's, compares the request's `Origin` with its `Host`, and refuses a request the browser marks `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` whatever its origin: 403. `Origin: null` passes only when the browser also says `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`. `NetjesOptions.AllowedActionOrigins` lists more origins, for a same-site origin such as a sibling subdomain; a cross-site post is refused even when its origin is listed.
- Behind a proxy that rewrites `Host`, every action fails the origin check until the app sees its public host. Use `UseForwardedHeaders`, or list the public origin in `AllowedActionOrigins`.

A page action that receives a form posted from another site (a payment or identity provider posting back) can turn both checks off with `.DisableAntiforgery()`. Check the post some other way, such as the provider's signature. On a server action `.DisableAntiforgery()` turns off the token check only; its origin check stays.

The antiforgery cookie keeps ASP.NET Core's defaults (`SameSite=Strict`, `HttpOnly`), so the same app works over plain HTTP in development. An app served only over HTTPS should make it a `__Host-` cookie, which a sibling subdomain or a plain-HTTP response cannot set or replace:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddAntiforgery(o =>
{
    o.Cookie.Name = "__Host-Antiforgery";
    o.Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always;
    o.Cookie.Path = "/"; // __Host- cookies need it, also under UsePathBase
});
```

With `SecurePolicy.Always`, ASP.NET Core refuses every antiforgery operation on a request that is not HTTPS (a 500), so behind a TLS-terminating proxy call `UseForwardedHeaders` first, and keep the default in development.

### Body limits

A server action's request body may be at most 1 MB (`NetjesOptions.ActionBodySizeLimit`, like Next.js's `serverActions.bodySizeLimit`); a larger one gets 413. The option only lowers the server's own limit (Kestrel's is 30 MB). Page actions keep the server's limit. An action that takes uploads sets its own with `[RequestSizeLimit(bytes)]`. [Body limits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md#body-limits) has the details.

### What a failed post hands back

A form whose action fails validation comes back with what was typed, so the user does not type it again. Only the fields the action declares come back, never files, and never a field whose name contains one of the words in `NetjesOptions.PrivateFormFields` (`password`, `token`, `card`, `pin`, `iban` and more). What comes back goes out `Cache-Control: no-store`: the page rendered again, or a server action's answer to a call from the client. [What a failed post hands back](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md#what-a-failed-post-hands-back) has the default words, how they match and the size limits.

The return page of a post without JavaScript is always a page of the app: a return URL that routes anywhere else renders the home page (or the error page with 422, where `/` is no page either). Middleware registered before `UseNetjes()` does not run again for that render, so protect pages with endpoint authorization, not with middleware ahead of `UseNetjes()` ([Forms without JavaScript](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md#forms-without-javascript)).

## Redirects

`Page.Redirect(url)` and `ServerAction.Redirect(url)` accept relative URLs and absolute `http` and `https` URLs, and throw for anything else, including a `%` before the first `:` or `/`, which could hide an encoded scheme (`javascript%3A`). Start a relative URL with `/` or `./`.

For a URL that comes from the request, such as a `returnUrl` query value, use `Page.LocalRedirect(url)`: it throws unless the URL is a path on this site (`/path`, not `//host` or `/\host`). `Page.IsLocalUrl(url)` checks one first, so you can fall back instead:

```csharp
return Page.IsLocalUrl(returnUrl) ? Page.LocalRedirect(returnUrl) : Page.Redirect("/");
```

The client router never loads a page from another origin: a redirect or link to another site is a full page load, handed to the browser.

Netjes's own redirect of another spelling of a page's URL ([One URL per page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#one-url-per-page)) is built from the URL the client sent, and never sends a location that could lead off the site. Under a root catch-all with `TrailingSlash.Never`, `//other.example/` would go to `//other.example`, `/\other.example/` to `/\other.example`, and `/%5Cother.example/` to a location that a client which decodes it reads as `/\other.example`: each of them is answered as it was sent, without a redirect. So is a URL whose location would hold a backslash, which browsers read as a slash, a `#`, which ends the path, a control character such as a tab, which browsers drop, or a character beyond ASCII, and one whose base path comes from a header, such as an `X-Forwarded-Prefix` taken from anyone, and would make the location start with `//` or `/\`.

## The image endpoint

`/_netjes/image` serves only the widths and qualities you configure, reads local images from `public/` only and only as their files are spelled, fetches remote images only from the hosts in `Netjes:Images:RemoteHosts` (https on the default port, public addresses only, no redirects followed, no proxy, within a size cap and a timeout), serves only PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP and AVIF bytes (SVG only with `AllowSvg`, sandboxed), and bounds how many images it reads, fetches and processes at once. The [images guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/images.md) has every limit and setting.

With `Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp`, native codecs parse whatever a file in `public/` or an allow-listed host holds, even limited to PNG, JPEG and WebP. Keep SkiaSharp current: when a fix ships before `Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp` moves to it, reference the newer `SkiaSharp` and `SkiaSharp.NativeAssets.Linux.NoDependencies` packages from your project.

## The Node sidecar

The Node processes that render pages listen on `127.0.0.1` only, on a random port. Each gets a random token from .NET when it starts and refuses every request without it (403); a process does not start without one. The process removes the token from its environment before any page code runs. If you start `sidecar/server.mjs` yourself, set `NETJES_TOKEN` to a non-empty value and send it as the `X-Netjes-Token` header.

Page code that runs on the server runs in those processes, not in .NET. It sees the environment the app was started with, except the token.

## The layout key secret

On client navigations the router sends keys for the layouts it already shows, and the server skips the loaders of those layouts while the keys still match. A key is an HMAC of the layout's folder, the build, the user (authentication type, name, identifier and roles) and the layout's own route values, signed with `NetjesOptions.SegmentKeySecret`, so a client cannot make up a key for a layout it was not given, or reuse one across users.

- By default the secret is random per process. Set it, at least 32 bytes, when several instances should accept each other's keys (see [deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md#several-instances)); a shorter one stops the app at startup. Keep it out of source control like any secret.
- A layout loader binds only the route values of its own URL, and is skipped while they and the user stay the same. So an access check on a route value deeper than the layout's URL belongs in the page's loader, which runs on every navigation. [Data loading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md) explains this.

## Hosts and HTTPS

- `AllowedHosts`: the template's `appsettings.json` allows any host (`*`), and its `appsettings.Development.json` allows only `localhost;127.0.0.1;[::1]`, so a page that rebinds its DNS name to your machine cannot reach the dev app. Pin `AllowedHosts` to your host names in production: the output cache keys entries on the host, and every made-up host would otherwise get entries of its own.
- HSTS and HTTPS redirection are ASP.NET Core's. The template calls `UseHsts()` and `UseHttpsRedirection()` outside Development.
- Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, call `UseForwardedHeaders()` first, trusting only that proxy's network, so the app sees the original scheme, host and client address. [Deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md#proxies-and-base-paths) has an example.

## Errors and configuration

- Error pages show exception messages and stacks only in Development (`IncludeErrorDetails`). In production an `error.tsx` gets the status's reason phrase as `error.message`, marked with `error.withheld`, and no stack. A failed `Page.Defer` value goes to the browser with an empty message, and a server action's 5xx with none; the browser marks both as withheld.
- Everything in `Netjes:PublicConfig` is sent to the browser as it is. Never put a secret there.
- The generated file names the app's endpoints: `api` its JSON endpoints, and `endpointUrl()` the method and route of each endpoint that has a key, an endpoint the app maps only in Development included, since the file is generated in Development. The routes are one map in that file, so once any component calls `endpointUrl`, all of them reach the browser in the chunk that holds the file. Pages share that chunk, usually through the root layout, so expect every page to load it, also one that never calls `endpointUrl`. While nothing calls it, the build leaves the map out. `api` ships its keys the same way. A route in the file is no easier to reach than one outside it: authorization stays on the endpoint (`RequireAuthorization()`) ([Endpoint URLs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md#endpoint-urls)).
- Output-cached pages are served to every visitor; keep per-visitor data out of them. See [caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md#shared-props-and-cookies).

## The development server

The Vite dev server binds to `localhost`. `NETJES_VITE_HOST=0.0.0.0` (in the environment of `npm run dev`) exposes it to the network, and with it the workspace. The Vite plugin denies the backend's files to the dev server, on top of Vite's own list (`.env` files, certificates, `.git`): settings files, C# sources and build output, dev certificates and keys, SQLite databases and Compose files, all listed in the [Vite plugin reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/vite-plugin.md#the-dev-server). Everything else under the workspace root (or your own `server.fs.allow`) is readable by anyone who can reach the port, so only expose it on a network you trust. The template's development Compose file binds its ports to `127.0.0.1`.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md -->

# Testing

This guide is for app developers writing tests for a Netjes app: component and page tests in Vitest with the `netjes/testing` harness, tests of C# loaders and actions with `WebApplicationFactory`, end-to-end tests in Playwright, and the checks to run in CI. An app made with `netjes new` has two component tests to start from, in `components/`, and a test of the home page's whole document, `app/document.test.ts`.

## Vitest

The template runs Vitest with `npm test` (`vitest run`). The `netjes()` Vite plugin sets these defaults under Vitest, each only when the app's own `test` config does not set it:

- `environment: 'jsdom'`, when `jsdom` is installed;
- `exclude`: `node_modules/`, `dist/`, `bin/`, `obj/`, `e2e/` (Playwright's folder) and `.git/`;
- a setup file that unmounts what each test rendered (Testing Library's `cleanup`), when `@testing-library/react` is installed and the app sets no `setupFiles` of its own. An app that sets them lists `netjes/testing/setup` there itself.

Whatever the app's config says, it also adds two settings to it:

- a setup file of its own, in `setupFiles` after the app's own setup files. It lets Testing Library work with Vitest's fake timers ([Fake timers](#fake-timers)), and hands `createTestApp()` the app's query defaults;
- `provide['netjes:query']`: the `defaultOptions` of `netjes({ query })` (`{}` when there are none, and nothing with `query: false`), which that setup file reads ([Queries that fail](#queries-that-fail)). The app's own `provide` keys stay as they are.

There is no `include` default, so Vitest finds `*.test.*` and `*.spec.*` files outside those folders. `netjes({ test: false })` adds none of these settings ([Vite plugin](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/vite-plugin.md#vitest-defaults)).

An inline project in `test.projects` is the exception. Under Vitest 5, one that changes no Vite options shares the Vite server of the config that declares it, and Vitest builds its `test` options from that config's as written, before any plugin adds to them: neither these defaults nor Netjes's setup file reaches its tests. Set `sharedViteServer: false` in the root's `test` options, and each project gets them.

## Component and page tests

`createTestApp()` from `netjes/testing` gives a component what a Netjes page has around it: the router, the page payload, the query client and the public config. Pass its `Wrapper` to Testing Library:

```tsx
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { createTestApp } from 'netjes/testing';
import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { Greeting } from './Greeting.tsx';

describe('Greeting', () => {
  it('links to the about page without a full page load', async () => {
    const app = createTestApp();
    render(<Greeting message="Hello" renderedAt="2026-10-28T12:00:00Z" />, { wrapper: app.Wrapper });

    await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('link', { name: 'About this app' }));

    expect(app.navigations).toEqual([{ type: 'push', href: '/about' }]);
  });
});
```

The router is a fake. `<Link>`, `router.push` and `router.replace` move to the new URL, so hooks such as `usePathname()` and `useSearchParams()` see it, but no page is loaded. Every navigation, router call, form post and server action call is recorded in `app.navigations`, in order:

| Entry | For |
|---|---|
| `{ type: 'push' \| 'replace', href }` | A link, `router.push`, `router.replace` |
| `{ type: 'refresh' \| 'back' \| 'forward' }` | `router.refresh()`, `router.back()`, `router.forward()` |
| `{ type: 'submit', action, data }` | A `<Form method="post">` post, with its fields as `URLSearchParams` or `FormData` |
| `{ type: 'action', name, input }` | A server action call, with its input (an object, or the form's `FormData`) |

### Options

| Option | What it sets |
|---|---|
| `url` | The current URL. Default `/`. |
| `route` | The page's route pattern, such as `/blog/[slug]`. |
| `params` | What `useParams()` returns. |
| `shared` | The shared props, as the server would send them. |
| `queries` | Entries seeded into the query client, as `.WithQuery` seeds them: `[{ key, data }]`. |
| `defaultOptions` | TanStack Query defaults, like `netjes({ query: { defaultOptions } })`, merged over the app's own and the harness's. Failed queries and mutations are tried as often as in the app, with no wait between the tries ([Queries that fail](#queries-that-fail)). |
| `queryClient` | A client of your own instead, used as it is, without any of those defaults. |
| `actions` | Answers for server action calls, by name (below). |
| `navigation` | What `useNavigation()` returns. Default idle. |
| `antiforgery` | The token `<Form method="post">` adds. Default a test token; `false` for none. |
| `publicConfig` | What `usePublicConfig()` returns. |
| `locale` | What `useLocale()` returns. |
| `draftMode` | What `useDraftMode()` reports. |

`createTestApp()` returns `{ Wrapper, navigations, queryClient }`. The [React API reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/react-api.md#createtestapp) has the types.

### Answering server actions

`actions` answers calls by name, as the C# action would. An action without an answer succeeds with no result. A failure can name the fields its state's `values` keep, as the server does for the fields an action declares:

```tsx
const app = createTestApp({
  actions: {
    'home.greet': () => ({ ok: false, status: 422, errors: { name: ['Tell us your name.'] }, fields: ['name'] }),
  },
});
render(<HelloForm />, { wrapper: app.Wrapper });

await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Say hello' }));

expect(await screen.findByText('Tell us your name.')).toBeDefined();
```

An answer can also carry `queries` (`[{ key, data }]`) and `invalidate` (query keys), like `.WithQuery` and `.Invalidate` on a C# result.

A failure other than a 422 throws a `ServerActionError` into the nearest error boundary, as it does in the app. `message` is what the server would send: the status's reason phrase for a call it refused, or the exception's message with error details on. Without one, the call fails as a 5xx does with error details off, whatever its status: the error is [`withheld`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/react-api.md#errorpageprops), and an error page that renders the message only when `!error.withheld` leaves it out. So a test of a refused call sends the server's message:

```tsx
const app = createTestApp({
  actions: { 'posts.archive': () => ({ ok: false, status: 403, errors: {}, message: 'Forbidden' }) },
});
```

The `Wrapper` puts its stand-in for the router in place before the components inside it run any effect, so an action a component calls from `useEffect` or `useLayoutEffect` as it mounts is answered and recorded like any other call. Render such a component inside the `Wrapper`: outside it there is no router to wait for, and the call fails at once with "called before the page was ready".

### Pages

A page file's default export is a component like any other. Render it with the props its loader would send; `definePage` checks them against the generated schema, as it does in the app, so a test with props the schema rejects fails the way the page would:

```tsx
import Guestbook from './page.tsx';

it('shows the validation errors the action sent back, next to their fields', () => {
  const app = createTestApp({ url: '/guestbook' });

  render(<Guestbook entries={[]} errors={{ name: 'Tell us your name.' }} values={{ name: '', message: 'Hi' }} />, {
    wrapper: app.Wrapper,
  });

  expect(screen.getByText('Tell us your name.')).toBeDefined();
});
```

A component that fetches its own data with `useQuery` gets seeded data from `queries`. For what it fetches after that, answer the requests with a mock server such as [MSW](https://mswjs.io), as the Blog example's `LikeButton.test.tsx` does.

### Queries that fail

In the browser a failed query is tried three more times, after 1, 2 and 4 seconds (TanStack Query's defaults for `retry` and `retryDelay`), unless the app's `netjes({ query: { defaultOptions } })` says otherwise. `createTestApp()` builds its client from those same defaults, which the plugin hands to the tests, with the harness's own over them and the test's `defaultOptions` over those:

- A failed query or mutation is tried as often as in the app, but with no wait between the tries. So a test sees what the app shows in the end: the error once every try has failed, or the data that a later try got.
- The app's `staleTime`, `retry`, refetch options and mutation `retry` apply in tests. Its `retryDelay` and its queries' `gcTime` do not: the harness sets `retryDelay: 0`, and keeps every query's data for the whole test (`gcTime: Infinity`).
- `defaultOptions: { queries: { retry: false } }` shows the error after the first request. To test the waits themselves, pass a `retryDelay` of your own, such as TanStack Query's `(attemptIndex) => Math.min(1000 * 2 ** attemptIndex, 30_000)`, and move the clock on with [fake timers](#fake-timers).
- Under fake timers, each try after the first still waits on a timer of 0 ms, which runs only when the fake clock moves on. `findBy…` and `waitFor` move it on as they wait.
- Seeded data is fresh for the app's `staleTime`, counted from when `createTestApp()` is called. With a `staleTime` of 0, a component fetches its seeded query again as it mounts, as it does in the browser; with a longer one, only a component that mounts after that time, such as one rendered after the test moved [fake timers](#fake-timers) on. Answer that request, or set `defaultOptions: { queries: { staleTime: 60_000 } }`.

A Vitest config without `netjes()` hands over no app defaults, and `createTestApp()` starts from the Netjes defaults (a `staleTime` of one minute) and the harness's ([ADR 0028](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0028-test-harness-starts-from-the-apps-query-defaults.md)). In Vitest's browser mode, Vitest sends provided values to the test page as JSON, so an `Infinity` in `netjes({ query })`, such as `staleTime: Infinity`, reaches `createTestApp()` as `null`, and seeded data is stale at once: pass such a value in the test's `defaultOptions` there.

### Fake timers

A component that waits, such as a search box that searches once the typing stops, is tested with Vitest's fake timers. Testing Library's queries and user-event work with them:

```tsx
import { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { createTestApp } from 'netjes/testing';
import { afterEach, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';
import { SearchBox } from './SearchBox.tsx';

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

it('searches once the typing stops', async () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  const user = userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime });
  const app = createTestApp({ url: '/search' });
  render(<SearchBox />, { wrapper: app.Wrapper });

  await user.type(screen.getByRole('searchbox'), 'tea');

  await waitFor(() => expect(app.navigations).toEqual([{ type: 'replace', href: '/search?q=tea' }]));
});
```

- `findBy…` queries and `waitFor` move the fake clock on by their polling interval (50 ms) while they wait, and their `timeout` (1 s by default) runs on the fake clock.
- user-event moves it on through its `advanceTimers` option: create the user with `userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime })`. Without that option, as with user-event's direct API (`userEvent.click(...)` with no `setup()`), user-event waits out its own delays on the fake clock, and the call never returns.
- `fireEvent` dispatches the event at once. To run a timer it started, move the clock on inside `act`: `await act(() => vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(300))`.

Testing Library moves fake timers on only through a `jest` global, which Vitest does not have, so Netjes's setup file defines one while Vitest's timers are fake. `typeof jest` is `'object'` then and `'undefined'` with real timers, and `'jest' in globalThis` is always true. A test on `vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true })`, whose fake clock also follows real time, takes Testing Library's path for fake timers too. A `jest` global that the app's own setup file defines, or that a test assigns, is kept instead of Netjes's ([ADR 0027](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0027-testing-library-advances-vitest-fake-timers.md)).

### The document

`renderDocument()` from `netjes/testing` renders a page's whole document, from `<!DOCTYPE html>` to `</html>`, as the Node process renders it for a crawler: the page inside the layouts the server wraps it in, the head with the metadata of the page and its layouts, Netjes's inline scripts and the page payload. It returns the HTML. Name the page by its file, as `app/` holds it, and pass what the C# side would send with it:

```ts
// @vitest-environment node
import { renderDocument } from 'netjes/testing';
import { expect, it } from 'vitest';

it('renders the post inside the blog layout, which lists the categories', async () => {
  const html = await renderDocument('app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx', {
    url: '/blog/hello',
    params: { slug: 'hello' },
    props: { title: 'Hello', body: 'The first post.' },
    layouts: { 'app/blog/layout.tsx': { categories: ['react', 'dotnet'] } },
    shared: { siteName: 'Shop' },
  });

  expect(html).toContain('<h1>Hello</h1>');
  expect(html).toContain('<li>dotnet</li>');
});
```

- The test file runs in Vitest's node environment: start it with `// @vitest-environment node`. The server renders without a DOM, and parts of a page take another path where there is one, such as a `<Form>` for a server action, which renders with the action's URL only on the server. In a DOM environment, such as the jsdom the plugin sets by default, `renderDocument` rejects with an error that says so.
- The Vitest config has the `netjes()` plugin, as the template's `vite.config.ts` does. The plugin provides the pages map: the page, layout and boundary files in `app/`, from which `renderDocument` builds the segments the server would send, by the server's rules ([ADR 0038](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/decisions/0038-netjes-testing-renders-a-pages-document.md)). A test can pass a map of its own as `modules`, keyed `/app/...` as `import.meta.glob` keys it.
- No C# runs. The props, each layout's props (by the layout's file), the shared props, the route values and the URL are what the test passes, and a layout that `layouts` does not name gets no props. Nothing else the server would send with the page is in the document (below).
- It renders a page file, or a `not-found`, `error`, `forbidden`, `unauthorized` or `global-error` file, with the status the server gives it (404, 500, 403, 401 and 500) unless `status` sets another. An error file gets the props the test passes and no others: the server sends an error page `{ status, message, stack }`, with `withheld: true` when the message stands in for an exception's (error details off), from which Netjes builds the `error` prop that `error.tsx` reads, so pass those. A page in a parallel route slot (`app/@modal/...`) is refused, and so is any page in or below a folder that has a slot, since the server chooses what each slot renders.
- A boundary file renders as the server renders it in place of a page in or below its folder: inside the layouts down to its own folder, that folder's layout included, and `global-error` without any layout. The payload's route is `null`, which the server sends only when no page matched; in place of a page, it sends that page's route. One case renders otherwise: for a user who fails the authorization of a section's layout loader, the server renders the section's own `forbidden` or `unauthorized` file without the section's layout, and `renderDocument` renders that file inside it.
- The document is a crawler's: it waits for every Suspense boundary and renders what they hold in place.

What the server adds to a page's document, and a test cannot pass, is left out, so a page that reads it renders as it does without it:

- The TanStack Query entries a loader seeds with `.WithQuery`. A component that reads one with `useQuery` renders as it does before its data arrives, where the server's document has the data.
- Metadata from a C# loader (`.WithMetadata(...)`). The head has what the files' `metadata` exports give, and the elements the page and its layouts render there, such as a `<title>`.
- The antiforgery token: a `<Form method="post">` renders without its token field.
- The request's locale, draft mode and base path: `useLocale()` returns `null`, `useDraftMode()` reports draft mode off, and `useBasePath()` returns `''`.
- The image optimiser's settings from `Netjes:Images`: `<Image>` builds its URLs from the default path and widths, with the quality it is given.
- The build's stylesheets and module scripts, and the styles that development inlines.

| Option | What it sets |
|---|---|
| `props` | The page's props, as its C# loader sends them. A Promise in them is a `Page.Defer` value. |
| `params` | The route values, as `useParams()` returns them: a string for `[slug]`, an array for a catch-all. Default none. |
| `url` | The page's URL, path and query. Default `/`. |
| `layouts` | Each layout loader's props, by the layout's file: `{ 'app/blog/layout.tsx': { categories } }`. A Promise in them is a `Page.Defer` value. |
| `shared` | The shared props, as the server sends them (`UseSharedProps`). Default `null`. |
| `status` | The page's status. Default 200, or the boundary file's (above). |
| `nonce` | A Content-Security-Policy nonce, which goes on every script and stylesheet, as under a policy with `{nonce}`. |
| `lang` | `<html lang>`. Default `en`. |
| `publicConfig` | What `usePublicConfig()` reads, as the `Netjes:PublicConfig` section. |
| `modules` | The pages map, keyed `/app/...`. Default the app's, from the plugin. |
| `signal` | Stops the render, which then rejects with the signal's reason. |

A Promise in the props, at any depth, or in a layout's props, is a `Page.Defer` value, which reaches the page as the server's does. One that resolves renders in place. One that rejects leaves the fallback of the Suspense boundary that reads it in the document, with the error's message in the script that hands the failure to the browser, as the server sends a value that failed with error details on (with them off, it sends an empty message: [Page.Defer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md#on-the-wire)); the error is also logged with `console.error`, as the Node process logs it. One that never settles keeps the render waiting, and the test runs into Vitest's timeout: pass `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(1000)`, and `renderDocument` rejects with the signal's reason instead.

A Content-Security-Policy without a nonce lists the hash of each inline script a page runs ([hash-based policies](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#hash-based)). `inlineScriptHashes(html)` returns the hashes of those in a document, as `'sha256-…'` sources in their quotes: one for each script element without `src` that a browser runs and checks against the policy, with no type, a JavaScript type, `module`, `importmap` or `speculationrules`, in the order they first appear, each once. The payload and the entry of an external `beforeInteractive` `<Script>`, both `type="application/json"` data blocks, are not. A page that renders no inline scripts of its own has only Netjes's in its document, whose hashes `CSP_SCRIPT_HASHES` holds, as the new app's `app/document.test.ts` checks for the home page:

```ts
// @vitest-environment node
import { CSP_SCRIPT_HASHES } from 'netjes';
import { inlineScriptHashes, renderDocument } from 'netjes/testing';
import { expect, it } from 'vitest';

it('has no inline script in its document but the one whose hash Netjes lists for a policy without a nonce', async () => {
  const html = await renderDocument('app/page.tsx', {
    props: { message: 'Hello from C#', renderedAt: '2026-11-05T12:00:00Z' },
    shared: { siteName: 'Shop' },
  });

  expect(await inlineScriptHashes(html)).toEqual(CSP_SCRIPT_HASHES.split(' '));
});
```

The policy in C# is built from `NetjesContentSecurityPolicy.ScriptHashes`, which holds the same hashes. When the app's pages or layouts render inline code of their own, in `<script>` elements or in `beforeInteractive` `<Script>`s, such as a theme script, the policy lists their hashes too, and so does the test's expected list. A page with `Page.Defer` values has one more inline script per value in its document, which carries the value, so no fixed hash covers it: under a hash-based policy such a page must not stream.

The check sees the document a crawler gets. A visitor's browser also gets inline scripts that are not in it, which a policy without a nonce checks too:

- React's scripts that reveal a Suspense boundary still waiting when a visitor's shell goes out. A crawler's document waits for every boundary, so it has none of them, and no hash covers them, since they name the boundaries of that render. Under a hash-based policy no boundary may still wait when the shell goes out, lazy code under `loading.tsx` included ([hash-based policies](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md#hash-based)), and this check cannot show that none does.
- The inline code of an `afterInteractive` or `lazyOnload` `<Script>`, which `<Script>` adds in the browser. It is in no document, so it stays out of the test's expected list, and its hash goes in the policy. A `beforeInteractive` `<Script>`'s inline code is in the document, so its hash is in both.

## C# tests of loaders and actions

### Loaders as plain methods

`Page.Props(x)` returns a `PageResult<T>` whose `Props` holds `x` (null for a redirect or not-found), so you can call a loader written as a method from a test:

```csharp
public static class HomePage
{
    public sealed record HomeProps(string Message, DateTimeOffset RenderedAt);

    public static PageResult<HomeProps> Home(TimeProvider time) => Page.Props(new HomeProps("Hello from C#", time.GetUtcNow()));

    public static void MapHomePage(this IEndpointRouteBuilder app) => app.MapPageLoader("/", Home);
}

[Fact]
public void Home_SaysHello() => Assert.Equal("Hello from C#", HomePage.Home(TimeProvider.System).Props?.Message);
```

### The app over HTTP

`WebApplicationFactory` from `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing` runs the real app in memory, with its pipeline, authorization and services. Two settings let it run without a client build or Node: development mode, so the routes come from the files in `app/`, and a stand-in for the renderer, so no sidecar starts. The TaskBoard example's tests do this:

```csharp
public sealed class AppFactory : WebApplicationFactory<Program>
{
    public FakeRenderer Renderer { get; } = new();

    protected override void ConfigureWebHost(IWebHostBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.UseEnvironment("Testing");
        // Development mode reads the routes from app/ on disk; nothing is rendered, so no Vite or Node is needed.
        builder.UseSetting("Netjes:Mode", "Development");
        builder.ConfigureServices(services => services.AddSingleton<ISsrRenderer>(Renderer));
    }
}

/// <summary>Keeps the payload of the last document instead of rendering it.</summary>
public sealed class FakeRenderer : ISsrRenderer
{
    public string? Last { get; private set; }

    public Task<string> RenderAsync(string payloadJson, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        Last = payloadJson;
        return Task.FromResult("<!DOCTYPE html><html><body>rendered</body></html>");
    }
}
```

The factory runs the app in the `Testing` environment, with Netjes in development mode, rather than in `Development`. In the Development environment Netjes output-caches no page: each request renders the page again, and an output-cached page goes out `no-store` there ([caching](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/caching.md#in-the-development-environment)). So a test of what `CachePage` or other output caching stores runs in `Testing`, or any environment other than `Development`; a test of what Development does sets `UseEnvironment("Development")`.

The test project references the app's project and `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing`; ASP.NET Core 10 makes the `Program` class of top-level statements public, so `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` can start it. In development mode the app also writes `generated/netjes.ts` at startup when it is out of date, as `dotnet run` does.

When the app cannot start, `CreateClient()` throws why, as an `InvalidOperationException` whose message says what to do: `No production build found at …` for a test that runs the app in Production without a build, or `Could not start 'node'. …` for one that renders with the real Node processes where Node.js is not installed. Run as its own program, the app logs that message in one line and exits with code 1 instead ([deployment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md#what-the-server-needs)).

A host that the test project builds itself with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`, rather than `WebApplicationFactory`, has the test assembly's name, so Netjes takes it for the program: when its Node processes cannot start, `StartAsync()` returns, and the app logs why and stops. Give it another name with `WebApplicationOptions.ApplicationName`, as `WebApplicationFactory` gives the app its own, and `StartAsync()` throws instead.

Talk to it as the client router does. A request with `X-Netjes-Data: 1` gets the page payload as JSON:

```csharp
public sealed class HomePageTests(AppFactory app) : IClassFixture<AppFactory>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task TheHomePage_HasTheLoadersMessage()
    {
        var client = app.CreateClient();
        var request = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Get, "/");
        request.Headers.Add(NetjesHeaders.Data, "1");

        var response = await client.SendAsync(request, TestContext.Current.CancellationToken);
        var payload = JsonNode.Parse(await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(TestContext.Current.CancellationToken))!;

        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode);
        Assert.Equal("Hello from C#", (string?)payload["props"]!["message"]);
    }
}
```

A page with `Page.Defer` values answers with NDJSON: the payload on the first line, then one line per value. A document request (without the header) goes through the fake renderer, whose `Last` then holds the payload the sidecar would have rendered.

The factory's server, TestServer, passes on no request target (`IHttpRequestFeature.RawTarget` is empty), and Netjes redirects another spelling of a page's URL only when the target shows that the client sent it ([One URL per page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#one-url-per-page)). So in these tests `/About` renders the page `/about` does, where the app on Kestrel answers 308. Test the redirect end to end, or give each request the target Kestrel would, from a startup filter, which runs ahead of the app's pipeline:

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Extensions; // GetEncodedPathAndQuery
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Features;   // IHttpRequestFeature

// In AppFactory.ConfigureWebHost:
builder.ConfigureServices(services => services.AddTransient<IStartupFilter, RequestTargets>());

/// <summary>Gives each request the target its client sent, as Kestrel does.</summary>
public sealed class RequestTargets : IStartupFilter
{
    public Action<IApplicationBuilder> Configure(Action<IApplicationBuilder> next) => app =>
    {
        app.Use((http, inner) =>
        {
            http.Features.Get<IHttpRequestFeature>()!.RawTarget = http.Request.GetEncodedPathAndQuery();
            return inner(http);
        });
        next(app);
    };
}
```

A server action needs an antiforgery token. Get one from `/_netjes/antiforgery`, which also sets the antiforgery cookie (the factory's client keeps cookies), and send it as the header the response names:

```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task Greeting_WithoutAName_IsAFieldError()
{
    var client = app.CreateClient();
    var token = JsonNode.Parse(await client.GetStringAsync("/_netjes/antiforgery", TestContext.Current.CancellationToken))!;
    var request = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Post, "/_netjes/actions/home.greet")
    {
        Content = new FormUrlEncodedContent([new("name", "")]),
    };
    request.Headers.Add(NetjesHeaders.Data, "1");
    request.Headers.Add((string)token["headerName"]!, (string)token["requestToken"]!);

    var response = await client.SendAsync(request, TestContext.Current.CancellationToken);
    var result = JsonNode.Parse(await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(TestContext.Current.CancellationToken))!;

    Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.UnprocessableEntity, response.StatusCode);
    Assert.Equal("Tell us your name.", (string?)result["errors"]!["name"]![0]);
}
```

Without `X-Netjes-Data` the same post is a form post without JavaScript: put the token in the form field `token["formFieldName"]` instead, and expect a 303 redirect on success, or the form's page rendered again with status 422.

`tests/TaskBoard.Tests` has a fuller harness: a `Browser` type that keeps cookies and the last token, signs up users and calls actions, against Postgres in Testcontainers.

A test about every page at once, such as one that checks that each page `CachePage` caches has a tag to revalidate it by, needs no request: it walks the app's endpoints and reads the metadata Netjes puts on them ([endpoint metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/csharp-api.md#endpoint-metadata)).

## End-to-end tests

Playwright tests the app in a real browser. The examples run each suite against two servers at once, one in Development (the Vite dev server) and one in Production (the build), since some failures show in one only. A server in the Playwright config waits for the app's health check:

```ts
webServer: [
  {
    command: 'dotnet run --no-build --no-launch-profile',
    url: `${DEV_URL}/healthz`,
    env: { ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT: 'Development', ASPNETCORE_URLS: DEV_URL, Netjes__ViteDevPort: VITE_PORT },
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  },
  {
    command: 'npm run build && dotnet run --no-build --no-launch-profile',
    url: `${PROD_URL}/healthz`,
    env: { ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT: 'Production', ASPNETCORE_URLS: PROD_URL },
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  },
],
```

`--no-build` starts the last build, so build the app first: the examples' `test:e2e` script is `dotnet build && playwright test`. Give each development server its own `Netjes__ViteDevPort`, so two of them can run side by side. Put the specs in `e2e/`, which the Vitest defaults leave out, and install the browser once with `npx playwright install chromium`. `examples/Blog/playwright.config.ts` also runs the app under a base path, with no Node process ready (the client-rendered fallback), and as a static export.

### Wait for hydration

Until the page has hydrated, a `<Link>` loads the next page in full, a `<Form>` posts natively and an `onClick` handler does not run, so a test that clicks or types too early can pass on the path a browser without JavaScript takes. Once the client router runs in the document, Netjes puts `data-netjes-hydrated` on `<html>`, with an empty value. After each full page load, wait for it before the test's first click or keystroke:

```ts
await page.goto('/guestbook');
await page.locator('html[data-netjes-hydrated]').waitFor({ state: 'attached' });
```

`waitFor` waits as long as the test may run, unless the config sets an `actionTimeout`. The same wait as a web-first assertion, which retries for `expect`'s timeout instead (5 seconds by default):

```ts
await expect(page.locator('html')).toHaveAttribute('data-netjes-hydrated', '');
```

What the mark says, and what it does not:

- The client router runs in this document. React has hydrated the page (all but the content of its Suspense boundaries, below), or rendered it in the browser when no Node process was ready ([the client-rendered fallback](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md#when-no-sidecar-is-ready)). The router has keyed the history entry, listens for back and forward, and is the page's action client, so a server action call goes out at once.
- Each document gets its own. After a reload, or a back or forward that loads the page again, the new document has no mark until its own router runs. A client navigation keeps it.
- It does not say that every Suspense boundary has hydrated. React hydrates the content of a boundary (a `loading.tsx`, or one of the page's own) in a pass of its own after the rest of the page, and content that is still streaming in once it arrives. When a click lands on such content before React gets to it, React hydrates it at once and then handles the click. Content that has not arrived cannot be clicked: wait for it to show, as Playwright's actions do.
- The server never renders it, so a test with JavaScript turned off never sees it. A page whose modules fail to load never gets it either: the page stays as the server rendered it, without the client router, and a test that waits for the mark there times out.

Do not wait for the router's key in `history.state` instead. It is internal, and the browser keeps a history entry's state when it loads the document again, so after a reload the key is there before any of the page's scripts has run.

### Focus, announcements and other spellings

A browser sees a few things that a component test does not:

- After a client navigation to another page, the focus starts over at the top of the document, on `body` ([Focus and announcements](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#focus-and-announcements)). A test that types right after one focuses its field first, as `locator.fill()` does; `page.keyboard.type()` on its own types into `body`.
- After a navigation to another path or query, the router puts the new page's name in a live region after the app's content. A test that reads the text of a whole container, such as `body`, gets the region's text too, so read the element you mean. The region has no role; find it as `page.locator('[data-netjes-route-announcer]')`.
- A URL in another case of a page's literal segments, such as `/About` for `app/about/page.tsx`, answers 308 to the file's spelling on Kestrel, where the `WebApplicationFactory` tests above get the page ([One URL per page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#one-url-per-page)).

## In CI

```bash
npm ci
npx netjes generate --check            # the committed generated/netjes.ts matches the C# code
npm run typecheck
npm test                               # Vitest
dotnet test -c Release                 # loaders and actions
dotnet build                           # the Debug build that dotnet run --no-build starts
npx playwright install --with-deps chromium && npx playwright test
```

`netjes generate --check` runs the app once in command mode, without a build or a Node process and on a throwaway loopback port, and exits 1 when the generated types are out of date. An app that does not start, such as one with a loader or action minimal APIs cannot bind, fails the check with the exception's message. Startup code that needs a database can skip that work with `app.GetNetjesCommand()`; see the [CLI reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/cli.md#netjes-generate).

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/deployment.md -->

# Deployment

This guide is for app developers taking a Netjes app to production: what `dotnet publish` produces and what the server needs, the template's Docker and Compose setup, configuration, running several instances behind a load balancer, health checks, telemetry and logs, and running behind a proxy or under a base path. Security settings to review before you go live are in [security](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/security.md).

## Build and publish

A Netjes app is an ASP.NET Core app with a client build next to it. `dotnet publish` makes both:

```bash
dotnet publish -c Release -o bin/publish
```

The build leaves `bin/`, `obj/` and a `publish/` folder in the project out of the app's content, so `-o publish` works as well as `-o bin/publish`. A folder with another name is not left out: the Web SDK takes the JSON and config files under the project folder as content, so it would be copied into the next build's output. The template's `.gitignore` and `.dockerignore` list `publish/`.

The Netjes package's `build/Netjes.targets`, imported into every project that references it, runs `npm run build` during publish (`vite build && vite build --ssr` in the template) and ships `dist/` with the app:

- `dist/client/`: the browser's JavaScript and CSS, content-hashed under `assets/`, and the files from `public/`, with Vite's manifest in `.vite/`.
- `dist/server/`: the server bundle the Node processes import, with React and every other dependency bundled in, and the sidecar script (`netjes-sidecar.mjs`).

The published folder runs without `node_modules`. Three MSBuild properties change what publish does:

| Property | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `NetjesSkipClientBuild` | unset | `true` publishes a `dist/` that is already built, for a CI step or Docker stage that builds the client on its own. |
| `NetjesBuildCommand` | `npm run build` | The command that builds the client. |
| `NetjesRoot` | the project's folder | Where `package.json` and `dist/` are. |

`netjes build` does the client build on its own (it also writes the generated types first), and `netjes start` runs the app in Production from the project or a published `.dll` (run from the `.dll`'s folder). See the [CLI reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/cli.md).

## What the server needs

- The ASP.NET Core runtime, 10.0.14 or newer.
- Node.js `^22.22.2 || ^24.15.0 || >=26.0.0` (Node.js 22.22.2 or a later 22, 24.15.0 or a later 24, or 26 or newer), as `node` on the path (or `NetjesOptions.NodeExecutable`). Netjes starts the Node processes itself; you do not run them.
- The published folder, with `dist/`. In Production the app reads `dist/client/.vite/manifest.json` at startup and stops when it is missing.

The app runs in Production mode whenever the environment is not Development (`ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT`); `Netjes:Mode` sets the mode outright.

When the app finds no build, or cannot start Node.js, it says so in one line and exits with code 1. It logs the reason as a critical entry, the last thing it logs, with what to do:

```text
crit: Netjes.Rendering.ViteManifestProvider[0]
      No production build found at '/app/dist/client/.vite/manifest.json'. To develop, run `npm run dev`, or start the app with ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development. To run in production, build first: `npm run build` in '/app'.
```

For Node.js the line is `Could not start 'node'. Is Node.js installed and on the PATH? Set Netjes:NodeExecutable to use another executable.`, and for a build without the sidecar script `` Cannot find the netjes sidecar at '/app/dist/server/netjes-sidecar.mjs'. Run `npm run build` in '/app'. ``. A container runtime or process manager sees exit code 1 for these failures. In a test host such as `WebApplicationFactory`, the start fails with that message instead ([testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md#the-app-over-http)).

Exit code 1 is for these failures only, and in Development for a Vite dev server that does not start ([the sidecar pool](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md#the-sidecar-pool)). An exception that nothing catches, such as one thrown from `Program.cs` or on a thread the app starts itself, ends the app as .NET ends any process that crashes: it prints the exception with its stack and aborts, which is exit code 134 (SIGABRT) on Linux and macOS. That includes Netjes's other startup checks, such as page files in a `pages/` folder or two pages that match the same URLs: `UseNetjes()` and `MapPages()` throw their exception into `Program.cs`. `Environment.FailFast` and a stack overflow end it the same way. A request's exceptions do not end it: ASP.NET Core catches them, and Netjes renders a page's as its [error page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md#error-pages). The host catches one from a `BackgroundService`, logs it and stops the app with exit code 0. In a container, the abort ends the process only under an init; see [a crash in a container](#a-crash-in-a-container).

## Docker

Every app made with `netjes new` has a `Dockerfile` and three Compose files. An app scaffolded from a Netjes checkout references that checkout instead of the packages, and the Docker build cannot see the checkout, so pass `--packages` there.

```bash
docker compose up                                                     # development: dotnet watch + Vite HMR on http://localhost:8080
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d  # the production image, on port 8080
```

Both stacks publish the app on port 8080 of the host. To use another port, set `APP_PORT`, in the shell or in a `.env` file next to the Compose files: `APP_PORT=8090 docker compose up` serves development on http://localhost:8090, and the same variable moves the production stack. The app listens on 8080 inside the container either way, and Vite's port, 5173, does not move.

The `Dockerfile` has these stages:

| Stage | What it does |
|---|---|
| `deps` | `npm ci`, cached until `package.json` or the lockfile changes. |
| `dev` | The .NET SDK with Node, running `dotnet watch run`; the source is bind-mounted. |
| `client` | `npm run build`: `dist/client` and `dist/server`. |
| `build` | `dotnet publish` with `-p:NetjesSkipClientBuild=true`, taking `dist/` from `client`. |
| `tini` | Ubuntu's `tini` package, installed in the SDK image, for the static binary that `production` copies. |
| `production` | The ASP.NET Core runtime image plus the `node` and `tini` binaries and the published app. tini starts the app (`tini -s -- dotnet MyApp.dll`, see [below](#a-crash-in-a-container)) as the non-root `app` user, and a `HEALTHCHECK` checks `/healthz`. |

The Compose files:

- `docker-compose.yml` defines the `app` service from the `production` stage, with `pull_policy: build`, so `up -d` always builds and never reuses a stale or development image.
- `docker-compose.override.yml`, which Compose loads by default, switches to the `dev` stage, bind-mounts the source, and publishes the app's port (8080, or `APP_PORT`) and Vite's 5173 on `127.0.0.1` only: development error pages show stack traces and Vite serves the source.
- `docker-compose.prod.yml` publishes the app on port 8080, or `APP_PORT`, and runs the container read-only, with a `tmpfs` at `/tmp`, `no-new-privileges`, every capability dropped, limits of one CPU and 512 MB, `restart: always`, and a named volume for ASP.NET Core's Data Protection keys, which sign antiforgery tokens and the draft mode cookie, so they survive restarts and new images.

ASP.NET Core logs a warning at startup that those keys are not encrypted at rest. Encrypt them with one of the `ProtectKeysWith...` methods (a certificate, Azure Key Vault) if that matters where you run.

### A crash in a container
