When the Vite dev server or the Node.js processes cannot start, such as for an error in `vite.config.ts` or a package it imports that is not installed, the app logs why in one log entry and exits with code 1, and `dotnet watch` waits for a file to change before it starts the app again (Ctrl+R starts it at once).

Stop it with Ctrl+C. `dotnet watch` does not stop on SIGTERM, so a tool that runs `netjes dev` for you (an IDE task, a process manager) should stop it with SIGINT.

## netjes build

```text
netjes build
```

Writes `generated/netjes.ts` (as `netjes generate` does), then runs `vite build` and `vite build --ssr`, which write `dist/client/` and `dist/server/`. It stops at the first step that fails, with that step's exit code. It runs the vite installed in the app's `node_modules`; when there is none it says to run `npm install`, and never downloads one.

`dotnet publish` runs `npm run build` itself (through `build/Netjes.targets`) and ships `dist/` with the app.

## netjes start

```text
netjes start [--dll <path>]
```

Runs the app in Production: `dotnet run -c Release` in the project, or `dotnet <path>` for a published app. In Production the app in the project serves the build in `dist/`; when `dist/` has none, netjes says to run `netjes build` first and starts the app anyway (an app can keep its build elsewhere with `NetjesOptions.DistDirectory`), which then stops with one line saying there is no build, and exit code 1. A published app runs from the folder the `.dll` is in, as it does when you start it by hand there: it serves the published `dist/` and reads the published `appsettings*.json`, not the project's. A relative path is resolved against the folder `netjes` runs in, or `--cwd`. `netjes` stops with an error when the path is not a file.

| Option | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--dll <path>` | Run a published app's `.dll` (from `dotnet publish`) instead of the project, and run it from the `.dll`'s folder. | `dotnet run -c Release` in the project |

```bash
netjes build && netjes start
dotnet publish -c Release -o bin/publish && netjes start --dll bin/publish/MyShop.dll
```

ASP.NET Core listens on `http://localhost:5000` unless `ASPNETCORE_URLS` says otherwise.

## netjes generate

```text
netjes generate [--check]
```

Writes `generated/netjes.ts`: zod schemas for what the loaders and actions return, typed server action references, typed routes and typed endpoint URLs. The app also rewrites it when it starts in Development; commit it.

| Option | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--check` | Write nothing, and exit 1 when `generated/netjes.ts` is out of date. For CI. | off |

When `--check` finds the file out of date, the error shows where it differs: the first block of changed lines, as `- 12: old line` from the committed file and `+ 12: new line` from the generated one, with line numbers, up to 20 lines and then a count of the rest. When the file differs again further down, a last line says up to which line. A missing file is reported as missing.

Like `routes`, it runs the app once in command mode: the app starts as usual, so every `Map...` call and option applies, but it binds only a throwaway loopback port, starts no Node sidecar and needs no build; it writes its result and exits. Startup code that needs a database can skip that work with `if (app.GetNetjesCommand() is null)`. A `Map...` call that throws, such as a loader whose parameters minimal APIs cannot bind, stops the app before it writes anything: the app prints the exception's message, then its stack trace, and the command exits with the app's exit code, which is not 0. It exits 2 when `NetjesOptions.TypesFile` is null.

## netjes routes

```text
netjes routes [--json]
```

Prints the pages as the app maps them (pattern, file, loader, page action, props type, output caching, authorization), the other endpoints (the built-in ones such as `/_netjes/image`, your own minimal API endpoints and the [server actions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md) at `/_netjes/actions/<name>`), and the [route warnings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#route-warnings). Warnings do not change the exit code.

| Option | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--json` | Print the report as JSON. | off: a table |

The report is the only thing on stdout; the build and app output go to stderr, so `netjes routes --json | jq` works. Its shape:

```json
{
  "routes": [{ "pattern": "/blog/[slug]", "template": "/blog/{slug}", "file": "app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx", "layouts": ["app/layout.tsx"],
               "loader": true, "action": false, "props": "PostProps", "cached": true, "authorized": false }],
  "endpoints": [{ "method": "*", "route": "/healthz", "name": "Health checks" }],
  "warnings": [{ "kind": "overlap", "message": "…", "files": ["app/[id]/page.tsx", "app/[...rest]/page.tsx"] }]
}
```

`method` is the HTTP method an endpoint answers, or `"*"` for one that answers every method, as `MapHealthChecks` does. A warning's `kind` names one of the [route warnings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#route-warnings): `query-binding` for a loader parameter that reads the query string instead of a route value, `overlap` for two pages that match the same URLs, `ambiguous-endpoint` for an endpoint that ties with a page, and `form-input` for a form input that refuses a post without a checkbox. `files` lists the page and layout files the warning is about, and is empty for a server action's form input.

## netjes export

```text
netjes export [dir] [--no-build]
```

Builds the app (as `netjes build` does), then runs it once in Production and writes every page as static HTML into `dir`, with `404.html`, the client assets, and a file for each endpoint marked `.IncludeInExport()`, such as `sitemap.xml` and `robots.txt` from `MapSitemap` and `MapRobotsTxt`. [Static export](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md) has the rules: which pages and endpoints can be exported, `.StaticParams(...)` for dynamic pages, and where the output may go.

The export logs a warning, in the category `Netjes.Export.QueryString`, for each page loader of a page it writes, and each layout loader above one, that reads the query string, which the export never sends. The page is still written and the exit code does not change. A loader that requires a query value still fails the export, and its warning says so ([loaders that read the query string](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/static-export.md#loaders-that-read-the-query-string)).

| Argument or option | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `[dir]` | The folder to write the site to, inside the app. A relative path is resolved against the folder `netjes` runs in, or `--cwd`. | `out` |
| `--no-build` | Export the build already in `dist/`. | off: build first |

Before it builds, netjes checks that `dir` is inside the folder it runs in. A folder outside it, such as `..`, `../site` or a path elsewhere on the disk, or that folder itself, ends the command with one line on stderr and exit code 1, and nothing is built:

```console
$ netjes export ../site
netjes export: the output folder /home/me/site must be inside the app (/home/me/my-shop), such as 'out'; nothing was built
```

On macOS and Windows that check ignores letter case, as .NET does. On macOS and Linux, netjes takes the folder it runs in by its real path, with any symlink resolved, since that is the folder the app finds itself in, and resolves a relative `dir` against it. After the build, the app checks the folder again, with the rest of the rules, against `Netjes:Root`. With `--no-build`, netjes still resolves a relative `dir` that way, but does not check the folder, and the app alone decides: an app whose `Netjes:Root` is above the project folder can export to a folder inside it, such as `../site`, and a folder the app refuses costs a compile and a start before the export stops.

## netjes info

```text
netjes info
```

Checks the tools and the project, one line each: `✓` for what is in order, `!` for a warning, `✗` for a problem. Every `!` and `✗` line is followed by an indented line that says how to fix it. It exits 1 when there is a `✗`, and 0 otherwise.

```text
netjes 0.0.2 in /home/me/my-shop

✓ Node.js 24.15.0
✓ .NET SDK 10.0.403 (MyShop.csproj targets net10.0)

✓ npm packages: netjes 0.0.2, vite 8.3.5, react 19.3.1, react-dom 19.3.1
✓ MyShop.csproj references Netjes 0.0.2, the version of the npm package
✓ vite.config.ts uses netjes()
✓ package.json has a build script (dotnet publish runs it)
✓ app/ has 2 pages
! generated/netjes.ts is older than Features/Home/HomePage.cs
  Run `netjes generate` if the C# types changed; `netjes generate --check` tells for sure
```

| Check | Fails (`✗`) when | Warns (`!`) when |
|---|---|---|
| Node.js | outside `^22.22.2 \|\| ^24.15.0 \|\| >=26.0.0`: older than 22.22.2, or a 24 older than 24.15.0 | an odd release line (23, 25), which falls between the supported ones |
| .NET SDK | `dotnet` is missing, `dotnet --version` fails (often a `global.json` that asks for an SDK that is not installed), or the SDK is older than the app's `TargetFramework` (and 10.0): any .NET 10 SDK builds an app that targets `net10.0` | |
| npm packages | `netjes`, `vite`, `react` or `react-dom` is not installed, or a version is outside the installed netjes's peer range | the netjes running `info` is another version than the app's (run `npx netjes info`) |
| Netjes reference | the `.csproj` references an exact Netjes version (`x.y.z` or `[x.y.z]`) other than the npm package's, or a checkout that is not there. A range, a floating version or an MSBuild property such as `$(NetjesVersion)` is shown, not compared. | the `.csproj` references no Netjes package (fine when `Directory.Packages.props` does) |
| Vite config | there is no `vite.config.*`, or it does not use `netjes()` | |
| `package.json` | it is missing, is not valid JSON, or has no `build` script | |
| `app/` | it is missing; or `pages/` still has pages router files (named with their `app/` files) or API routes in `pages/api/` | it has no `page.tsx` |
| `generated/netjes.ts` | it is missing | a `.cs` file in the app is newer (a hint only: `netjes generate --check` is exact) |

## netjes agents

```text
netjes agents [dir] [--name <Name>] [--force]
```

Writes what `netjes new` gives coding agents into an existing app: `AGENTS.md` (how this app is built and tested, with links to the Netjes docs and `llms.txt`), a `CLAUDE.md` that imports it, and the Netjes skill in `.claude/skills/netjes/`. It prints each file as `wrote` or `kept`: a file that exists is kept unless `--force` is given. When it keeps a `CLAUDE.md` that does not import `AGENTS.md`, it says to add the `@AGENTS.md` line. When the folder has no `.csproj` (or more than one) and `--name` is not given, it warns on stderr that the app is named after the folder, and still writes the files. After upgrading Netjes, `rm -r .claude/skills/netjes && npx netjes agents` refreshes the skill and keeps the rest. The [coding agents guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/coding-agents.md) has more.

| Argument or option | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `[dir]` | The app folder. | the current folder |
| `--name <Name>` | The app's name in `AGENTS.md`. | the name of its `.csproj`, else the folder name |
| `--force` | Replace the files that exist. | off: keep them |

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Success. |
| 1 | A usage error; a check that failed before anything ran (no `.csproj`, packages not installed, the port is in use, a name or folder that `netjes new` refuses, an output folder outside the app, which `netjes export` refuses before it builds); or a failed check (`netjes info` found a `✗`, `netjes generate --check` found the types out of date). |
| 127 | `dotnet` or `npm` is not installed, or not on `PATH`. netjes says what to install. |
| 130 | Ctrl+C at the `netjes new` prompt. |
| other | The exit code of the process netjes ran (`dotnet`, `npm` or `vite`), passed on unchanged; 128 + n when signal n ended it (130 for SIGINT, 143 for SIGTERM). |

## Output

- Results go to stdout: help, the version, the route table or its JSON, the `info` report, what `new` created. Errors and hints go to stderr.
- A reader that stops early, as in `netjes routes | head`, is not an error: netjes drops the rest of its output and exits as it would have.
- `dotnet`, `npm` and `vite` write to the terminal directly, with their own formatting. Under `routes`, the app's stdout goes to stderr, so that stdout holds only the report.
- In command mode (`generate`, `routes`, `export`) the host's own lifetime messages ("Now listening on" a throwaway port, "Press Ctrl+C to shut down") are left out; the app's other logs are not.
- Colour only where it helps: the marks of `netjes info` and the label of an error, when the stream is a terminal. See `NO_COLOR` and `FORCE_COLOR` below.
- netjes asks a question in one case only: `netjes new` without a folder, in a terminal. Everything else takes its input from arguments, so it runs the same in scripts and CI.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `NO_COLOR` | Any non-empty value turns colour off ([no-color.org](https://no-color.org)). It wins over `FORCE_COLOR`. |
| `FORCE_COLOR` | Colour even when the output is not a terminal; `0` or `false` turns it off. |
| `TERM=dumb` | No colour. |
| `ASPNETCORE_URLS` | Where the app listens. `netjes dev` sets `http://localhost:5080` unless it is set; `start` leaves it to ASP.NET Core; command mode uses `http://127.0.0.1:0`. |
| `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` | `dev`, `generate`, `routes` and the type step of `build` run in `Development`, `start` and `export` in `Production`, unless it is set. |
| `Logging__LogLevel__Microsoft.Hosting.Lifetime` | In command mode netjes sets it to `Warning`, unless it is set. |
| `NETJES_COMMAND`, `NETJES_OUTPUT`, `NETJES_CHECK` | Set by netjes to put the app in command mode. netjes removes inherited ones (in any letter case) from every process it starts, so a leftover one cannot turn `netjes start` into an export. The app reads them only from its process environment. |
| `NETJES_VITE_HOST`, `NETJES_VITE_ORIGIN` | Passed on to the app's sidecar: the Vite dev server's host (localhost unless set; `0.0.0.0` exposes it, see [the dev server](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/vite-plugin.md#the-dev-server)) and origin. `netjes dev` checks the Vite port on that host. |
| `Netjes__*` | ASP.NET Core configuration for `NetjesOptions`, passed on, such as `Netjes__ViteDevPort=5174`. |

## In CI

```bash
npm ci
npx netjes generate --check                # the committed types match the C# code
npm test
dotnet publish -c Release -o bin/publish   # runs npm run build, and ships dist/ with the app
```

To build the client in a step of its own (`npx netjes build`), pass `-p:NetjesSkipClientBuild=true` to `dotnet publish`, as the template's `Dockerfile` does, so that it is not built twice.

`netjes info` makes a quick first step in a CI job, too: it fails, with a reason, on a missing or old SDK or Node.js and on packages that do not match.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/reference/vite-plugin.md -->

# Vite plugin

`netjes()` from `netjes/vite` is the Vite plugin every Netjes app uses. This page lists its options and everything it adds to the Vite config, for when you need to change the build, turn part of the default stack off, or understand what the dev server serves.

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import netjes from 'netjes/vite';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [netjes()],
});
```

The plugin returns a list of plugins: `@vitejs/plugin-react`, the Netjes plugin itself, and `@tailwindcss/vite` unless Tailwind is off. Put any plugins of your own next to it in `plugins`.

## Options

```ts
netjes({
  appDir: 'app',
  basePath: '/docs',
  tailwind: true,
  query: { defaultOptions: { queries: { staleTime: 5 * 60_000 } } },
  test: true,
});
```

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `appDir` | `string` | `'app'` | The folder of page files, relative to the Vite root. It must match `Netjes:AppDirectory` in the .NET app. |
| `basePath` | `string` | none | The path the app is mounted under with `app.UsePathBase(...)`, such as `'/docs'`. Built asset URLs get it (Vite's `base`); links, forms, redirects and router calls get it from the server at runtime. It must match the base path in `Program.cs`. |
| `tailwind` | `boolean` | `true` | Adds `@tailwindcss/vite`. Import Tailwind with `@import "tailwindcss";` in a stylesheet that a layout imports. With `false`, `tailwindcss` and `@tailwindcss/vite` need not be installed. |
| `query` | `boolean \| { defaultOptions?: DefaultOptions }` | `true` | The built-in TanStack Query client, which loaders seed with `.WithQuery(key, data)`. `false` removes it, and TanStack Query with it, from the bundle. An object configures the client; its `defaultOptions` are merged over the Netjes defaults (`staleTime` of one minute, so seeded data is not fetched again at once). Under Vitest the plugin hands the same `defaultOptions` to `createTestApp()`, which keeps all of them but `retryDelay` and the queries' `gcTime` ([Vitest defaults](#vitest-defaults)). |
| `test` | `boolean` | `true` | Vitest defaults, below. `false` adds none. |
| `react` | `Options` of `@vitejs/plugin-react` | none | Passed to `@vitejs/plugin-react`, which the plugin includes. |

`query` options are written into the browser bundle as literals, so they can be plain values only: numbers (`Infinity` too), strings, booleans, `null`, arrays and plain objects. A function, such as a `retry` callback, fails when the config loads, with an error naming the option; set those per query, as in `useQuery({ retry })`.

With Tailwind on, a missing `@tailwindcss/vite` fails the config with a message saying to install it (`npm install -D tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite`) or to pass `tailwind: false`.

## What it adds

### The page module map

The plugin provides `virtual:netjes/pages`, a map of every convention file under `appDir`: `page`, `layout`, `template`, `loading`, `error`, `not-found`, `forbidden`, `unauthorized`, `global-error` and `default`, as `.tsx` or `.jsx`. The client entry and the server entry load pages from it by the path the server names in each payload. The module also exports `appDir` as the plugin has it, which `renderDocument` in `netjes/testing` builds a page's route and segments from ([the document](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md#the-document)). Other files in `appDir` are colocated code and not routes, except a route handler, which stops the build ([Builds](#builds)).

In development the map is rebuilt when Vite's watcher reports a page file added or removed. When the server routes a page file the map does not have yet, the Node process that renders pages asks the plugin to build the map again from the files on disk and renders once more, so a new page works on its first request.

### The query client

`virtual:netjes/query` holds the TanStack Query shell: a `QueryClient` per render on the server and per page load in the browser, hydrated from each payload's seeded queries. With `query: false` the module exports nothing and pages render without it.

### Builds

`vite build` builds the client:

- input: the Netjes client entry; output: `dist/client/`, emptied first;
- a manifest in `dist/client/.vite/manifest.json`, from which the .NET app learns the routes and the assets of each page in production. The app never serves the `.vite/` folder: a request for it answers 404.

`vite build --ssr` builds the server bundle:

- input: the Netjes server entry; output: `dist/server/server-entry.js`, as an ES module, with every dependency bundled in, so production needs no `node_modules`;
- the script of the Node process that renders pages, copied to `dist/server/netjes-sidecar.mjs`;
- no copy of `public/`.

Both builds stop on a route handler in `appDir`: a file named `route` plus one extension (`route.ts`, `route.js`; a test such as `route.test.ts` is not one), outside private folders (`_lib/`) and slots (`@modal/`). The error names the first in ordinal order, with the message the app stops with in development: route handlers are C# in Netjes, and an API is a minimal API endpoint (`app.MapGet`, `app.MapPost`; [What is not there](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/routing.md#what-is-not-there)).

`netjes build` runs both, after regenerating `generated/netjes.ts`, and `dotnet publish` runs `npm run build`, which the template defines as `vite build && vite build --ssr`.

### Resolution and dependencies

- `react`, `react-dom` and, with the query client, `@tanstack/react-query` are deduplicated, so the app and `netjes` share one copy even when `netjes` is linked from elsewhere (a `file:` dependency or `npm link`). Under Vitest, `@testing-library/react` is too.
- Dependencies are pre-bundled from the page files (there is no `index.html` to scan), including `react`, `react-dom/client`, TanStack Query and, when it is installed, `web-vitals`. `netjes` itself is left out: it imports the plugin's virtual modules (the page module map and the query shell), and the app's pages and the plugin's entries must share one copy of each of its modules. For the same reasons Vite processes it for server rendering in development too (`ssr.noExternal`).
- `appType` is `'custom'`: the .NET app serves the documents, and Vite serves modules.

### TypeScript setup

`netjes` ships its modules as JavaScript with declaration files (`.d.ts`), so the app's `tsc` checks the app's own code against the declarations of `netjes`, not against its sources. The app may add stricter compiler options, such as `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` or `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature`: the declarations pass under them, with `skipLibCheck` on or off. They resolve under `moduleResolution` `bundler` (the template's), `node16` and `nodenext`, which read the package's `exports`.

The TypeScript sources ship in the package too: the declaration maps and source maps point at them, so an editor's go to definition and a stack trace lead to the TypeScript.

### Vitest defaults

Under Vitest, unless `test` is `false`, the plugin sets these, each only if the app's own `test` config leaves it unset, with two exceptions, which it adds to what the app sets: Netjes's own setup file, in `setupFiles`, and `provide['netjes:query']`.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| `environment` | `'jsdom'`, when `jsdom` is installed |
| `exclude` | `node_modules`, `dist`, `bin`, `obj`, `e2e` (for Playwright) and `.git` folders |
| `setupFiles` | In every app, Netjes's own setup file, which lets Testing Library work with Vitest's fake timers ([Fake timers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md#fake-timers)) and hands `createTestApp()` the app's query defaults; Vite puts it after the app's own setup files. Before it, when `@testing-library/react` is installed and the app sets no `setupFiles`, a setup file that unmounts what each test rendered (Testing Library's `cleanup`, `netjes/testing/setup`); an app that sets them lists `netjes/testing/setup` there itself |
| `provide` | `'netjes:query'`: the `defaultOptions` of the `query` option, `{}` when there are none, which Netjes's setup file reads with `inject()`. `createTestApp()` merges them over the Netjes defaults, with its own `retryDelay: 0`, and `gcTime: Infinity` for queries, over them ([Queries that fail](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md#queries-that-fail)). Not set with `query: false`. The app's own `provide` keys are kept. In Vitest's browser mode the value travels as JSON, so an `Infinity` in it arrives as `null` |

It sets no `include`, so Vitest's own pattern (`*.test.*` and `*.spec.*` files) applies outside those folders. Tests then render with `createTestApp()` from `netjes/testing`; see [Testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md).

Under Vitest 5, an inline project in `test.projects` that changes no Vite options shares the Vite server of the config that declares it (`sharedViteServer`, on by default), and Vitest builds its `test` options from that config's as written, before any plugin adds to them. Such a project gets none of the plugin's `environment`, `exclude` and setup files, so its tests get neither the [fake-timer bridge](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/docs/guides/testing.md#fake-timers) nor the app's query defaults in `createTestApp()`. Set `sharedViteServer: false` in the root's `test` options, and Vitest resolves the config for each project, with the plugin's settings.

## The dev server

In development the .NET app starts a Node process that runs the Vite dev server with this config, and renders pages through it. The browser loads modules and hot updates from that server, on its own port.

- It listens on port 5173, which `Netjes:ViteDevPort` changes, with `strictPort`: the browser loads modules and hot updates from that port, so when something else has it the dev server does not move to another one. The app logs that the port is in use and how to move Vite (`Netjes__ViteDevPort=5174`), in one line, and stops with exit code 1; `netjes dev` checks the port before it starts the app.
- When it does not start for another reason, such as an error in `vite.config.ts` or a package the config imports that is not installed, the app logs what Vite reported, its code frame included, and what to do (`npm install` for a package it cannot find), in one log entry, and stops with exit code 1.
- It binds to `localhost`. `NETJES_VITE_HOST=0.0.0.0` in the environment of `npm run dev` exposes it to the network, as the template's development container does; `NETJES_VITE_ORIGIN` sets the origin the browser uses, when it reaches the server by another address.
- It may read files from the workspace root, unless your config sets `server.fs.allow`, and from the `netjes` package.

The dev server's root is the app's folder, which also holds the .NET side, so the plugin denies these to the dev server, on top of Vite's own defaults (`.env`, `.env.*`, certificates and `.git`):

- `appsettings*.json`, `launchSettings.json`, `secrets.json`, `nuget.config` and `*.user` files;
- `*.cs`, `*.csproj`, `*.pdb` and `*.dll` files, `Directory.Build.*` and `global.json`;
- dev certificates and keys (`*.pfx`, `*.p12`, `*.key`) and SQLite databases (`*.db`, `*.sqlite`, `*.sqlite3`);
- Compose files (`compose*.yml`, `docker-compose*.yml`, and `.yaml`);
- the `bin/`, `obj/` and `dist/server/` folders below the workspace root.

A `server.fs.deny` of your own is added to that list. Everything else under the allowed folders is readable by anyone who can reach the port, which is why the server binds to localhost: expose it only on a network you trust.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/packages/netjes/README.md -->

# netjes

The npm half of [Netjes](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes), a React framework for building apps and sites on ASP.NET Core: pages in `app/` with the Next.js App Router conventions, C# loaders and server actions, server rendering, client navigation. This package holds the Vite plugin, the client router and components, the Node sidecar that renders pages for the .NET app, the `netjes` command and the app template. The ASP.NET Core half is the [`Netjes`](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Netjes) NuGet package, released at the same version.

## Start an app

You need Node.js `^22.22.2 || ^24.15.0 || >=26.0.0` (Node.js 22.22.2 or a later 22, 24.15.0 or a later 24, or 26 or newer) and the .NET 10 SDK.

```bash
npx netjes new my-app
cd my-app
npm run dev          # http://localhost:5080
```

`netjes new` writes an ASP.NET Core app with React pages, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query, zod, Vitest and Docker files, and references `netjes` and `Netjes` at the same exact version.

## Add it to a project

```bash
npm install netjes@0.0.2 react react-dom zod @tanstack/react-query
npm install -D vite tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite
```

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import netjes from 'netjes/vite';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [netjes()] });
```

Tailwind CSS and the TanStack Query client are on by default; `netjes({ tailwind: false, query: false })` turns them off, and then they need not be installed. `vitest`, `jsdom`, `@testing-library/react` and `web-vitals` are optional peers, used when installed. Use the version of `netjes` that matches the app's `Netjes` NuGet package; `npx netjes info` checks it.

## Entry points

| Import | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `netjes` | Components and hooks: `Link`, `Form`, `Image`, `Script`, `definePage`, `useAction`, `useRouter` and the rest, and `CSP_SCRIPT_HASHES`, the hashes of Netjes's inline scripts for a Content-Security-Policy without a nonce |
| `netjes/vite` | The Vite plugin |
| `netjes/testing` | `createTestApp()`, for rendering pages and components in Vitest, and `renderDocument()` and `inlineScriptHashes()`, for a page's whole document and the inline scripts in it |
| `netjes/vitals` | `useReportWebVitals` and `<WebVitals />` |
| `netjes/zod` | `deferred(schema)`, for values that loaders stream with `Page.Defer` |
| `netjes` (bin) | The command: `new`, `dev`, `build`, `start`, `generate`, `routes`, `export`, `info`, `agents` |

Each import is an ES module with its type declarations, so an app's `tsc` reads the declarations and checks only the app's own code, also under stricter compiler options such as `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` or `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` (see [TypeScript setup](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/reference/vite-plugin.md#typescript-setup)). The TypeScript sources are in the package too, for the source maps: an editor's go to definition and a stack trace lead to them.

## Documentation

- [Getting started](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md)
- [All guides](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/README.md)
- [React API](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/reference/react-api.md)
- [Vite plugin](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/reference/vite-plugin.md)
- [The netjes command](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/reference/cli.md)

Report bugs in the [issue tracker](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/issues), and security problems privately, as the [security policy](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/security/policy) describes. MIT licensed.

# Netjes

The ASP.NET Core half of [Netjes](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes), a React framework for building apps and sites on ASP.NET Core. Pages live in `app/` with the Next.js App Router conventions; this package turns them into endpoints, runs their C# loaders and server actions, renders them through a supervised pool of Node processes, and handles caching, images and the generated TypeScript types. The npm package [`netjes`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/netjes), released at the same version, is the other half: the Vite plugin, the client router and the renderer.

## Start an app

```bash
npx netjes new my-app
```

That writes an app with both halves set up. To add Netjes to a project you have, reference this package and install the npm half at the same version (0.0.2 here; the two are released together):

```bash
dotnet add package Netjes --version 0.0.2
npm install netjes@0.0.2 react react-dom zod @tanstack/react-query
```

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc; // for [FromForm]

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddNetjes();

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseNetjes();
app.UseAntiforgery(); // after authentication, if you have it

app.MapPageLoader("/", (TimeProvider time) => Page.Props(new HomeProps("Hello from C#", time.GetUtcNow())));
app.MapAction("home.greet", ([FromForm] GreetInput input) => ServerAction.Ok(new Greeting($"Hello, {input.Name}!")));
app.MapPages(); // every other page file, plus the 404 fallback

app.Run();

public sealed record HomeProps(string Message, DateTimeOffset RenderedAt);
public sealed record GreetInput { public string? Name { get; init; } }
public sealed record Greeting(string Text);
```

The package adds build targets to the project: `using Netjes` when implicit usings are on, `node_modules` and `dist` kept out of the build, and `dotnet publish` running `npm run build` and shipping `dist/`. The app needs the .NET 10 SDK and, at build time and in production, Node.js `^22.22.2 || ^24.15.0 || >=26.0.0` (Node.js 22.22.2 or a later 22, 24.15.0 or a later 24, or 26 or newer).

- [All guides](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/README.md)
- [C# API](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/reference/csharp-api.md)

# Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp

Image processing for the [Netjes](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Netjes) `<Image>` endpoint, built on SkiaSharp (MIT). Without it the endpoint serves originals (cached); with it, images are resized to the requested width, never larger than the source, and encoded as WebP.

## Install

```bash
dotnet add package Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp --version 0.0.2
```

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNetjes();
builder.Services.AddNetjesSkiaImages();   // before or after AddNetjes()
```

Options:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNetjesSkiaImages(o =>
{
    o.MaxPixels = 40_000_000;                    // refuse images whose header declares more (default)
    o.MaxConcurrency = Environment.ProcessorCount; // images decoded and encoded at once (default)
});
```

## What it does

- Decodes PNG, JPEG and WebP only, and only bytes that start with the declared format's signature. Output is WebP when the browser accepts it, otherwise JPEG and WebP sources keep their format and PNG stays PNG.
- Applies the EXIF orientation, and decodes large JPEGs at a reduced size.
- GIFs (possibly animated) and AVIFs pass through unchanged. Every other format (BMP and ICO, for example), bytes that do not match their declared format, and images that fail to decode are refused, not passed through.
- Images whose header declares more than `MaxPixels` are refused before decoding (refused like any other image it cannot process), since a small file can claim a huge size.
- A refused image answers 400 from the endpoint when it is a local file and 502 when it is a remote image (the remote host supplied bad bytes).
- Linux builds use `SkiaSharp.NativeAssets.Linux.NoDependencies`, so it runs in the slim ASP.NET Core images.

## Security

This package decodes bytes that visitors and remote hosts control, with native codecs (libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp and others inside SkiaSharp's Skia build). Native image codecs have a history of memory-safety vulnerabilities, so keep the SkiaSharp packages current: update `Netjes.Images.SkiaSharp` and watch SkiaSharp releases and advisories. The pixel limit and concurrency cap bound resource use but do not protect against a codec bug. Restrict `Netjes:Images:RemoteHosts` to hosts you trust and leave `AllowSvg` off.

Use the same version as `Netjes` (0.0.2 above); the two are released together. The [images guide](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/images.md) covers `<Image>`, the endpoint's limits and `IImageProcessor`. MIT licensed.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/packages/netjes/skills/netjes/SKILL.md -->

# Building a Netjes app

Netjes renders React pages from ASP.NET Core. C# receives every request and owns routing, loaders, server actions, authorization and caching. A Node sidecar renders the React tree to HTML; the browser hydrates it, and later navigations fetch the next page's props as JSON from the same C# endpoints. The file conventions in `app/` are the Next.js App Router's, but there are no React Server Components and no `route.ts`: data comes from C# loaders, and APIs are minimal API endpoints.

## Where things go

- `app/**/page.tsx`: a page. `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` serves `/blog/{slug}`. Layouts, boundaries and folder rules: [references/routing.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/packages/netjes/skills/netjes/references/routing.md).
- `Features/<Feature>/*.cs`: the C# side of a feature, mapped by an extension method that `Program.cs` calls before `app.MapPages()`. Loaders and actions: [references/data-and-actions.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/packages/netjes/skills/netjes/references/data-and-actions.md).
- `generated/netjes.ts`: zod schemas and typed references generated from the C# types and the page files. Read it to see what a page receives; never edit it.
- `components/`: React components and their tests. Testing: [references/testing.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/packages/netjes/skills/netjes/references/testing.md).

## The loop for any change

1. Write the failing test first: a Vitest component test, or a C# test for loader and action logic.
2. Change the C# record, loader or action, then run `npx netjes generate` so `generated/netjes.ts` matches (a running `npm run dev` rewrites it when it restarts).
3. Use the generated names in React: `pages['/pattern']`, `layouts['app/folder']`, `serverActions['name']`, `api['GET /api/...']`, `route('/pattern', params)`, `endpointUrl('GET /api/...', params)`.
4. Check: `npm test`, `npm run typecheck`, `dotnet build` (warnings are errors), `npx netjes generate --check`, and `npm run routes` for route warnings.

## A page with data, end to end

```csharp
// Features/Posts/PostPages.cs
namespace MyApp.Features.Posts;

public static class PostPages
{
    public sealed record PostProps(string Slug, string Title, string Body);

    public static void MapPostPages(this IEndpointRouteBuilder app)
    {
        // The parameter name matches [slug]; Page.Props names the props type for the generated schema.
        app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, PostStore posts) =>
            posts.Find(slug) is { } post
                ? Page.Props(new PostProps(post.Slug, post.Title, post.Body))
                    .WithMetadata(new PageMetadata { Title = post.Title })
                : Page.NotFound());
    }
}
```

```tsx
// app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx
import { Link, definePage } from 'netjes';
import { pages, route } from '../../../generated/netjes.ts';

export default definePage(pages['/blog/[slug]'], function Post({ title, body }) {
  return (
    <article>
      <Link href={route('/blog')}>All posts</Link>
      <h1>{title}</h1>
      <p>{body}</p>
    </article>
  );
});
```

`Program.cs` calls `app.MapPostPages();` before `app.MapPages();`. A page without a loader is a plain default export with no props.

## Rules

- Decisions live in C#: data access, validation, authorization (`.RequireAuthorization()`, `Page.Forbidden()`), redirects, caching. React renders what it is sent.
- Loaders and actions return Netjes results (`Page.Props(...)`, `Page.NotFound()`, `ServerAction.Ok(...)`), so their types reach `generated/netjes.ts`. Use records for everything that crosses to the browser.
- zod at every boundary: `definePage`/`defineLayout` with the generated schemas, `useSearchParams(schema)` and `useParams(schema)` (schemas at module level), `api[...].response.parse(...)` for fetched JSON (from `useHref(endpointUrl(...))`, never a hand-built URL), `usePublicConfig(schema)`, `Href.parse(...)` or `isHref(...)` for URLs from a CMS. A link C# sends to one of the app's pages is a `Href` in the record (`new Href("/about")`), generated as the `Href` schema, so it reaches `<Link href>` checked; a link to an endpoint or a file stays a `string`. No `any`, no casts of server data.
- Server state goes through TanStack Query, seeded from the loader with `.WithQuery(key, data)`; no `useEffect` fetching.
- Internal links use `<Link>` and `route()`; forms use `<Form>` with `useAction`, and must work without JavaScript.
- Give each page a title of its own (`metadata`, or `PageMetadata` from C#), and keep the "Skip to content" link the first thing in `app/layout.tsx` that takes the focus: after a client navigation the router announces the page by its title and starts the focus over at the top ([references/routing.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/packages/netjes/skills/netjes/references/routing.md)).
- Never edit `generated/netjes.ts`; regenerate it and commit it with the change.
- Anything in `Netjes:PublicConfig` or shared props is sent to the browser. So is the route of each endpoint with an `endpointUrl` key, one mapped only in Development included, once any component calls `endpointUrl`: keep secrets out of routes, and authorize on the endpoint.
- Caching, streaming and static export have sharp edges: read [references/caching-and-streaming.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/packages/netjes/skills/netjes/references/caching-and-streaming.md) before using `.CachePage`, `Page.Defer` or `netjes export`.
- Shipping: [references/deployment.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/packages/netjes/skills/netjes/references/deployment.md).

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm run dev` | `dotnet watch` with Vite HMR on http://localhost:5080 |
| `npm test`, `npm run typecheck` | Vitest; strict TypeScript |
| `npx netjes generate [--check]` | Rewrite `generated/netjes.ts`; `--check` fails when it is stale |
| `npm run routes` (`netjes routes [--json]`) | The route table and route warnings, as ASP.NET Core sees them |
| `npx netjes build` | Types, then the client and server bundles |
| `npx netjes start` | Run in Production |
| `npx netjes export [dir]` | Write the site as static HTML |
| `npx netjes info` | Versions and a check of the project setup |

## More

The guides go further than these references: [routing](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/routing.md), [data loading](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md), [actions and forms](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md), [rendering and streaming](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/rendering-and-streaming.md), [caching](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/caching.md), [images](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/images.md), [metadata](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/metadata.md), [security](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/security.md), [testing](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/testing.md) and [deployment](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/deployment.md), with the [React API](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/reference/react-api.md), the [C# API](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/reference/csharp-api.md) and the [options](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/reference/options.md) as reference.

The same docs as plain text: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/llms.txt (an index) and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/llms-full.txt (everything in one file). They follow the main branch; the installed version's sources and types are in `node_modules/netjes/`.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/packages/netjes/skills/netjes/references/routing.md -->

# Routing

ASP.NET Core does the routing: every page file becomes an endpoint with an ordinary route template, so precedence, constraints and conventions such as `RequireAuthorization()` work as for any minimal API. The browser never matches routes itself.

## Files in `app/`

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `page.tsx` | The page for its folder's URL. |
| `layout.tsx` | Wraps every page below it and stays mounted across navigations (its state survives). The root `app/layout.tsx` imports the global stylesheet. Netjes renders `<html>`, `<head>` and `<body>` around the root layout, with `suppressHydrationWarning` on `<html>` and `<body>`, so no layout renders them: the root one returns what goes inside `<body>`. |
| `template.tsx` | Like a layout, but remounted on every navigation. |
| `loading.tsx` | Suspense fallback, streamed first while the page below waits on deferred values or lazy code. |
| `error.tsx` | Error boundary below its layout; props `{ error, reset }` (`ErrorPageProps`), status in `error.status`. Render `error.message` only when `!error.withheld`: `withheld` marks a stand-in for a message Netjes does not show (an exception's with error details off, a thrown value without one). In development `error.message` can take several lines (a syntax error's code frame): render it with `whitespace-pre-wrap`. |
| `not-found.tsx` | Rendered for `Page.NotFound()` from a loader below it, and the root one for unknown URLs. |
| `forbidden.tsx`, `unauthorized.tsx` | Rendered for `Page.Forbidden()` / `Page.Unauthorized()` and for empty 403/401 responses from authorization; without one, the error page renders. |
| `global-error.tsx` | In `app/` only: rendered without any layout when even the error page fails. |

Built-in pages stand in for missing boundary files.

## Folders

| Folder | URL |
|---|---|
| `blog/[slug]` | `/blog/{slug}`: one segment |
| `docs/[...path]` | `/docs/a/b`: one or more segments; the loader gets them joined by `/` |
| `docs/[[...path]]` | `/docs` and anything below it |
| `(group)` | No URL segment: groups pages under a shared layout (`app/(marketing)/layout.tsx`) |
| `_private` | Not routed: components that live next to the pages |
| `@slot` + `default.tsx` | A parallel route: the layout gets the slot as a prop |
| `@modal/(.)photo/[id]` | An intercepting route, inside a slot only: a client navigation shows it in the slot, a reload shows the real page |

A literal segment beats a dynamic one (`blog/new` over `blog/[slug]`), as in Next.js. Two page files of the same shape (`[lang]/about` and `[slug]/about`) stop the app at startup. There is no pages router: Next.js pages router files in `pages/` stop the app at startup, and the message says where each goes (`pages/about.js` to `app/about/page.jsx`, `pages/404.tsx` to `app/not-found.tsx`, `pages/_app.tsx` and `pages/_document.tsx` to the root `app/layout.tsx`, `pages/api/` routes to minimal API endpoints). There are no route handlers either: a `route.ts` in `app/` stops the app in development and fails `vite build`, and an API is a minimal API endpoint in C# (`app.MapGet`, `app.MapPost`).

## One URL per page

A page answers its file's spelling: a `GET` or `HEAD` for `/About` for `app/about/page.tsx` gets a 308 to `/about`, and a client navigation a redirect payload, so links and crawlers see one URL, and the output cache stores no other case that a browser sends (`RedirectLiteralCase`, on by default; `options.RedirectLiteralCase = false`, or `Netjes:RedirectLiteralCase=false`, answers every case). Other methods are answered as sent: a `POST` to `/About` is not redirected. Only literal segments change; route values (`/Blog/Hello` goes to `/blog/Hello`), the query and the base path stay as sent, so a loader that redirected to its own spelling of a literal can drop that check, while one that checks a slug's case keeps it. A trailing slash is answered as it is (`TrailingSlash.Ignore`); `options.TrailingSlash = TrailingSlash.Never` (`Netjes:TrailingSlash=Never`) sends `/about/` to `/about` and drops a catch-all's last slash. The `/robots.txt` and `/sitemap.xml` that `MapRobotsTxt` and `MapSitemap` serve follow both. `WebApplicationFactory` tests run on TestServer, which passes on no request target, so they see no redirect: check it end to end with Playwright, or set `IHttpRequestFeature.RawTarget` in a startup filter, as the testing guide shows.

## Loader parameters and route warnings

Loaders bind like minimal APIs: a string or `TryParse` parameter takes the route value of the same name (any case), and otherwise the query string. `(string id)` on `/blog/[slug]` therefore reads `?id=`, never the slug, and `string[] path` on `[...path]` reads `?path=`. Netjes logs a warning for that at startup, and `npm run routes` prints it. Name parameters after the route segment, or mark query parameters `[FromQuery]`. Another warning is two pages that match the same URLs (`[id]` next to `[...rest]`); rename one, or accept it if the overlap is wanted. Others are an endpoint of the app that ties with a page (below), and a `[FromForm]` positional record with a `bool`, `bool?` or list field, which form binding refuses (400) when the post leaves that field out, as for an unchecked box: give the input `init` properties instead.

## Endpoints next to pages

ASP.NET Core ranks the endpoints a URL matches by order (pages and `MapGet` endpoints have 0), then route precedence (a literal, a constrained parameter, a parameter, a constrained catch-all, then a catch-all), then HTTP methods, hosts and accepted content types, in that order. When two rank first together and both fit a request, it answers 500 (`AmbiguousMatchException`); Netjes warns about such an endpoint next to a page or a page action at startup and in `npm run routes`. A file next to a catch-all page, such as a Markdown copy of each docs page next to `app/docs/[...path]/page.tsx`, ranks the same as the page, so map it ahead of it and for HEAD as well: `app.MapMethods("/docs/{**path:regex(\\.md$)}", [HttpMethods.Get, HttpMethods.Head], ...).WithOrder(-1)`. Link it with `<a href={useHref(endpointUrl('GET /docs/{**path:regex(\\.md$)}', { path }))}>`; a bare `<a href>` misses the base path.

## Links and navigation

- `<Link href={route('/blog/[slug]', { slug })}>`: client navigation with prefetch on hover and focus; takes a `ref`, as `<Form>`, `<SubmitButton>` and `<Image>` do. `route()` and the `Href` type come from `generated/netjes.ts`, so a wrong path or a missing parameter is a type error.
- `route(pattern, params, search, { hash })` builds the query from `search` and a `#fragment` from `hash`, the id of an element on the page: `route('/docs/[...path]', { path }, undefined, { hash: 'keys' })`. Pass `undefined` as `search` for a link with a fragment and no query.
- `aria-current="page"` goes on a link to the page on screen: the same path (`/x` and `/x/` are one) and the page's values for every query parameter the link names. Parameters it leaves out do not count, and a `#` link is never marked. Pass `aria-current` to decide yourself: `undefined` on an "All" filter (`/blog`) while a filter is on, `"true"` on a section link (Docs) below the section's page, from `useSelectedLayoutSegments()` or `usePathname()`.
- `useRouter()`: `push`, `replace`, `prefetch`, `refresh`, `back`, `forward`. The promises of `push`, `replace` and `refresh` resolve once the router has handed the page to React, when the old page can still be on screen; code that needs the new page runs in an effect of that page, or in one that depends on `usePathname()` and `useSearchParams()`.
- After a navigation to another page the router announces it in a polite live region (its title, else its first `h1`, else its path) and starts the focus over at the top of the document. A link to a `#fragment`, on the page on screen or on another, moves the focus to that element instead, which is how the skip link works; Back and Forward restore the scroll position and give a fragment no focus. The region speaks only when the name differs from the previous page's, so give each page its own title, and keep the skip link first in the root layout: `<Link href="#content" prefetch="none" className="sr-only focus:not-sr-only">Skip to content</Link>` and `<main id="content">`. The focus stays on the same page (query changes, refreshes, a post that stays, a modal), on an `autoFocus` element or wherever the app's code moved it during the navigation (a link's `onClick` and a form's `onSubmit` included), on a `scroll={false}` link that still has it, and in a field the user types into. To put it elsewhere on the new page, do it in that page's `useEffect`, which runs after the router's. If a menu closes in an effect after the navigation, give the focus back to its button only while the focus is still inside the menu. In end-to-end tests, focus a field before typing after a navigation (`locator.fill()` does), and read the element you mean rather than a container's whole text.
- `usePathname()`, `useSearchParams(schema?)`, `useParams(schema?)`: with a schema the values are parsed; catch-all params are arrays. Search values a schema rejects are dropped so its defaults apply; a rejected route param goes to the error page, so constrain route params in C#.
- `useSelectedLayoutSegment()`, `useSelectedLayoutSegments()`: the active child segment in a layout (tabs).
- `useNavigation()`: `idle`, `loading` or `submitting`, for progress indicators.
- External URLs, `target`, `download` and modified clicks behave like a plain `<a>`; `reloadDocument` forces a full load.

## Metadata

- `export const metadata: Metadata = { title: 'About' }` on pages and layouts; a layout's `title: { default, template: '%s · Site' }` applies to the pages below it. A `default` below the root goes through the nearest template above it, like a string (`'Docs'` under `'%s · Site'` is `Docs · Site`), never through the one beside it; `{ absolute: 'Docs' }` skips every template.
- From C#: `.WithMetadata(new PageMetadata { Title = post.Title, Description = ... })` on the loader's result, merged over the files' metadata.
- Below a layout that sets a title, use `metadata`, not a `<title>` element (that makes a second title).
- Code the first paint needs, such as a theme set on `<html>`, goes in `<Script id="theme" strategy="beforeInteractive">{code}</Script>` first in the root layout: the server writes inline code where it stands and the parser runs it there. An external `beforeInteractive` script runs once the shell is parsed, in order, before the page's code; hydration waits for it, and inline code runs before it. Keep them outside Suspense boundaries. Under a hash-based policy, list the hash of the code as the document carries it, which `inlineScriptHashes` from `netjes/testing` gives.

## Protecting sections

`app.MapLayoutLoader("/dashboard", ...).RequireAuthorization()` protects every page below `app/dashboard/`; `app.MapPages().RequireAuthorization()` protects every page that has no loader of its own; a page loader takes `.RequireAuthorization()` itself. With cookie authentication, answer 401/403 instead of redirecting (`OnRedirectToLogin`, `OnRedirectToAccessDenied`) so `unauthorized.tsx` and `forbidden.tsx` render.

A check that depends on data (is this user a member of this project?) goes in the page loader as well as in the layout loader: a page's loader runs before its layouts' loaders, and a layout loader is skipped on client navigations within its section while its own route values, the user and the roles stay the same. A layout loader also binds only the route values of its own URL, so it cannot check a deeper one.

## Base path and locales

`app.UsePathBase("/docs")` with `netjes({ basePath: '/docs' })`; links, forms and redirects add it, and app code is written as if at the root (`useHref(path)` for a plain `<a>`). Locale routing is a `[lang]` folder with `AddNetjesLocalization`, `UseNetjesLocalization` and `MapLocaleRedirect`; `useLocale()` reads it.

## More

[Routing](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/routing.md) and [Metadata](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/metadata.md) in the guides, and the [React API](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/reference/react-api.md) for every component and hook.

<!-- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/main/packages/netjes/skills/netjes/references/data-and-actions.md -->

# Data and actions

Everything a page shows comes from C#: page loaders, layout loaders, shared props and JSON endpoints. Everything a page changes goes through C#: server actions. Their C# types become zod schemas and typed references in `generated/netjes.ts`.

## Page loaders

```csharp
app.MapPageLoader("/projects/[id]", async (string id, ClaimsPrincipal user, AppDb db, CancellationToken ct) =>
{
    var project = await db.FindProjectAsync(id, ct);
    if (project is null) return Page.NotFound();
    if (!project.HasMember(user)) return Page.Forbidden();
    return Page.Props(new ProjectProps(project.Name, project.Tasks))
        .WithQuery(["projects", id, "stats"], await db.StatsAsync(id, ct))
        .WithMetadata(new PageMetadata { Title = project.Name });
});
```

- It binds like a minimal API: route values by name, services, `ClaimsPrincipal`, `HttpContext`, `CancellationToken`, `[FromQuery]`.
- It reads no request body, so a complex type that is not a registered service needs `[AsParameters]` or a static `BindAsync`. A loader or action whose parameters minimal APIs cannot bind stops the app at startup, saying which and why. So does a loader parameter that reads the body (`[FromBody]`, `[FromForm]`, `IFormFile`): posted data belongs in a page action or a server action. A page loader stops the app too for a type that adds accepts metadata (`IAcceptsMetadata`) for itself, and must not get `.Accepts<T>()`: routing would match the page only for requests with that Content-Type, and navigations would get the not-found page. Repeated query values bind to an array (`int[] ids`); `List<int>` and `IEnumerable<int>` stop the app at startup, the latter because minimal APIs would bind it from services.
- `Page.Props(record)` names the props type for `pages['/projects/[id]']`. `Page.NotFound()`, `Page.Forbidden()`, `Page.Unauthorized()` render the nearest boundary file; `Page.Redirect(url)` and `Page.LocalRedirect(returnUrl)` (for URLs from the request) redirect, and the client router follows them. `.WithStatus(422)` changes the status.
- A link to one of the app's pages is a `Href` in the props record (`public sealed record NavLink(Href Href, string Label)`, `new Href($"/projects/{Uri.EscapeDataString(id)}")`, with each value encoded), root-relative, in the page file's spelling (the props parse compares literal segments with their case, so `/About` fails for `app/about/page.tsx`) and without the base path. It is generated as the `Href` schema, so the props parse checks it against the pages and the component passes it to `<Link href>` as it is. `new Href(url)` throws `ArgumentException` unless the URL starts with `/` (and not `//` or `/\`), `?`, `#`, `http:`, `https:`, `mailto:` or `tel:`, and also for a control character anywhere in it or a space at either end; `Href.TryCreate` returns false instead. C# checks only that shape: a root-relative `Href` that no page serves fails the whole props parse and the page shows its error boundary (a 500 from the server only when no Suspense boundary, such as a `loading.tsx`, is above the component that parses; otherwise the server sends that boundary's fallback with the loader's status), so a link to an endpoint or a file, such as `/llms.txt`, stays a `string`, rendered with `useHref`, and so does a link from a CMS, checked with `isHref` where it is rendered. No query or route value binds to an `Href`: a `returnUrl` stays a `string` for `Page.LocalRedirect`, and a `[FromForm]` input takes a `string`, since form binding reads no `Href` from the field of its name. `LinkGenerator`'s `HttpContext` overloads add the base path, so pass `pathBase: PathString.Empty`.
- It returns a `RouteHandlerBuilder`: `.RequireAuthorization()`, `.CachePage(...)` and filters apply.
- A page's loader runs before its layouts' loaders, so a page under a layout that checks access checks it too.

## Layout loaders

`app.MapLayoutLoader("/projects/[id]", ...)` loads the data of `app/.../projects/[id]/layout.tsx` (by URL, or by folder: `app/(shop)`). The layout reads it with `defineLayout(layouts['app/(app)/projects/[id]'], function Layout({ project, children }) { ... })`. Its conventions (`.RequireAuthorization()`) apply to every page below. `NotFound`/`Forbidden` from it render the nearest boundary above the layout.

- It binds only the route values of its own URL (`id` here, never a deeper `taskId`; a `[FromRoute]` naming one stops the app at startup), the query string and services. Nothing binds from a body: a complex type needs to be a service, `[AsParameters]` or bind itself, and `[FromBody]`, `[FromForm]` or a file stops the app at startup.
- On client navigations within the section it is skipped while its route values, user and roles are unchanged, so checks that must run on every request belong in conventions or page loaders, and it must not depend on the query string or cookies.

## Shared props

`options.UseSharedProps(http => ValueTask.FromResult(new SiteProps(...)))` in `AddNetjes` gives every page and layout the same props: `useSharedProps(sharedProps)`. Typical: the signed-in user, from `http.User`. They are sent to the browser.

## Server actions

```csharp
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc; // [FromForm]: not in the implicit usings

public sealed record Renamed(string Name);

public sealed record RenameInput
{
    [Required] public string Id { get; init; } = "";
    [Required(ErrorMessage = "Give it a name."), StringLength(100)] public string Name { get; init; } = "";
}

app.MapAction("projects.rename", async ([FromForm] RenameInput input, AppDb db, CancellationToken ct) =>
    await db.TryRenameAsync(input.Id, input.Name, ct)
        ? ServerAction.Ok(new Renamed(input.Name)).RevalidatePath($"/projects/{input.Id}")
        : ServerAction.Invalid("name", "That name is taken."));
```

```tsx
const [state, formAction, pending] = useAction(serverActions['projects.rename']);
const nameError = state?.ok === false ? state.errors.name?.[0] : undefined;

<Form action={formAction}>
  <input type="hidden" name="id" value={id} />
  <input name="name" defaultValue={state?.ok === false ? String(state.values?.name ?? '') : name} aria-invalid={nameError ? true : undefined} />
  {nameError && <p>{nameError}</p>}
  <button disabled={pending}>Rename</button>
</Form>
```

- Results: `ServerAction.Ok(result)` or `Ok()`, `Invalid(field, message)` or `Invalid(errors)` (422), `Redirect(url)`, `Forbidden()`, `NotFound()`. Chain `.Revalidate(tags)` and `.RevalidatePath(paths)` (evict output-cached pages and refresh the page), `.Refresh()`, `.Invalidate(queryKey)` and `.WithQuery(queryKey, data)` (TanStack Query on the client).
- `[FromForm]` inputs make the form work without JavaScript: the browser posts, a success redirects back, a failure renders the page again with the errors and the typed values. Keep that working.
- An input without `[FromForm]` binds JSON: `await serverActions['posts.like']({ slug })` resolves to `{ ok: true, result }` or `{ ok: false, errors }`; server failures throw to the nearest error boundary.
- Validation: DataAnnotations (`[Required]`, `[StringLength]`, `[Range]`, `[EmailAddress]`) and `IValidatableObject` on an action's input are checked before the action runs (for a polymorphic JSON input, those of the `[JsonDerivedType]` the call sends). Failures come back as field errors (422, `state.errors`), also without JavaScript, and the action is not called. This needs no setup: `builder.Services.AddValidation()` is for your other minimal API endpoints, not for `MapAction` or `MapPageAction`. An attribute that cannot be read, such as a `[Display]` whose resource type has no such name, stops the app at startup, also on a derived type a JSON input lists with `[JsonDerivedType]`. A `[FromForm]` input is never `null` (unless declared nullable): a post with none of its fields, such as a form of unchecked checkboxes, gets an empty input, checked like any other. Give form inputs `init` properties, as above, not constructor parameters: a field the post leaves out (an unchecked checkbox, a list with nothing chosen) keeps its default, while form binding refuses such a post (400) for a positional record. A form input, and each type its properties and lists hold, needs exactly one public constructor: form binding never builds a type with several or none, or an abstract class or an interface, so that stops the app at startup. Bind a checkbox group or a list as a property of the input type (`public string[] Tags { get; init; } = [];`), not as a top-level `[FromForm]` parameter: a top-level list or dictionary reads fields named `[0]` or `[key]`, not its own name, and is `null` when none is posted.
- Optimistic UI: `useAction(action, { onSubmit(formData) { setOptimistic(...) } })` with React's `useOptimistic`.
- Every action needs `app.UseAntiforgery()` (after authentication) and checks the origin; `<Form>` and `serverActions` send the token. `MapAction` bodies are limited to 1 MB (`ActionBodySizeLimit`); an upload action sets `[RequestSizeLimit(bytes)]`. Page actions keep the server's limit.
- Name actions `feature.verb`. Check authorization inside the action, or with `.RequireAuthorization()`, as for any endpoint.
- `app.MapPageAction("/guestbook", ...)` is the other kind: a POST to the page's own URL from `<Form method="post">`, fields typed in `forms['/guestbook']`. Its input's DataAnnotations and `IValidatableObject` are checked as for `MapAction`: on a failure the delegate does not run, the page renders again from its loader (422), and `const failed = usePageActionState()` gives `failed.errors` and `failed.values` (null otherwise). Checks that need data stay in the delegate: return `Page.Props(...)` with your own errors and the typed values (`.WithStatus(422)`), or `Page.Redirect(...)` after a change.
- An action or post that sets or deletes a cookie (signing in or out) makes the client router forget the pages it keeps for back and forward, reload the page on screen and clear the query cache, in every tab of the app in that browser. Nothing to do in the action; a proxy must pass `X-Netjes-Cookies` through.

## JSON endpoints and TanStack Query

```csharp
app.MapGet("/api/projects/{slug}/stats", async Task<Results<Ok<ProjectStats>, NotFound>> (string slug, AppDb db) => ...)
    .RequireAuthorization();
```

```ts
async function fetchStats(url: string) {
  const response = await fetch(url);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Stats request failed with ${response.status}`);
  return api['GET /api/projects/{slug}/stats'].response.parse(await response.json());
}
const url = useHref(endpointUrl('GET /api/projects/{slug}/stats', { slug }));
const stats = useQuery({ queryKey: ['projects', slug, 'stats'], queryFn: () => fetchStats(url) });
```

Typed results (`TypedResults`, `Results<...>`) give the endpoint its `api` schemas, keyed by method and route template. `endpointUrl(key, params, search)` builds the URL of the app's endpoints that are not pages, JSON or not (a JSON endpoint has a key per method except `HEAD`, any other endpoint one for `GET`, if it answers `GET`), by the same key: the route values and the query values its handler binds are typed from C#, an enum as its C# names and values, and `search` adds others. It has no base path: `useHref` adds it, for a `fetch` or an `<a href>`. `<Link>` refuses it, as an endpoint is not a page. Seed the same query key from the loader with `.WithQuery(key, data)` and the query renders on the server with no fetch; keep the key in one place on each side. Seeded data is fresh for the default `staleTime` (one minute).

`MapGet` answers `GET` only: a `HEAD` to its URL goes to whatever else matches it, often the not-found page. For an endpoint that crawlers, link checkers or monitors ask with `HEAD`, map `app.MapMethods(pattern, [HttpMethods.Get, HttpMethods.Head], handler)`; its `api` key stays `GET` and the route. Pages, `/sitemap.xml`, `/robots.txt`, `/_netjes/image` and the locale redirect answer `HEAD` already.

## More

[Data loading](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/data-loading.md) and [Actions and forms](https://github.com/DennisVerhoeven/netjes/blob/main/docs/guides/actions-and-forms.md) in the guides.

# Caching, streaming and static export

## Output-cached pages

```csharp
builder.Services.AddOutputCache();
// ...
app.UseNetjes();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.UseAntiforgery();
app.UseOutputCache();          // after UseNetjes and after UseAuthentication, so signed-in users bypass it

app.MapPageLoader("/blog/[slug]", (string slug, PostStore posts) => ...)
    .CachePage(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), "posts");
```

- A stored page is served to every visitor, shared props included. Cache only pages that are the same for everyone: their loaders and shared props must not depend on cookies or other per-visitor state (Netjes warns once per page when a cached render reads `Request.Cookies`). Signed-in users and requests with an `Authorization` header bypass the cache.
- Evict from an action with `ServerAction.Ok().Revalidate("posts")` or `.RevalidatePath("/blog/hello")`, and from anywhere else (a webhook, a background job) with `IPageCache.RevalidateTagAsync(tag)` / `RevalidatePathAsync(path)`.
- Cached pages carry no antiforgery token: forms on them fetch one first, so they need JavaScript.
- A Content-Security-Policy is off unless the app sets one. A document with a CSP nonce is never stored, so cached pages under a policy need a hash-based one (`ContentSecurityPolicy` without `{nonce}`), and under such a policy a page must not stream. Build it from `NetjesContentSecurityPolicy.ScriptHashes`, the hashes of Netjes's inline scripts, never from a pasted hash, which a Netjes upgrade can make stale: `$"script-src 'self' {NetjesContentSecurityPolicy.ScriptHashes}; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'"`. Keep `'self'` for the built app's module scripts, and leave out `'strict-dynamic'`, which needs a nonce. In the Development environment the module scripts come from the Vite dev server, so add its origin there, and only there, from a variable:

  ```csharp
  builder.Services.AddNetjes(options =>
  {
      var devServer = builder.Environment.IsDevelopment() ? $" http://localhost:{options.ViteDevPort}" : "";
      options.ContentSecurityPolicy =
          $"script-src 'self'{devServer} {NetjesContentSecurityPolicy.ScriptHashes}; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'";
  });
  ```

  When browsers reach the dev server at another address, the one set in `NETJES_VITE_ORIGIN`, list that origin instead. In Development a policy also needs these, or set it outside Development only:

  - With `connect-src`, or `default-src` without `connect-src`: Vite's HMR socket, `ws://` (`wss://` for an https origin) and the dev server's host and port, such as `ws://localhost:{options.ViteDevPort}`, which neither `'self'` nor a nonce covers.
  - With `style-src-elem` or `style-src`, or `default-src` without them: the document's nonce or `'unsafe-inline'`, for the CSS that Development inlines.
  - With `img-src` or `font-src`, or `default-src` without them: the dev server's origin, for the images and fonts Vite serves.

  Neither the nonce-based nor the hash-based policy needs `'unsafe-eval'`: zod parses without compiled code in the browser, from zod 4.4.0 on. Under a hash-based policy, give forms server actions through `useAction` and `<Form action={formAction}>`: any other function action, and any function on `<SubmitButton formAction>`, makes React add an inline script whose hash follows the React version and is not in `ScriptHashes`. In JavaScript, such as a static host's headers for exported pages, the same value is `CSP_SCRIPT_HASHES` from `netjes`. A nonce-based policy that the app writes itself takes its nonce from `HttpContext.GetCspNonce()`, the one Netjes puts on the document. Netjes logs a warning, once per policy, when the policy on a document refuses what the document needs (images and fonts aside).
- Keys include the host and the full URL, case included. In production pin `AllowedHosts` and set the output cache's `SizeLimit`.
- Pages the output cache does not store go out `Cache-Control: no-store, private`, for visitors and signed-in users alike, unless the page sets its own header.
- In the Development environment pages are never output-cached: each request renders the page, nothing is stored, and an output-cached page goes out `no-store, private` unless it sets its own `Cache-Control`, so `UseOutputCache()` can stay in every environment, with no Development guard. Cache slow or billed upstream data in the service that loads it (`IMemoryCache`, `HybridCache`). Try caching on the built app (`npx netjes build && npx netjes start`); a `WebApplicationFactory` test of it runs in the `Testing` environment with `Netjes:Mode=Development`.
- Draft pages and draft redirects (a loader's `Page.Redirect` in draft mode), the client-rendered fallback, the page for a failed form post, action answers and antiforgery tokens always go out `no-store`, and without the headers a CDN reads ahead of `Cache-Control` (`CDN-Cache-Control`, any other `*-Cache-Control`, `Surrogate-Control`, `Edge-Control`, `X-Accel-Expires`), whatever the page set.

## Endpoints that are not pages

JSON APIs, text files and webhooks are not pages, unless `CachePage` is put on them or on their group. The page rules do not apply to their cache entries.

- Netjes adds no `Cache-Control` to their answers, including the 400 that minimal API binding answers, and none under `CachePage` either (the page rules decide entries, not headers): the handler's own goes out as set, and the output cache sends the headers set before the body is written again with every stored answer, with `Age`, and adds none. Netjes's own endpoints: `/_netjes/image` (`public, max-age=` the image `CacheDuration` with an image or a 304, none with an error), `MapSitemap` (`public, max-age=` its `cacheFor`), action answers and `/_netjes/antiforgery` (`no-store`); `MapRobotsTxt` and `MapLocaleRedirect` send none.
- ASP.NET Core's keys apply. The path in any case shares one entry, route values included (`/codes/Ab` and `/codes/aB`): `AddOutputCache(o => o.UseCaseSensitivePaths = true)` gives each spelling its own entry, app-wide, and `.CacheOutput(p => p.With(c => c.HttpContext.Request.Path.Value == "/llms.txt"))` stores that one spelling only. Every query key varies the entry: `SetVaryByQuery([])` keeps one entry whatever the query (there is no call without arguments), `SetVaryByQuery("page")` varies on the keys it lists. Both are safe only when the answer does not depend on the keys they leave out and its body does not repeat the URL.
- Only the answer to a `GET` or `HEAD` without an `Authorization` header or a signed-in user is stored, when it is a 200 that sets no cookie. `RevalidatePath` never evicts these entries: give the policy a tag (`.CacheOutput(p => p.Tag("docs"))`) and use `.Revalidate("docs")` or `IPageCache.RevalidateTagAsync("docs")`.
- They stay output-cached in the Development environment, where only pages are not. Draft mode bypasses them, the image endpoint apart.

## TanStack Query

Netjes creates one `QueryClient` per server render and per page load. `.WithQuery(key, data)` on a loader result seeds it, so `useQuery` with that key has data on the first render and fetches nothing until the data is stale (default `staleTime` one minute). Data the browser fetched more recently is kept. After an action, `.Invalidate(key)` refetches and `.WithQuery(key, data)` sets the new value. A fresh query is not fetched again on a mount or a window focus, whatever `Cache-Control` its endpoint sent; the `fetch` of a refetch can be answered by the browser's HTTP cache, and `staleTime: 0` leaves a query to HTTP caching. Configure the client with `netjes({ query: { defaultOptions } })` in `vite.config.ts`.

## Streaming slow data

```csharp
public sealed record TaskPageProps(TaskDetail Task, Deferred<IReadOnlyList<ActivityItem>> Activity);

app.MapPageLoader("/tasks/[id]", (string id, IDbContextFactory<AppDb> contexts, HttpContext http) =>
    Page.Props(new TaskPageProps(LoadTask(id), Page.Defer(ActivityAsync(contexts, id, http.RequestAborted)))));
```

```tsx
// The generated schema types `activity` as a promise, validated when it arrives (deferred() from netjes/zod).
<Suspense fallback={<p>Loading activity…</p>}>
  <ActivityFeed activity={activity} />
</Suspense>

function ActivityFeed({ activity }: { activity: PromiseLike<ActivityItem[]> }) {
  const items = use(activity);
  return <ol>{items.map((item) => <li key={item.id}>{item.summary}</li>)}</ol>;
}
```

- The shell goes out first, with `loading.tsx` or the Suspense fallback where a value is pending, and each value streams in when its task completes. Client navigations stream the same way.
- A deferred task runs alongside the rest of the request: give it its own `DbContext`, never the request's, and pass `http.RequestAborted`. Either create one from `IDbContextFactory<T>`, as above, or use the overload that runs the work in its own DI scope, started once the page's payload is written: `Page.Defer(services => services.GetRequiredService<AppDb>().ActivityAsync(id, http.RequestAborted))`.
- Without JavaScript, a fallback that is still pending stays. Crawlers (`CrawlerUserAgents`), apps with `StreamDocuments = false` and `netjes export` get the complete document.
- A boundary that is ready when the shell goes out is written in place, so it shows without JavaScript too.

## Static export

`npx netjes export [dir]` builds, runs the app once in Production and writes every page as static HTML (default `out/`). `dir` must be inside the app: `netjes export` refuses any other folder before it builds. Dynamic pages need `.StaticParams(...)` (`.StaticParams<PostStore>(s => s.All.Select(p => new { slug = p.Slug }))`, arrays for catch-all parameters); pages that need a server take `.ExcludeFromExport()`. The export fails before writing anything for a dynamic page without static params, a page with a page action, or a page that requires authorization. Exported pages navigate with full page loads and carry no antiforgery token.

It also writes `sitemap.xml` and `robots.txt` when the app maps `MapSitemap` and `MapRobotsTxt`, the sitemap listing only exported pages (none marked `.ExcludeFromExport()`), and any other `GET` endpoint marked `.IncludeInExport()` as a file at its URL: `app.MapGet("/llms.txt", ...).IncludeInExport()` writes `out/llms.txt`, the body only. The export requests it with no query string, and any status but 200, a redirect included, fails the export; one that reads the query string is warned about in `Netjes.Export.QueryString`, and one that requires a value there fails the export. Such an endpoint needs a URL with a file extension and no route parameters, and must allow anonymous requests; a file in `public/` with its path (a `public/robots.txt` next to `MapRobotsTxt`) fails the export. `.ExcludeFromExport()` on the Map call leaves a file out, and wins over `.IncludeInExport()`; when you leave `MapSitemap` out, leave `MapRobotsTxt` out too, since `robots.txt` always names the sitemap.
